Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89], and He said: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder that you may clarify to mankind what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl 44], and He said: ﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation (18). Then upon Us is its clarification﴾ [al-Qiyamah 18, 19]. This includes both verbal clarification and clarification of meaning. So know that there is nothing in the Qur'an whose meaning people do not understand; never. They must understand its meaning. So if something is found whose meaning is not known, that means it has no meaning. This is the first point.

Second: if we apply these letters to the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down (193) upon your heart that you may be of the warners (194) in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193-195], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand﴾ [al-Zukhruf 3], we say: these letters, in the language of the Arabs, what is their meaning? They have no meaning. So the requirement that the Qur'an be in a clear Arabic tongue is that these letters have no meaning, because these letters have no meaning in the Arabic language. This is what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, transmitted from the imam of the commentators of his time, Mujahid ibn Jabr, may Allah have mercy on him, who took the tafsir of the Qur'an from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, who said: these disjointed letters have no meaning[[Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir (1/67) from Mujahid that he said: "Alif Lam Mim, Ha Mim, Alif Lam Mim Sad, and Sad are openings with which Allah began the Qur'an."]]. Do we affirm this with certainty or not? We affirm it with certainty, not by conjecture, but by reasoning from the Qur'an and reasoning from the state of the Qur'an:

Reasoning from the Qur'an: because it was revealed in the Arabic language, and these alphabetic letters have no meaning in the Arabic language.

Reasoning from the state of the Qur'an: that there is nothing in the Qur'an that people do not know the meaning of, all of them. There must be something known; accordingly, we affirm with certainty that these letters themselves have no meaning.

But then a problem arises for us: if we say they have no meaning, their revelation and the Lord's speech with them, Mighty and Majestic, would be pointless, and Allah, blessed and exalted, does nothing in vain.

We say: it is not pointless. They themselves have no meaning, but they have a purpose connected with the challenge, namely: you Arabs compose your speech from these letters, and the Qur'an did not come with any letter you do not speak. Rather all of it is from the letters you speak with. Here is an example: ha, mim, 'ayn, sin, qaf. Yet you were unable to produce the like of it. So in this there is a great purpose: that the Qur'an which has defeated you, O Arabs, although you are the masters of eloquence, did it bring letters that are new, so that you would say, "By Allah, we do not know these letters," or is it from the letters you pronounce? The answer is the second, and yet it defeated you.

This purpose, which Shaykh al-Islam and those before and after him affirmed, is supported by the fact that you hardly find a surah beginning with these letters without the mention of the Noble Qur'an after it, or the mention of what cannot be known except by revelation. Let us look now: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-Baqarah 1] at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and what follows? ﴿That is the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah 2]. In Al 'Imran: ﴿Alif Lam Mim (1) Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer (2) He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran 1-3]. In al-A'raf: ﴿Alif Lam Mim Sad (1) A Book revealed to you, so let there not be in your breast distress from it﴾ [al-A'raf 1, 2]. And so on; there are only two or three exceptions. But the reality is that what follows these letters cannot be known except through revelation.

﴿Ha Mim (1) 'Ayn Sin Qaf﴾ — we say in its tafsir: these are alphabetic letters with no meaning, but they have a purpose.

(﴿Thus﴾ meaning: like that inspiration ﴿reveals to you, and﴾ [He revealed] ﴿to those before you, Allah﴾ [al-Shura 3], the doer of the inspiring.) ﴿Thus﴾ occurs often in the Qur'an. Its parsing, in all its places except a few, is that you say: the kaf is standing in place of (mithl, "like"), in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), and its governing word is what comes after it. The kaf in the sense of (mithl) is accusative as what? As an absolute object whose governing word is what comes after it. Convert the kaf into (mithl): you say "mithla dhalika." What governs it? What governs it is ﴿yuhi﴾ (reveals); that is: He reveals to you the like of that inspiration, Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.

As for his saying (dhalika), the thing referred to is the revelation sent down to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿Yuhi ilayka﴾: wahy (revelation) in the language means informing swiftly and secretly. It is also used for signalling, as in ﴿So he signalled to them that you should glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 11]; and it is used for inspiration, as in ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾ [al-Nahl 68], and ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa that you should nurse him﴾ [al-Qasas 7]. As for the technical sense, wahy is Allah the Exalted informing His prophets and messengers of the sharia.

As for ﴿and to those before you﴾: the waw is a conjunctive particle, and ﴿to those before you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿to you﴾. When it is conjoined to ﴿to you﴾, the implied verb is: "and it is revealed to those before you." But note that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, changed it, saying: (and [He] revealed ﴿to those before you﴾), so he estimated a past verb, although it is conjoined to the object of a present verb. Why? Because Allah's revelation to His Messenger Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, is continuous, while His revelation to those who came before is past and ended. For this reason the author estimated a past verb.

But we say: the default is not to estimate, because the Qur'an is complete and needs no estimation except where necessity calls for it, and here there is no necessity. We say: likewise He reveals to you and He reveals to those before you; and the mention of revelation to those who came before us is by way of depicting the situation, since when He, glorified and exalted, reveals to those before, He reveals in the present tense, so this is a narration of the present state.

As for ﴿and to those before you﴾, the intended ones are the prophets and messengers.

(﴿Allah﴾ is the doer of the inspiring.) Had he said: the subject of ﴿yuhi﴾, it would have been better in clarifying the parsing. So we say: ﴿yuhi﴾ is a present-tense verb, and ﴿Allah﴾ is its subject.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 1–3 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Allah﴾ Allah is the proper name of our Lord, Mighty and Majestic. It is said that its origin is al-Ilah (the God), and the hamzah was dropped due to frequent usage, just as the hamzah was dropped from (khayr) and (sharr) in their saying: "Fulan is khayrun min fulan" or "Fulan is sharrun min fulan," and the original form is akhyar and asharr.

﴿Allah﴾ As for the meaning of this great word: it is said that it is a rigid noun (ism jamid) with no meaning, and thus not derived. But this view is not correct, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And to Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ [al-A'raf 180], and a name stripped of meaning does not fall under "the Most Beautiful," nor even under "beautiful." Every name of Allah includes one attribute of Allah or more, and there is no name of Allah that is a rigid noun carrying no meaning at all.

Based on this, we say: (Allah) is derived from al-uluhiyyah (divinity), and al-uluhiyyah is submission and humility toward the one who is worshipped, together with love and exaltation. Therefore (Allah) means the one who is worshipped with love and exaltation.

﴿Allah, the Mighty﴾ The author said: (in His dominion) ﴿the Wise﴾ (in His creation). Firstly he said: (﴿the Mighty﴾ in His dominion), but he did not explain the meaning of "might" (al-'izzah).

(Al-'Aziz) originally means the Dominant, the one who overcomes and subdues all others, Mighty and Majestic. Listen to the saying of Allah about the hypocrites: ﴿They say: If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner therefrom﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8]. Whom do they mean by "the mightier"? They mean themselves, and by "the meaner" they mean the Messenger (ﷺ) and his companions. What did Allah say in reply to them? He said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8], i.e., dominance belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers.

Consider His saying: ﴿But might belongs to Allah﴾, and He did not say: "Allah is the mightiest," even though they themselves said: ﴿the mightier﴾ and ﴿the meaner﴾. He did not say, "Allah is mightier," but said: ﴿might belongs to Allah﴾, because had He said, "Allah is the Mightiest," that would have affirmed for the hypocrites an inferior kind of might. But the reality is that the hypocrite has no might at all; rather he is always overcome. Indeed, his condition shows that he is overcome, because he is hidden and cowardly, displaying that he is a Muslim while he is not a Muslim. For this reason we say that the open, clear disbelievers are braver than the hypocrites, because they declare openly and proclaim their stance. The hypocrite is humiliated; he displays Islam out of fear of the Muslims, and conceals disbelief, because he is a disbeliever, and we seek refuge with Allah.

Summary: The author, may Allah have mercy on him, did not explain the meaning of ﴿al-'Aziz﴾, so we say: what is "might" (al-'izzah)? It is dominance.

﴿the Wise﴾ He says: (in His creation). This is very deficient, because the wisdom of Allah the Exalted is in His creation and in His legislation (shar'). He is Wise in His creation, that is, in His making, and He is Wise in His legislation. Read the saying of Allah the Exalted in Surah al-Mumtahanah: ﴿So if you ascertain that they are believing women, then do not return them to the disbelievers. They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them [the disbelievers]. And give the disbelievers what they have spent. And there is no blame upon you for marrying them when you have given them their due compensation. And do not hold on to marriage with disbelieving women, and ask for the return of what you have spent, and let the disbelievers ask for the return of what they have spent﴾. All of these are legal rulings. Then He said: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you. And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. So He, may He be exalted, is Wise in His legislation and Wise in His creation, that is, in His creating. Everything that Allah has created, wisdom requires its existence, and everything that Allah has annulled, wisdom requires its non-existence; this is an established matter. Everything Allah has legislated, whether as obligatory, prohibited, or permitted, wisdom requires that it be legislated as such: wisdom requires the obligatory to be obligatory, the forbidden to be forbidden, and the permissible to be permissible. But the presence of wisdom in that does not necessarily mean that it is known to us. It contains wisdom; we may know it or we may not know it. Now, if its knowledge is hidden from us, does that mean it is non-existent? Answer, brothers.

* The students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, because we are deficient in everything. Man was created weak in everything: weak in his strength, in his perception, in his knowledge, in everything. For this reason, when they said, "What is the soul, O Muhammad?", Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is of the command of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra' 85]. He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾, as if He is saying: "Nothing of knowledge remains for you except the soul, that you should ask about it?" Rather, what has escaped you of knowledge is far more than what you have grasped. For this reason He said: ﴿and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾. Therefore the duty of the Muslim toward Allah's creation and Allah's legislation is to submit completely and to say: "This is the wisdom."

Let me give an example from the legislated rites: why do people take pebbles, small stones, and strike a specific place with them? Someone may say: what is the wisdom in this? What is the wisdom?

We say: the mere fact that Allah legislated it is evidence of wisdom, and we are content with this. Yet among the greatest wisdoms in it is the perfection of worship: that a person takes a stone and strikes with it a place merely in obedience to the command of Allah. There is perfection of worship in it, because the soul's submission to what it knows the benefit of is easier than its submission to what it does not know the benefit of, and its submission to what it does not know the benefit of is more eloquent in humility and worship toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Moreover, this act is accompanied by remembrance: with every pebble you throw, you say: "Allah is greatest." It is also accompanied by following: with every pebble you throw, you feel that you are following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

In any case, we say: the author's restricting ﴿the Wise﴾ to the wisdom of creation, what is wrong with that?

* The students: It is deficient.

* The Shaykh: Deficient, without doubt. He is Wise in His creation and Wise in His legislation, blessed and exalted is He.

We must know what wisdom is. The scholars say: wisdom is placing things in their proper places. That means that when Allah, glorified and exalted, creates something or legislates something, it is in its fitting place. For this reason some of the Salaf said: "Allah has not commanded a thing for which the intellect would say, 'Would that He had not commanded it,' and He has not forbidden a thing for which the intellect would say, 'Would that He had not forbidden it.'" So whatever is established by the Shari'ah does not contradict the intellect; rather the intellect supports it and bears witness to its soundness. Thus the Wise is the one who places things in their proper places, whether legislative or cosmic. He never commands a thing for which the intellect would say, "Would that He had not commanded it," and He never forbids a thing for which the intellect would say, "Would that He had not forbidden it."

As for cosmic matters, Allah, glorified and exalted, may decree things that you think are corruption, and then they turn out to be good and beneficial. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And if you dislike them, perhaps you dislike a thing while Allah has placed in it much good﴾ [an-Nisa' 19]. Allah, glorified and exalted, may decree things which, when a person first looks at them, he says: "There is no benefit in this," or he says: "This is harmful." But if he reflects, he finds that wisdom requires it. And you, O servant, when you believe that Allah is Wise in His legislation and Wise in His creation, there remains no doubt in you that what He legislated is good and what He decreed is good.

The Wise also has another meaning apart from wisdom, namely the Judge (al-Hakim), because this root (h-k-m) indicates both meanings: wisdom and judgment (hukm). He, glorified and exalted, is the Judge: He judges over people and judges between people. He judges over people by obligating them with legal rulings, and He judges between people in what they dispute. His judgment is founded on perfect justice; there is no injustice or tyranny, neither in what He judges between people nor in what He judges over people. All of it is justice, all of it is good. So the Wise has another meaning, which is what? Judgment (al-hukm).

Judgment is divided into: decreed judgment (hukm qadari) and legislative judgment (hukm shar'i). For this reason, when a person is afflicted with a calamity, he says: "This is the judgment of Allah" (this is a colloquial expression). This is the judgment of Allah; is it the decreed or the legislative? 

* The students: The decreed.

* The Shaykh: The decreed. But if it is said to him: "It is obligatory upon you to do such and such," he says: "Why is it obligatory?" It is said: "This is the judgment of Allah." This is the legislative judgment of Allah.

Both are in the Qur'an. From the first, namely the decreed judgment, is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, about the brother of Yusuf: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or Allah decides for me﴾ [Yusuf 80], i.e., decrees for me. He did not say "judge in me"; He said: ﴿or Allah decides for me﴾. So the judgment here is decreed.

An example of the second, the legislative judgment, is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, when He mentioned the rulings concerning the disbelieving women who come from the disbelievers to the believers: ﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges between you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 10]. ﴿The judgment of Allah﴾, i.e., the legislative or the cosmic?

* The students: The legislative.

* The Shaykh: The legislative.

Good. What is the difference between them, between legislative judgment and decreed judgment?

The difference is that decreed judgment occurs in what Allah loves and in what Allah does not love; the cosmic judgment occurs in what Allah loves and what He does not love. A man steals, commits adultery, drinks wine: is this the decreed or the legislative judgment of Allah?

* The students: The decreed.

* The Shaykh: The decreed, and Allah does not love this.

A person prays, gives charity, fasts, performs Hajj: this is the judgment of Allah, cosmic or legislative?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It is decreed, but does Allah love it or not?

* The students: He loves it.

* The Shaykh: Allah loves it. So the cosmic judgment, or decreed if you prefer, occurs in what Allah loves and in what Allah does not love.

As for legislative judgment, it occurs only in what Allah loves. Allah does not forbid anything except that He is pleased that it not be done, and He does not obligate anything except that He is pleased that it be done.

Likewise there is another difference: the cosmic or decreed judgment, and the meaning is one, must come to pass. When Allah decrees something cosmically, it must occur. Have you understood?

The legislative judgment may occur or may not occur. Are all people committed to the legislative rulings of Allah? No.

These are two differences between cosmic judgment and legislative judgment, and both are included in His saying: ﴿the Wise﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verses: the demonstration of the power of Allah, blessed and exalted, in that His speech sent down to His Prophet consists of the letters with which people speak and from which they compose their speech, yet it has rendered them incapable; the evidence: ﴿Ha Mim. 'Ayn Sin Qaf.﴾

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his family, by His saying: ﴿who reveals to you﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of prophethood among the earlier nations, by His saying: ﴿and to those before you﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely: ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾.

Know that the names of Allah, glorified and exalted, must each include two things:

The first: the affirmation that this is a name of Allah, blessed and exalted. For example, (al-'Aziz): we now testify that among the names of Allah is (al-'Aziz), and we also testify that among the names of Allah is (al-Hakim).

The second thing included: the attribute indicated by this name. For example, (al-'Aziz) indicates what? 

* A student: Might.

* The Shaykh: And (al-Hakim) indicates wisdom.

Each of these names must include both. A name may include a third thing, which is the action that follows from it; or if you wish, say: the effect that follows from it. For example, (al-Sami') includes affirming the name (al-Sami') for Allah, which is correct, and affirming hearing for Him (the attribute being an additional meaning beyond the essence), and the third: that He hears everything.

With (al-Hakim) we say likewise: affirming (al-Hakim) as a name of Allah; the second: affirming wisdom in one of its two meanings, and affirming judgment in the other meaning; and the third: that Allah, glorified and exalted, judges among His servants and judges over His servants.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the perfection of His might and the perfection of His wisdom, the perfection of might and the perfection of wisdom, because Allah joined al-'Aziz with al-Hakim, indicating that His might and His dominance are founded upon wisdom.

The might of a created being may lead him to act foolishly, as in the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," what? ﴿he is seized by pride in sin﴾ [al-Baqarah 206]. Here he had might, but it did not benefit him, because it was not joined with wisdom.

Likewise, the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is joined with His might. Because the wise may be weak, having no dominance, so he loses much, and loses resolve, because he says: "This is what? It is wisdom." But the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is joined with His might. For this reason we now benefit from joining the names with one another: through this we gain a meaning beyond what we gain from the mere name.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the laws sent down to the messengers are might and wisdom. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun 8], and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah has sent down to you the Book and wisdom﴾ [an-Nisa' 113]. So whoever holds fast to these laws attains both, namely might and wisdom, and judgment as well.

* * *

We seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. We have previously said that Surah ash-Shura has two names.

* A student: Surah "ash-Shura" and "Shura."

* The Shaykh: Yes, "Shura" and "ash-Shura," good. Is it Meccan or Madinan?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Meccan. What is the Meccan and what is the Madinan?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What was revealed in Makkah before the Hijrah; that is, two conditions: what was revealed before the Hijrah. And the Madinan?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Even if it was in Makkah?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Do you memorize anything revealed in Makkah after the Hijrah?

* The student: The saying of Allah: (...).

* The Shaykh: The saying of Allah: ﴿Today...﴾ [al-Ma'idah 3].

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Where was this revealed?

* The student: At 'Arafah.

* The Shaykh: At 'Arafah, may Allah bless you.

Now, the author excepted four verses from this surah. What is your opinion?

* A student: We demand evidence for (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, for this exception, we demand evidence for this exception, because the principle is that a Meccan surah all of whose verses are Meccan, and a Madinan surah all of whose verses are Madinan, is it not so? Whoever claims something contrary to the principle must provide the evidence.

Now, the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Ha Mim. 'Ayn Sin Qaf.﴾ What do you say about it?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the alphabetic letters are better than our saying "the disjointed letters," because they may be a single letter, such as ﴿Nun﴾ and ﴿Sad﴾.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is a difference of opinion, and the preferred view?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Excellent, may Allah bless you. What is the evidence for the preference of this view?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: In the Arabic language.

* The student: In the Arabic language we say these letters have no known meaning.

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is one point. Another point: Allah sent down the Book as an explanation of everything, and if we say these have no known meaning, then the Qur'an would contain something whose meaning is not known, and this contradicts His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [an-Nahl 89], and His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [an-Nahl 44].

* The Shaykh: ﴿the Wise﴾ [ash-Shura 3]. The commentator said: (in His creation). What is your opinion of this (...)?

* A student: (...).

The Shaykh: There is a deficiency in it. The correct wording is that He is the Wise in His creation and in His legislation. Complete.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 4 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah the Most High said, at the start of the new lesson: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura 4]. The pronoun in ﴿To Him﴾ refers to Allah. You know that ﴿lahu﴾ (to Him) is a predicate placed before its subject, and the subject is ﴿mā﴾ in His words ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, because ﴿mā﴾ here is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and the sense is: "To Him belongs that which is in the heavens." The rule among the eloquent (bulaghā') is that placing before what should be placed after implies restriction and exclusivity (ḥaṣr wa-ikhtiṣāṣ). So His words ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens﴾ mean: not to anyone else. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

The author said: (ownership, creation and servitude). It would have been better to begin with creation before ownership, because creation precedes ownership. In any case, this matter is not of great importance. The essential point is that to Him belongs what is in the heavens: (ownership) meaning He is the owner of their substances; (creation) meaning He is their creator; (servitude) in the sense of predestination (al-qadari), meaning that whatever is in the heavens and the earth is humbled before Allah the Most High, as He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam 93].

His words ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ use the plural, and ﴿whatever is on the earth﴾ use the singular, because the heavens are greater than the earth. For this reason, the heavens are frequently mentioned in the plural, and sometimes in the singular, as in the words of the Most High: ﴿Nothing is hidden from Allah on the earth or in the heaven﴾ [Ali 'Imran 5]. When it is in the singular, the intended meaning is the genus; when it is in the plural, the intended meaning is the number. The number of the heavens is seven, as the Most High said: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?﴾ [al-Mu'minun 86].

The earths are not mentioned in the Qur'an except in the singular, considering the genus. However, the Qur'an indicated that they are seven in the words of the Most High: ﴿Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12]. Is the likeness (al-mithliyyah) valid if you apply it to the manner (al-kayfiyyah), or not?
* Students: It is not valid.
* The Shaykh: It is not valid, because the heaven is greater and more vast. Therefore, nothing remains but to apply it to quantity, so the meaning of ﴿the like of them﴾ is what? In number: seven earths.

The Sunnah has also come with the word seven. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever takes a span of land unjustly, Allah will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection, from seven earths"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198), and Muslim (1610 / 137), with his wording, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Whoever takes a span of land unjustly, Allah will collar him with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths."]], and this is an explicit text. Likewise it is reported from him, peace and blessings be upon him, that when he approached a town he would say: "O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and what they shade, and Lord of the seven earths and what they carry"[[Recorded by al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (8775), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him).]]. "The seven earths": so they are seven earths.

But how are they seven earths? Does the meaning mean seven climes, or seven continents, or what?

We say: they are seven earths, layered (tibaq), just as the heavens are seven layers, so likewise the earths are seven layers. What indicates this is that the Prophet ﷺ said: "He will be collared with it on the Day of Resurrection from seven earths." For if they were climes or continents, then the one who owns a piece of land here would not own what is in the other place. But the one who owns a piece here has what is on the surface and what is beneath it down to the seventh earth. For this reason the scholars said: the air follows the ground, and the lower follows the higher. For example, I have a house whose area is ten meters by ten meters. I have in the air, in the sky, ten meters by ten meters. No one can raise a shelf over my land, even if it is very far. And an airplane may not pass over my land, is that so?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, how not? Yes, if we wished, we could forbid it. This is my land; turn right or left, because the air follows the ground.

But regarding the airplane, one may say that custom has established that it is not prohibited; this is why it passes near towns over the houses, and sometimes disturbs people with its noise, and no one prevents it. And if someone said, "I will prevent it from passing over my house," he would be considered foolish. Custom has its rulings.

We have said: whoever owns the upper owns the lower. For example, is the depth of the earth mine or not mine? It is mine. For this reason, if a person wanted to dig a tunnel beneath my land, may I prevent him? Yes, because the lower follows the upper.

The point, in any case: how many are the heavens?
* Students: Seven.
* The Shaykh: And the earths?
* Students: Seven.
* The Shaykh: Seven.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ (﴿And He is the Most High﴾ over His creation, ﴿the Most Great﴾, the Great). Yes, ﴿He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾. Allah joined these two in this verse and in the Verse of the Throne.

﴿al-'Aliyy﴾: its morphological pattern is (fa'il), an attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). The attributive adjective requires that the described attribute be constantly present in the one described. Have you understood now?

(fa'il) is an attributive adjective, and the attributive adjective requires what? It requires the continuity and permanence of the attribute's presence in the one described. Therefore (al-'Aliyy) is an attribute necessarily belonging to Allah, mighty and majestic, eternally and forever; it is impossible for it to be the opposite of highness at any time. Highness, then, is an essential attribute (sifah dhatiyyah).

From where did you derive that it is an essential attribute?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (fa'il) is an attributive adjective, and the attributive adjective requires permanence and continuity, and the continuous presence of the attribute in the one described. Therefore highness is an essential attribute of Allah, mighty and majestic; under no circumstances can He be described by its opposite.

Good. Is this highness the highness of attribute (ʿulū al-ṣifah) on which the Islamic community agreed, or is it the highness of essence (ʿulū al-dhāt) which whoever denied it denied?

Both: the highness of essence and the highness of attribute. As for the highness of attribute, all Muslims have agreed upon it, even the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, the Ash'ariyyah, the Maturidiyyah and others; all of them agreed upon the affirmation of the attribute of highness for Allah, mighty and majestic. Highness, what? The highness of attribute.

For this reason I say to you: the deniers of the attributes (al-mu'attilah), who deny the attributes, do you know why? They said: because we exalt Allah; the affirmation of these attributes necessarily implies, in their opinion, imperfection, so they negate them in order to exalt Allah, mighty and majestic.

Thus the highness that is the highness of attribute is established for Allah by the consensus of the community, and no one denies it.

The highness of essence is the matter on which people differed, and they divided into three main groups:

The first group: those who denied it, but made Allah the Most High present in every place. They say: Allah's place is not specifically on high; rather He is in every place. This is the view of the Jahmiyyah of incarnation (al-Jahmiyyah al-hulūliyyah), who state this openly. They say: it is not possible for Allah the Most High to be high above everything; rather He is in everything. If you are in the mosque, is He —
* Students: In the mosque.
* The Shaykh: In the latrine?
* Students: In the latrine.
* The Shaykh: Then He is in the latrine. May Allah fight them, and He is far above their saying, and they have a pretext.

The second view is the exact opposite. He said: it is not permissible to say that Allah is in a place, neither high nor low. Rather He, glorified and exalted, is not above the world, nor beneath it, nor to its right, nor to its left, neither joined nor separated, neither distinct nor immanent, and so on through negative attributes, the very opposite of the first group.

I ask you by Allah: where would God be if He were negated from all of this? He would be nonexistent. For this reason Mahmud ibn Subuktakin, may Allah have mercy on him, one of the famous commanders, said, when Muhammad ibn Fawrak, one of the theologians, was debating with him, and Muhammad ibn Fawrak said: "He is neither inside the world nor outside it..." until the end, he said to him: "Explain to me the difference between nonexistence and your Lord whom you describe with this attribute." What is the answer? There is no difference.

The third: they say that Allah the Most High is high by His essence above everything, nothing of His creation encompasses Him, His highness is necessary to His essence, and He, glorified and exalted, is distinct from His creation, meaning that He does not dwell in them nor do they dwell in Him. This is the doctrine of the People of Truth, indicated by the Qur'an, the Sunnah, reason, the innate nature (fitrah) and consensus. Five proofs, all of which indicate the essential highness, and they are also varied; that is, the indication of the Qur'an is not one verse nor in one way, but varied, and likewise in the Sunnah.

The Qur'an is full of affirmation of Allah's essential highness, such as His words: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la 1], ﴿He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [al-Baqarah 255], ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am 18], ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth﴾ [al-Sajdah 5], ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven?﴾ [al-Mulk 16], and countless proofs.

From the Sunnah there are verbal, practical and tacit evidences; that is, all kinds of Sunnah indicate Allah's essential highness:

As for verbal Sunnah, the Prophet ﷺ says in his prostration, what? "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High,"[[Recorded by Muslim (772 / 203), from the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman (may Allah be pleased with him).]] affirming His highness.

As for tacit approval, he asked the slave girl: "Where is Allah?" She said: "In the heaven." So he approved her.[[Recorded by Muslim (537 / 33), from the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

As for practical evidence: "He used to deliver a sermon to the people on the Day of 'Arafah and say: 'Have I not conveyed?' They say: 'Yes.' He raises his finger to the heaven and says: 'O Allah, bear witness.'"[[Recorded by Muslim (1218 / 147), from Jabir; his wording: "And I have left among you that which you will never go astray after if you hold fast to it: the Book of Allah. And you will be asked about me, so what will you say?" They said: "We testify that you have conveyed, fulfilled and advised." Then he pointed with his index finger to the heaven and lowered it toward the people: "O Allah, bear witness, O Allah, bear witness," three times... the hadith.]] Meaning: over these people, he points to the heaven. And this is what kind of indication? 
* Student: Practical.
* The Shaykh: Practical, by gesture.

As for consensus: the early generations (salaf), headed by the Companions, agreed that Allah the Most High is above everything, agreeing on this with definitive consensus, because all of them say in their prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High," and it was never transmitted from any one of them that he said Allah is not in the heaven, never. The absence of any transmitted opposition to what is in the Book and the Sunnah indicates consensus. This is a clear path: when nothing has come from the salaf that contradicts the indication of the Qur'an, they agree upon what? Upon what the Qur'an indicates.

As for the indication of reason, ask yourself: which of these is more worthy: a Lord described by what indicates nonexistence, or a Lord not exalted above the filthy places, or a Lord who is high above everything? Which?
* Students: The third.
* The Shaykh: The third, without doubt.

Furthermore, highness, as highness, is an attribute of perfection, is it not? And if it is an attribute of perfection, then Allah has affirmed for Himself every attribute of perfection, as the Most High said: ﴿To Allah belongs the highest description﴾ [al-Nahl 60]. This is the rational indication.

As for the indication of the innate nature (fitrah): the innate nature also indicates Allah's highness. Before a person learns anything, by his nature, where does he imagine Allah, mighty and majestic? In highness. For this reason, you will find the ordinary person who has not read this research, if he wants to supplicate to Allah, where does he turn? To the heaven. For this reason Abu al-'Ala' al-Hamadhani, may Allah have mercy on him, said to Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni, while he was asserting the denial of highness (meaning the denial of settling over the Throne (...)), and saying that Allah, the Most High, was and nothing was before Him, and He is now as He was. What does he want? To deny settling over the Throne and highness too. Abu al-'Ala' al-Hamadhani, may Allah have mercy on him, said to him: "O master, leave me the mention of the Throne and settling over the Throne. Tell us about this innate nature: no knower has ever said 'O Allah' without finding in his heart a necessary inclination to seek highness." Subhan Allah! Is it not so? No knower has said... and the "knower" (ʿārif) is used among them for the Sufi, but here what is meant is more general: no knower has ever said "O Allah" without finding in his heart a necessary inclination to seek highness. He began striking his head: "You have bewildered me, you have bewildered me, you have bewildered me." Why? Because he was unable to answer. This is an innate indication which no one can deny, and praise be to Allah who guided us to this.

So the highness of Allah, mighty and majestic, is divided into two kinds: essential highness and attributive highness. The second, the Islamic community has not differed about; the first, the essential highness, they divided over into three sects. The saved sect, may Allah make me and you among them, are those who affirmed His highness by His essence, glorified and exalted, above everything; nothing is equal to Allah, mighty and majestic, all creation is in His grip, all creation is nothing in comparison to Him. If the seven heavens and seven earths, despite their greatness and vastness, are compared to the Kursi as a ring thrown into a desert, and the Kursi is compared to the Throne likewise... The ring: the ring of a coat of mail, a narrow ring, thrown into a desert. Tell me, what does this ring occupy of this desert?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, nothing. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: "The superiority of the Throne over the Kursi is like the superiority of the desert over this ring."[[Recorded by Ibn Hibban (361), from the hadith of Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "And the superiority of the Throne over the Kursi is like the superiority of the desert over the ring."]] So what is the Kursi compared to the Throne? Nothing.

And the Lord, mighty and majestic, is above that; He, glorified and exalted, is above everything; nothing is equal to Him; all creatures are beneath Him, glorified and exalted, and He is above everything.

So we have established this highness and elaborated on it because it is important, and because there are now those who deny it, may Allah protect us. There is no doubt that these people, Allah has turned their hearts away; otherwise, if they returned to their innate nature, just their nature, they would know that Allah the Most High is above everything, and that this is part of His perfection.

As for his words, may Allah have mercy on him: (﴿al-'Aliyy﴾ over His creation). We cannot say that the author denied essential highness, nor can we say that he affirmed it definitively, because (﴿al-'Aliyy﴾ over His creation) may mean He is high over them by authority and dominion, in which case it is attributive highness, and it may mean He is high over them by His essence. In any case, we may not accuse the author of denying highness, nor testify that he affirmed it, because the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is an Ash'ari. But we do not know. However, we are obliged, when we hear words from our Muslim brothers that may have a correct interpretation, to interpret them as what? In the correct interpretation, as long as no indication prevents that. Otherwise, the principle is: if you hear a word from your brother, take it in its correct meaning. Even if you hear a word and think, "This man is mocking me," for example, or ridiculing, do not take it that way; take it in the true meaning.

As for (﴿al-'Azim﴾), he, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (the Great). But there is consideration here, because (al-kabir, the big) is not the same as (al-'Azim, the Mighty). Al-'Azim means the one possessing greatness, and the greatness of a thing or the greatness of the Great means the strength of authority, the strength of knowledge, the strength of whatever meanings it may bear; all of this falls within the word (al-'Azim).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of His words, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: the all-encompassing dominion of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, as shown by His words ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, because ﴿mā﴾ (whatever) is a relative pronoun that conveys generality.
* Among its benefits: that this dominion belongs exclusively to Allah, and no one shares it with Him. This is shown by the fronting of the predicate, and the rhetorical principle is that fronting what should be delayed conveys restriction and exclusivity (ḥaṣr wa-ikhtiṣāṣ).
If someone says: "Your statement is challenged by the fact that Allah has affirmed dominion for human beings. He said: ﴿except over their spouses or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 6], and He said: ﴿or that whose keys you possess﴾ [al-Nur 61], and similar verses."
The answer: a human being's ownership of a thing is neither absolute ownership nor general ownership. It is not absolute, because a person cannot dispose of his property however he wishes. If he wanted to burn his property, would he be permitted? No, he is not permitted to do so. And if he wanted to use it for what is forbidden, he would not be permitted. Nor is it general, because each one of our ownerships is specific to its owner. You do not own my property, and I do not own yours.
The dominion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is absolute and general. Thus the difference between the dominion of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and the dominion of the created being becomes clear, and there is then no contradiction. Is this clear, brothers?
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the number of the heavens, since it is stated in the plural. Allah has clarified in another place that they are seven heavens. As for the earth, it is mentioned in the Qur'an in the singular, but Allah indicated that it is plural in His words: ﴿and of the earth the like of them﴾ [al-Talaq 12].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the exaltedness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His words: ﴿And He is the Most High (al-'Aliyy)﴾.
* Among its benefits: that exaltedness is an inherent attribute, not one of the attributes of action which He does if He wills and does not do if He wills. The reasoning, brothers, is that al-'Aliyy is an adjective of the attributive form (ṣifah mushabbahah), and the attributive form conveys permanence and the absence of change.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the comprehensiveness of the exaltedness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which includes the exaltedness of His essence and the exaltedness of His attributes.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, by His words: ﴿al-'Azim (the Mighty)﴾.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿al-'Aliyy al-'Azim﴾. Know that every name of Allah indicates an attribute, but not every attribute has a name derived from it. Accordingly, it becomes clear that the attributes are broader than the names, because every name includes an attribute, while not every attribute has a name derived from it. For example, among the attributes of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is His plotting against whoever deserves it. Is it permissible for us to derive from this attribute a name from His names? No, it is not permissible, because the category of attributes is broader. Among the attributes of Allah is His craftsmanship (ṣun'): ﴿the craftsmanship of Allah, who perfected everything﴾ [al-Naml 88]. Can we derive from this a name for Allah, al-Sani' (the Maker)? No. Apply this reasoning to other cases.
Then know that the indication of an attribute on what it signifies is divided into three types: indication by correspondence (dalālat al-muṭābaqah), indication by inclusion (dalālat al-tadammun), and indication by implication (dalālat al-iltizām). The indication of a name on its whole meaning is called indication by correspondence, on part of it is indication by inclusion, and on its necessary concomitant is indication by implication.
So the types of indication are three: correspondence, inclusion, and implication. If the word indicates its whole meaning, it is correspondence; if it indicates part of it, it is inclusion; and if it indicates something external that necessarily accompanies it, it is implication.
We will now illustrate this with the perceptible and the intellectual. If you say: "This is a house" (dār), or "this is a building" (bayt), what does its indication on everything that enters the boundary (sūr) amount to?
* The students: Correspondence.
* The Shaykh: Indication by correspondence. That is, it includes the rooms (ḥujar), which are the lower chambers, and it includes the rooms in the second and third floors, and so on. We call this indication by correspondence. Its indication on one of these, such as the reception room (ṣāliyah), the kitchen, or the storeroom (ma'shsha), and similar things, is indication by inclusion, because it indicates part of the meaning. Its indication on a builder who built it is indication by implication, because a house cannot exist without a builder. This is an example from the perceptible. Is it clear?
Now, I have this pen with me. Does its indication on its cap and on its body amount to what?
* The students: Correspondence.
* The Shaykh: Good. And its indication on one of them?
* The students: Inclusion.
* The Shaykh: Inclusion. And its indication that someone made it?
* The students: Implication.
* The Shaykh: Indication by implication, this is the indication.
We come to the names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We say: among the names of Allah, the Creator (al-Khaliq), is it not so? Al-Khaliq, al-Bari', al-Musawwir.
Al-Khaliq indicates the divine essence and the attribute of creating together: this is indication by correspondence. Its indication on the essence alone, or on the act of creating alone, is indication by inclusion. And its indication on knowledge and power, because there is no creator except that he is knowing, and no creator except that he is able, this is indication by implication.
As for the first two types, correspondence and inclusion, these present no difficulty to anyone; every student of knowledge can understand them. But indication by implication is what is hidden from many people, and that is why scholars differ greatly over it.
Here we ask: is indication by implication necessarily binding in every statement, or only in what Allah and His Messenger said?
The answer is the second. This is because the indication by implication may be denied by the one who spoke the words. For example, we say: the Jahmiyyah say that Allah is in every place. Is it a necessary implication of their statement that He is in latrines and filthy places? They do not accept this. If they accepted it, they would immediately be disbelievers, and no one doubts their disbelief. But they do not accept it.
That is why scholars expressed this question as: is the implication of a statement itself a statement or not?
We say: as for the words of Allah and His Messenger, their implications are true and are part of the words of Allah and His Messenger. As for anyone else's words, no. This is because, if we attribute the implication to him, he may refuse it; he may abandon his statement to avoid that false implication; and he may not have thought of that implication when he spoke.
In any case, may Allah bless you, the most important thing to me is... these points have come out of me fluidly, but they may be somewhat difficult for you.
Now I say: the names of Allah indicate the exalted essence, the essence of Allah, and what else? And the attribute included in that name. So al-'Aliyy indicates the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and the attribute of exaltedness. Likewise al-'Azim indicates the Lord and the attribute of greatness.
* A student: Affirmation of (...).
* The Shaykh: The name and the attribute. This is necessary for every name.
* The student: The effect, I mean.
* The Shaykh: The effect, I mean that which results from it.
* The student: The name (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is the requirement of the name.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, not every name is like this. We have al-Hayy (the Living), which has no effect. Al-Hayy is an attribute inherent in His essence and does not transfer to anything else. But when you say al-Basir (the All-Seeing) or al-Sami' (the All-Hearing), these are transitive: al-Sami' transfers to the thing heard, and al-Basir transfers to the thing seen. So the rule is that the name requiring belief in its effect is the transitive name.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, this falls under our statement "the exaltedness of attribute." When we say "the exaltedness of attribute," it includes the exaltedness of rank, the exaltedness of dominance, and all types of exaltedness. This is more general. Some scholars say it is three types: exaltedness of essence, exaltedness of rank, and exaltedness of dominance. But when we say "exaltedness of essence and exaltedness of attribute," it becomes more comprehensive and more general.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Apparently, and Allah knows best, the earth from which creatures benefit and in which they have interest, and by which is meant mankind, is one earth. This is the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, well done. This is a good objection. He says: if we say that air follows what is below and the lower follows the higher, there are now mosques whose upper floor is a mosque and whose lower floor is shops. The original arrangement of a person for these was that he set up these as shops and this as a mosque. Similarly, there are now some buildings in which the ground floor is owned by Zayd, the one above it by 'Amr, and the one above that by Khalid. This exists. But if the land beneath it was not owned by anyone, then it belongs to him, because these buildings are according to how their owner arranged them. If he makes this part a mosque, it becomes a mosque; if he makes these dwellings, they become dwellings.
* A student: (...) the roof of the house.
* The Shaykh: No, sometimes it is ground and sometimes it is a roof.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is not permissible. That is, if this were a mosque like the one we are in now, and someone wanted to build something above it, we would say: no, it is not permissible.
* * *
Someone asks: if a man is an innovator (mubtadi') and makes a statement that could be understood according to the methodology of the early Salaf or according to the methodology of later scholars (Khalaf), should we interpret it as the methodology of the Salaf?
We mentioned a little earlier that if there is no indicator (qarinah), we interpret it according to the correct meaning. If there is an indicator, we do not interpret it according to the correct meaning; we interpret it according to what we know of the man's condition. This is why one of them, I think it is al-Bulqini, said: "I extracted the Mu'tazilite doctrines of the Kashshaf with tweezers."
The Kashshaf is a tafsir by al-Zamakhshari, a good tafsir in reality, both in terms of language and meaning. He sometimes discusses juristic matters, and everyone after him, as we have seen, draws from it in matters of rhetoric and grammatical analysis (i'rab), such as Abu al-Su'ud and others. But he is a pure Mu'tazilite. He disparages the People of the Sunnah and calls them the Hashwiyyah. You find in his words things that you would say are good, excellent speech, such as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾ [Al 'Imran 185]. He said: "What triumph is greater than being drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise?!"
When you hear a statement like this, what do you say? It is a good statement; there is no triumph greater than this. But he is pointing to the denial of the vision of Allah, because it is well known that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made His vision an addition to the bliss of the Hereafter: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and an addition﴾ [Yunus 26]. He says: "What triumph is greater than being drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise?!" Everyone will answer: nothing, there is no triumph greater than this. But he is alluding to the denial of seeing Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Who knows this? Had we not known from this man's school of thought that he is a Mu'tazilite who denies the vision of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, we would say it is not permissible to accuse him, because whoever enters Paradise will see Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42 (al-Shura), verse 5 (part 1 of 2):**

Then the Exalted said: ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them﴾. [al-Shura: 5].

* Student: ﴿yatafattarna﴾.
* Shaykh: What I have written is ﴿yanfatirna﴾. He said: ﴿takadu﴾. The commentator (al-Shaarih or al-Mufassir) says: "with the taa' and the yaa', *takadu* and *yakadu*." As for *takadu*, its agreement with its subject is clear, because *al-samawat* (the heavens) is plural, and as al-Zamakhshari said, every plural is feminine. So *takadu* agrees with its subject clearly. *Yakadu* is for the masculine, and *al-samawat* is feminine, so what is the answer? The answer is: a feminine plural that is metaphorical (majazi) may have its verb either masculine or feminine. You say *tala'a al-shams* and *talaat al-shams* (the sun rose), and both are permitted, because it is metaphorical. But if it is literal (haqiqi), meaning it has a female sex among Adam's descendants or others, then its verb must be feminine. You say *qamat imra'a* (a woman stood), not *qama imra'a*. Is *al-samawat* metaphorical or literal? Metaphorical. For this reason two readings came down: ﴿takadu al-samawat﴾ and *yakadu*. The meaning of *takadu* is "to come close to," and it is one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah).
﴿takadu al-samawat﴾, meaning the seven heavens, ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with the nun. There is also a reading with the taa' and the shaddah (doubling). Is this reading canonical (sab'iyyah) or not? It is canonical, because the rule of the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says "in a reading" or says "with the taa' and the yaa'" or says "with the madd and without it," the reading is canonical. So you may recite ﴿yanfatirna﴾ and ﴿yatafattarna﴾. *Infitar* means *inshiqaq* (splitting open). Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾ [al-Infitar: 1]. His saying ﴿from above them﴾ is not "from below," because Allah, glorified and exalted, is above, and the heavens are almost splitting apart from above them. The commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "That is, each one splits above the one next to it, from the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." If Allah had not held them, they would have split apart, just as when He, the Majestic and Exalted, manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble into dust. So the heavens, despite their magnitude, power and strength, are almost splitting apart from the greatness of Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, glorified and praised be He.
He said: ﴿and the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. Look at the greatness: a greatness from which the heavens almost split, and another greatness in His armies, the Majestic and Exalted. The angels glorify the praise of their Lord.
Who are the angels? We say that they are an unseen world, whom Allah created from light and subjected to His worship: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya: 20]. They are an unseen world that is not observed. The Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family, said: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a space of four fingers in it but there is an angel standing for Allah, or bowing, or prostrating." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2312) from the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording is: "I see what you do not see, and I hear what you do not hear. The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of four fingers in it but there is an angel placing his forehead in prostration to Allah." The hadith.]
*Atta* (it creaked). That is, it made a sound like the creaking of a loaded saddle. Perhaps you have known a loaded saddle! When a camel's load is heavy, the saddle creaks with the movement of walking. The heaven has this because of the multitude of angels upon it. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "It has the right to creak."
So the angels, by their description, are an unseen world, created by Allah from light, as is established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and subjected to His worship: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾. When Allah commands them to do something: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6]. Their opposites are the devils (shayatin). The devils are an unseen world, created from fire, disobedient to Allah, arrogant toward His worship, and their great father is Iblis (Satan).
If someone says: "You said they are an unseen world. Did not the Prophet, peace be upon him, see Iblis in his own form, with six hundred wings that filled the horizon?"
The answer: Yes. But this does not contradict that they are, in origin, an unseen world. Allah may manifest them so that people see them, and they may also take forms. An angel may take the form of a human, as Jibril (Gabriel) once came in the form of a stranger with no trace of travel, and once in the form of Dihyah al-Kalbi. So they may take human forms. Is this transformation by their own will or by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
Asking about this is a bid'ah (innovation). That is, is there any benefit for us in knowing whether Jibril transforms himself into a human form, or whether Allah turns him into one? We have no benefit in that. But we know that it did not happen except by the will of Allah, whether it was an act of choice by Jibril or a creative act of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We have no right to ask about it. Do not ask about any matter of the unseen. Accept it as it came, because someone before you was more eager than you for knowledge, stronger in faith than you, and encountered those who could answer and respond. Who are they?
* Students: The Companions.
* Shaykh: And yet they did not ask. If what the Companions were content with does not suffice you, then may Allah not grant you abundance. For this reason, we must say to some of the young people now who investigate the names and attributes of Allah and delve deeply into them: we must forbid them and say: Fear Allah. Believe in the Qur'an and the Sunnah as they came in the Book and the Sunnah, and do not investigate. Someone better than you and more eager for knowledge came before you and did not ask. Then, if they did ask, whom would they ask? The Messenger, to whom revelation may descend and whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informs about what they asked. But would you ask a person who errs and is correct, when you and he are equal in knowledge of the unseen? This is error and folly, and a departure from the path of the early generations (al-salaf). How excellent is what Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said to the one who asked him about the manner of the istiwa' (establishment on the Throne): "The question about it is an innovation, and I see you only as an innovator."
So my advice to you, if you want safety, is to abandon asking about unseen matters. Leave it, or else this will recur in a person's mind. I mean: can the angel transform into a human form, or is this by the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning he cannot do it by himself but Allah transforms him? We say: this question comes to mind, but what is the proper way to answer it? Answer.
* Students: The question about it is an innovation.
* Shaykh: We say: The question about this is an innovation in the religion of Allah. Whoever is better than you did not ask about it. Leave it.
Are angels bodies? The answer: Yes, without doubt. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Who made the angels messengers having wings, two or three or four﴾ [Fatir: 1].
As for the one who says that the angels are a metaphor for forces of good and the devils are a metaphor for forces of evil, this means denying angels and devils. Rather, we say: the angels are bodies with wings, and the devils are bodies that eat and drink. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And incite against them your horsemen and your footmen, and share with them in wealth and children, and promise them; but Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾ [al-Isra: 64]. May Allah protect us and you from Satan.
The important point is that we believe the angels are bodies and the devils are bodies. But do we know their nature? We do not know except what Allah has taught us. What Allah taught us to know, we know; what He did not, we do not know, because they are an unseen world. He said: ﴿The angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 5], meaning: while clothed in praise.
The author's statement, "meaning while clothed in praise," informs us that the *ba'* here is for accompaniment and association. The meaning of *yusabbihu* is "they glorify, declare Allah free from imperfection." The meaning of *bi-hamd* is "glorification mixed with praise," because *tasbih* is declaring Allah free from defects and emptying Him of them, while *hamd* is the reverse, affirmation. So in this, when you say *Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi* (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him), there is combined in it declaring Allah free from every deficiency and affirming every perfection for Him. From where do we derive the affirmation of perfection? From *hamd* (praise). And the declaration of freedom from defect is from *tasbih* (glorification).
﴿glorify the praise of their Lord﴾, where *Rabb* means: Creator, Owner, Manager.
﴿and ask forgiveness for those on the earth﴾. In ﴿yastaghfirun﴾ the object is omitted because it is known. Who is the one asked for forgiveness? Allah. And they ask Allah for forgiveness. *Istighfar* is seeking forgiveness, because the form *istaf'ala* (form X) almost always and usually means seeking. You say *istasqa* meaning he sought water, *istaghfara* meaning he sought forgiveness, *istarhama* meaning he sought mercy, and similar. It may also come for other meanings, as in your saying *istakbara* (he acted arrogantly), where there is no seeking of arrogance, but he reached the furthest extent of pride.
﴿yastaghfirun﴾ means: they seek forgiveness from Allah. So what is forgiveness (maghfirah)? They said it is derived from *al-mighfar*. *Al-mighfar* is something a fighter puts on his head, covering the head and protecting it from arrows. It has covering and protection. So when you say "I ask Allah's forgiveness" or "My Lord, forgive me," you are seeking two things.
The first thing: covering, covering your faults from people. If people knew the sins you have, they would not return your greeting, as al-Qahtani, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
By Allah, if they knew the hidden secret of my heart, they would refuse to greet anyone who met me.
So you ask Allah to cover you. The second: you ask Allah for protection from sin. Protection from what? From punishment. Every sinner deserves punishment. So if a person says, "Forgiveness is not holding someone accountable for sin," we say: this is part of its meaning; its meaning is covering the sin and not holding one accountable for it.
His saying ﴿for those on the earth﴾: *man* here is a relative pronoun indicating generality. Is it general? No. This is a general term intended in a specific sense, as shown by another verse: ﴿And they ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way"﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. So *man* here is general in form, intended in a particular sense.
If someone says it is general and was specified, we say no, because it was not intended for generality from the outset; rather, specificity was intended: those who believe. ﴿And they ask forgiveness for those on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. For this reason the author said: "from the believers."
﴿Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. *Ala* is an interrogative particle of introduction that begins a sentence, and it indicates two things: the first is alerting, and the second is emphasis. *Inna Allah*: *inna* is a particle of emphasis. *Huwa*: is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and the separating pronoun indicates emphasis. Then it is right for us to say that this sentence is emphasized by three emphatics: *ala*, *inna*, and *huwa*, which is the separating pronoun: ﴿Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. For this reason the angels asked Him for forgiveness, because He, glorified and exalted, is worthy of it, as He said: ﴿He is worthy of piety and worthy of forgiveness﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 56]. ﴿Surely Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. By My forgiveness, displeasing things disappear, and by My mercy, beloved things are attained. May Allah forgive us and you.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿The heavens are almost splitting apart from above them﴾ [al-Shura: 5], to the end of the verse. This noble verse clarifies the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that these heavens, despite their strength and power, almost split from the greatness of Allah. This is like His saying when Musa (Moses) asked to see his Lord: ﴿He said: "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me." But when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble into dust, and Musa fell down unconscious﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Indeed, even the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is His speech, if it descended upon a mountain, you would see it humbled and split from fear of Allah.

* In this verse: a clarification of the greatness of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
* Among its benefits also: a clarification of Allah's essential highness (al-'uluw al-dhati), by His saying ﴿from above them﴾.
* Among its benefits: an affirmation of the angels, by His saying ﴿and the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 5]. It is obligatory for us to believe in the angels as an unseen world, that they have bodies, and that they have wings, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the perfection of the angels' worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying ﴿they glorify the praise of their Lord﴾. They combine for Him declaring Him free from imperfection and glorifying Him: the declaring free in His saying ﴿they glorify﴾, and the glorifying in His saying ﴿the praise of their Lord﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the angels are better than the children of Adam, because the children of Adam do not have this state, that is, glorifying with the praise of Allah. Rather, some of them are believers and some disbelievers. So the angels would be better than the children of Adam. This is one of the opinions on this question. Some scholars say: rather, the righteous among mankind are better. That is, believing humans are better than believing angels. For this reason the angels were subjected to them. This view is the one stated explicitly by Imam Ahmad: that the righteous among mankind are better than the angels, because the angels were created for worship and have no distractions that turn them away from the worship of Allah, whereas humans were created for worship without doubt, but there are distractions that turn them away, namely doubts and desires.
It is well known that realizing faith in the presence of distractions is more arduous and requires more struggle than realizing faith in the absence of distractions. For this reason a man who holds fast to the religion of Allah in the last times is better than fifty of the Companions, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "For the one who acts in those times is the reward of fifty of you." [Narrated by Abu Dawud (4341) with his chain from Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet, peace be upon him, who said: "Indeed, behind you are days of patience; patience in them is like grasping a hot coal. The one who acts in them will have the reward of fifty men who do the same deeds as he." Someone else added to me: He said: O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty of them? He said: "The reward of fifty of you."]. This is so because worship is harder under such circumstances, among a corrupt community.
Shaykh al-Islam (Ibn Taymiyyah), may Allah have mercy on him, chose to make a distinction on this matter. He said: The angels are better in terms of the beginning, and the humans are better in terms of the complete end. Because humans in the end enter Paradise, and the angels enter upon them from every gate: "Peace be upon you, for what you endured patiently" [al-Ra'd: 24]. It is as if they were created to congratulate them and reassure them. So in this there is a distinction: the angels are better in terms of the beginning, because they were created from light and the children of Adam from clay, and because they are in the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But in terms of the end, humans are better.
Beyond this, delving into this matter is not among the important issues, because we may say: what we know of their merits and the merits of humans, we believe in. As for preference in the sight of Allah, they are degrees with Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do. We do not know. In terms of what appears to us, we give each person what distinguishes him. In terms of what is with Allah, Allah knows it. We will not be held accountable if we stop at this matter.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the virtue of combining glorification (tasbih) and praise (tahmid); by His saying ﴿they glorify the praise of their Lord﴾. It has been established from the Prophet, peace be upon him, his saying: "Two words are beloved to the Most Merciful, light on the tongue, heavy in the scale: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him; Glory be to Allah the Mighty." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7563) and Muslim (2694/31) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]. How worthy we are for these two words to be always on our tongues, because they are light on the tongue, with no hardship in them, beloved to the Most Merciful, heavy in the scale. What would it cost us if a person kept saying: "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him, Glory be to Allah the Mighty," while he works, while he walks, while he lies down, while he sits? We would obtain much good, and by Allah's permission we would reach the love of Allah for us, because whenever we come to and persist in what He loves, He, the Mighty and Majestic, is more generous than us.

Among the benefits of these noble verses: the angels are servants who are nurtured (marbubun), having no share in lordship (rububiyyah); this is shown by His words: ﴿with the praise of their Lord﴾. On this basis, whoever calls upon Jibril, or Mikail, or Israfil, or Malik, or other than them, is a disbeliever who associates partners with Allah. This is why the people of the Fire did not say, "O Malik, take us out of the Fire," but rather they said as Allah related of them: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord decree upon us [our end]." He will say, "Indeed, you will remain"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 77], and the Exalted said: ﴿And those in the Fire will say to the keepers of Hell, "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment"﴾ [Ghafir 49]. Observe the shame and embarrassment, and we seek refuge with Allah: they did not say, "Call upon our Lord," but rather, "Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the punishment" [Ghafir 49], because they considered themselves too lowly to call upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, saying, "O our Lord, lighten for us a day of the punishment."

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the superiority of the angels over mankind, in the sense that they have a favour and a blessing upon them; this is shown by His words: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾, and there is no doubt that whoever asks forgiveness for you has a favour and a bounty over you.

Among its benefits: Allah's blessing upon us in subjecting the angels to us, so that they seek forgiveness for us; for if Allah had not subjected them to us, they would not have sought forgiveness for us. But Allah subjected them, and in this there is a bounty and blessing from Allah the Exalted upon the believers, in that the angels seek forgiveness for them.

Among the benefits of the noble verse: the emphasis that Allah the Exalted is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and how emphatic is this? It is emphasized by three emphatics: ﴿Unquestionably, indeed Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

Among its benefits: the affirmation of three of Allah's names, namely Allah, al-Ghafur (the Oft-Forgiving), and ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful). Are the names of Allah derived? The answer: yes, they are derived without doubt. Allah is from divinity (al-uluhiyyah), al-Ghafur from forgiveness (al-maghfirah), and ar-Rahim from mercy (ar-rahmah). He has not named Himself with these names except that He is characterized by what they indicate of attributes. For this reason we say: every name of Allah includes an attribute, or two attributes, or more, according to what these names indicate by correspondence (al-mutabaqah), inclusion (at-tadammun), and implication (al-iltizam).

Among the benefits of this noble verse: when we know that Allah is Oft-Forgiving and Most Merciful, it is fitting for us to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, since He is worthy of that. In this there is education for a person and guidance for his journey to Allah the Mighty and Majestic: that he knows He is Oft-Forgiving, so he seeks forgiveness, and that He is Most Merciful, so he seeks mercy.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: it encourages a person to abandon sins and to perform acts of obedience. The reason is that forgiveness requires righteous deeds and repentance by which Allah forgives the sin, and mercy requires acts of obedience by which a person reaches the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the clarification of the wisdom in Allah's cosmic, predestined decree, for His words ﴿Unquestionably, indeed Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ serve as a reason for His words ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾. It is as if someone says: why do they seek forgiveness for those on the earth? He says: because Allah is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Most Beautiful Names are perfect both individually and collectively, for when He combined al-Ghafur and ar-Rahim, there arose from them a third attribute, other than forgiveness and mercy, namely the combination of these two names indicating the description pertaining to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Through forgiveness He erases sins, and through mercy the sought-after goal is attained.

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Earlier, did the author mention two readings in His words ﴿takādu as-samāwātu﴾?
* Student: ﴿takādu﴾ and ﴿yakādu﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿takādu as-samāwātu﴾ is feminine, and there is no difficulty in it, but (yakādu) how did it come masculine while ﴿as-samāwātu﴾ is plural?
* Student: The feminine is metaphorical (majāzī at-ta'nīth).
* Shaykh: Yes, and a verb whose subject is a metaphorically feminine noun may be made masculine or feminine. May Allah bless you.

Mentioned in the verse: ﴿takādu as-samāwātu﴾. Did he mention two readings for ﴿yatafaṭṭarna﴾? ﴿yanfaṭirna﴾ and ﴿yatafaṭṭarna﴾.
His words: ﴿min fawqihinna﴾. Why are they nearly splitting? From the greatness of Allah. Is this the highness of Allah? It indicates the highness of Allah.
His words, the Exalted: ﴿wa-yastaghfirūna li-man fi al-arḍi﴾. What do you say? Is it general in its entirety or what?
* Student: For mankind.
* Shaykh: Mankind only? Meaning that wolves and beasts of prey are not forgiven!
* Student: It is specific to the believers.
* Shaykh: What is the evidence for its being restricted to the believers? In another verse: ﴿wa-yastaghfirūna li-alladhīna āmanū, Rabbanā wasi'ta kulla shay'in raḥmatan wa-'ilmā﴾ [Ghafir 7].
What is this type of generality called? The general term that is intended to be specific (al-'āmm alladhī urīda bihi al-khuṣūṣ).
