Can you bring us a clear example? His words, the Exalted: ﴿alladhīna qāla lahumu an-nāsu inna an-nāsa qad jama'ū lakum﴾ [Ali 'Imran 173]. What is meant by "an-nās" in the two places?
* Student: Abu Sufyan and his companions.
* Shaykh: And the first is meant to be those who informed the Prophet ﷺ, namely Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud ath-Thaqafi or others; the point is those who informed the Prophet ﷺ.
What is the difference between the general term intended to be specific and the general term that has been specified (al-'āmm al-makhṣūs)?
* Student: The general term intended to be specific is specific from its origin, unlike the general term that has been specified, which is general at first and then the specification comes upon it.
* Shaykh: Well said. The general term intended to be specific was never intended in its generality from the beginning; rather something particular is meant by it. As for the general term that has been specified, it is a general term whose generality was intended, and then some of its individuals were excluded, so it was specified. Clear. The evidence for the general term intended to be specific is rational ('aqlī), meaning that it is impossible for its generality to be intended.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him—Allah is Watcher over them﴾. First, in terms of grammar: ﴿Those who took﴾ (alladhina ittakhadhu) is a subject (mubtada'); ﴿protectors﴾ (awliya'a) is the second object (maf'ul thani) of ﴿took﴾, because the implied meaning is: they took the idols as protectors. ﴿Allah﴾ is a subject (mubtada'). ﴿Allah is Watcher over them﴾, with ﴿Watcher﴾ (hafiz) as its predicate, and the sentence made of the subject and predicate is in the position of a nominative predicate (khabar) of the first subject. Where is the first subject? It is ﴿those who﴾.

If someone says: it is well known among the grammarians that a sentence functioning as a predicate must contain a pronoun referring back to the subject, so that its connection to it is recognized.

We say: here the apparent noun has taken the place of the pronoun, which is the phrase ﴿Allah is Watcher over them﴾; meaning, those who took protectors besides Him, He (i.e., Allah) is Watcher over them. It is also permissible that the linking element is the phrase ﴿over them﴾, that is, the pronoun. In any case, Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾. Took whom? They took the idols; this is why the author said: (namely, the idols). This specification is to clarify the second object, as if he is saying: the second object is omitted, its implied meaning being the idols. ﴿Protectors﴾ is the plural of (wali), meaning they take these idols as allies, worship them, slaughter for them, and make vows to them, while they are heedless of Allah.

(﴿Allah is Watcher﴾, one who counts, ﴿over them﴾ to recompense them.) Explaining (hafiz) as "one who counts" is an explanation by a necessary consequence, but what is meant by hafiz is one who guards their deeds, a watcher over them, to whom nothing of their deeds escapes. ﴿Allah is Watcher over them﴾; and since He is their guardian and watcher, He must count their deeds against them and recompense them for them.

(﴿And you are not over them a disposer﴾, you do not secure what is sought from them; your duty is only to deliver the message.) ﴿And you are not over them﴾: the address is to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿A disposer﴾ means a guardian. The verse is clear: as if Allah is saying, "I am the Watcher over them; as for you, you are not a guardian. What is incumbent upon the Messenger? Upon you is only the delivering (of the message)." He is only required to deliver; as for guiding anyone or counting anyone's deeds, that is not up to him, but up to Allah, mighty and majestic. Indeed, Allah said to him in Al-Imran: ﴿You have no part in the affair, whether He accepts their repentance or punishes them, for indeed they are wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Imran 128]. ﴿And you are not over them a disposer﴾, and so on.

* In this verse: a demonstration of the foolishness of those who take protectors besides Allah. The aspect of foolishness is His saying: ﴿protectors besides Him﴾, meaning that they have completely neglected Allah, mighty and majestic, and taken these idols as protectors.

* Among its benefits: a warning to those who take protectors besides Allah, by His saying: ﴿Allah is Watcher over them﴾, which is a threat, just as one says to a person: "Go, and I am with you; I am behind you; I am counting against you."

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a demonstration of the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge, mighty and majestic, by His saying: ﴿Allah is Watcher over them﴾, since His saying ﴿Watcher over them﴾ encompasses all that they do of deeds, and this indicates the vastness of Allah's knowledge and His awareness, glorified and exalted is He.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ is a human being, who does not know the unseen and does not count the deeds of the servants, by His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a disposer﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the Messenger ﷺ, who is the master of callers and the leader of callers, is only obligated to deliver, by His saying: ﴿And you are not over them a disposer﴾. This verse has verbal and conceptual parallels; Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Will you then compel people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus 99], meaning you cannot. And if the master and leader of callers cannot guide them, then what of anyone else?

* Among the benefits of this verse: consolation for the callers to Allah when people do not obey them. Most people, meaning callers, when people do not obey them, their hearts are torn apart and their bodies wither. We say: "My brother, gently. Who prevented them from obeying you? Who prevented them from obeying you?" We say: it is Allah, mighty and majestic. I said: "Who prevented them from not obeying you?" Then I said: "from obeying you?" Both expressions are correct. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [Al-A'raf 12]. And He said: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?﴾ [Sad 75]. Both expressions are correct.

In any case, we say to this caller, eager for the guidance of people: do not grieve over them, do not be in distress over what they plot; perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they do not believe. Your duty is what it is, which is delivering, while guidance is in the hand of Allah, mighty and majestic, and had Allah willed, they would have been guided. When this occurs by the will of Allah, the person is reassured; but if his heart is broken with grief, he occupies himself with the faults of people instead of his own faults. This is why you find the caller with this description always preoccupied with the conditions of people and forgetting himself. If you were to examine him, you would find him falling short in worship; when he comes to worship and attends, his heart is in another valley. This is an error. Before everything, you are commanded to reform yourself; you are also commanded to be content with the decree of your Lord. Allah, mighty and majestic, has decreed that these people should not be guided. The command is His, and the servants are His servants. It is true that a person grieves, but he should not reach a degree where he becomes heedless of himself, as is the case with some callers. When a person is like this, be assured that he will be balanced in calling to Allah; otherwise he will be reckless and bring about what has an unpraiseworthy outcome. Therefore, be a caller to Allah, mighty and majestic, as the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is a human being, having no share in the affair; by His saying: ﴿Allah is Watcher over them, and you are not over them a disposer﴾ [Al-Shura 6]. The Messenger, peace be upon him, is a human; he cannot guide anyone, nor count anyone's deeds. Had he been able to guide anyone, he would have guided his uncle Abu Talib, who had the great merit in support of the Islamic call that is well known, but it benefited him only in one matter, a reality that did not avail him anything: he interceded for him with Allah, so his punishment was lightened, and he is in a shallow fire, with two sandals of fire on him from which his brain boils, yet he thinks he is the one with the most severe punishment. For had he thought he had the lightest punishment, the matter would have been easier for him and he would have been consoled by others. But he thinks he has the most severe punishment. We ask Allah for well-being.

Allah has indicated that sharing in punishment lightens it, in His saying: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you have wronged, that you are sharing in the punishment﴾ [Al-Zukhruf 39]. In this world, sharing benefits a person when others share with him, but in the Hereafter it does not benefit.

* Student: For instance, some university studies occupy the researcher after the study; is it permissible (...) to say this statement?

* The Shaykh: As I told you: regarding matters of the unseen, any person who asks about something the Companions did not ask about is an innovation. This is the criterion, especially regarding what relates to the names and attributes of Allah. Even the conditions of the Last Day, which are matters of the unseen, you must only affirm what you have heard. But research concerning the names and attributes of Allah is more serious and greater.

* Student: (...) an indication that it is derived from truthfulness itself; meaning the names, and among the names..

* The Shaykh: One of its meanings.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, all this is research with no need for it. The origin, undoubtedly, is the meaning; you cannot say "so-and-so is a striker" unless the striking has occurred from him. This is the origin. The verbal noun is the origin; this is the position of the Basran grammarians, and it is the truth, God willing. The Kufans say no, the origin is the verb, so they say: "darb" (striking) is derived from "daraba" (he struck); the correct view is the reverse.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The specified general (al-'am al-makhsus) is that whose generality was intended first, then some of its members were excluded, such as your saying: "The people stood except Zayd." The general term intended to mean the particular was never intended in its generality at all, and its indication is rational. For example: ﴿Those to whom people said: Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾ [Al-Imran 173]. "Those to whom people said" — are they all people? Does anyone understand from this word that all people said it? No one understands that.

﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: First, may Allah bless you. You will not find in the Qur'an that the protectors are the idols, but the commentators explain them as idols by way of example; otherwise the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Wretched is the slave of the dinar, wretched is the slave of the dirham, wretched is the slave of the khamisa, wretched is the slave of the khamila." [Narrated by al-Bukhari (2886) and al-Tabarani (2595), and the wording is his, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Wretched is the slave of the dinar, wretched is the slave of the dirham, wretched is the slave of the khamisa."] He made the one whose speech, love, enmity and dislike are tied to these things a slave to them.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: There is an indication in it: "They glorify the praise of their Lord and seek His forgiveness."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 7–8 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you﴾. The kaf (ك) here is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), and it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). For this reason the author estimated it with his words: "like that revelation" (mithl dhalika al-iyha'). The first: He said: ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾ [al-Shura 3], and did not specify what is revealed. Here He said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Qur'an﴾ [al-Shura 7], so it specified the revealed thing. Therefore there is here a detail after a generality. Where is the generality? ﴿He reveals to you﴾, because it did not specify what is revealed. And here ﴿We have revealed to you a Qur'an﴾, so it is a detail after a generality. It is not hidden from us that detail after generality is one of the great rhetorical styles of the language, because when a thing is stated in general terms, the soul remains looking forward, longing and eager for its details. When it comes detailed, it arrives like water on dry land. Water on dry land, what does it do? You drink it immediately. Likewise, when detail follows generality, it arrives at a heart that is wholly eager for the detail.

﴿And thus﴾, i.e., like this revelation, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾. The address is to the Messenger, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, through whom? Through Jibril. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down (193) upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193-194]. ﴿We have revealed to you a Qur'an in Arabic, that you may warn﴾ [al-Shura 7]. ﴿Qur'an﴾ means either "that which is recited" (maqru') or "one who recites" (qari'). As for the word itself, it is a verbal noun (masdar): qur'an is the masdar of qara'a, like ghufran is the masdar of ghafara and shukran is the masdar of shukr.

So qur'an is a masdar, but is it in the sense of the active participle, or the passive participle, or both together?

We have a principle that was mentioned earlier: if a verse or a hadith admits two meanings equally, with no contradiction between them, it must be understood as both together. So qur'an means both "one who recites" and "that which is recited." How can qur'an mean "one who recites" (qari')? Qari' means "one who gathers" (jami'), and from this the village (qarya) is named, because it gathers people. So qur'an means "one who gathers." Undoubtedly the Qur'an gathers the sciences of the first and the last and every beneficial knowledge and righteous deed.

His words ﴿Arabic﴾ mean: in the tongue of the Arabs. Does the Arabness here refer to Arab lineage (nasab) or Arab language (lisan)?
* Students: The language.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning is Arabness of language, but the reality is that Arabness of language originally derives from Arabness of lineage. Even if someone who is not Arab speaks the Arabic language, its origin is Arabness of lineage. For this reason, those people of Persia and Rome, we say they are Arabs in language, not Arabs in lineage. Do they then share in the praise of the Arabs? The answer: No, it does not extend to them, because the praise of the Arabs is only for Arab lineage. As for the description of being Arab by language, it does not deserve this praise. Therefore, if we were asked: Who are the most noble of people in lineage? Answer.
* Students: The Arabs.
* The Shaykh: Arabs by language, or Arabs by lineage?
* Students: Lineage.
* The Shaykh: Arabs by lineage.

We have explained earlier that Allah the Exalted gave a generality and then a detail: at the beginning He said ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾. Here He said ﴿And thus We have revealed to you﴾, and He attributed the revelation to Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, because the matter is extremely important, and what is revealed is the noblest speech.

﴿Qur'an﴾: We said that qur'an is a masdar like al-ghufran and al-shukran. Is it in the sense of the active participle or the passive participle? That is, does it mean that it is one who recites, or that it is that which is recited? We mentioned that both are permissible. As for its being one who recites, it is because it gathers all perfections in speech. From it comes "al-qarya" (the village), because it gathers people. As for its meaning as a passive participle, it is because it is recited and read. Both are suitable descriptions of the Qur'an and neither negates the other. On this basis it is understood as both meanings together, as is the rule in tafsir and in the Prophetic hadith: when a word may have two meanings with no preponderance of one over the other and no contradiction between them, it is obligatory to understand both.

﴿A Qur'an in Arabic﴾, i.e., in the language of the Arabs. Does the intended language of the Arabs refer to pronunciation or lineage? The original is lineage, because the language of the Arabs spread after the Islamic conquests; otherwise it was only in the Arabian Peninsula.

Then He said: ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾. The lam is for causation. What is the caused thing? His words ﴿We have revealed﴾. On this basis the lam is connected to His words ﴿We have revealed﴾. ﴿That you may warn﴾. The author said: (to warn ﴿the Mother of the Cities and those around it﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah and all other people).

His words ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾: the Mother of the Cities is Makkah, and it was so named because it gathers the cities, since all cities turn to it. Undoubtedly all Muslims turn toward the Mother of the Cities, because the Ka'bah is there. It also gathers the cities in the sense that all Muslims are obliged to perform Hajj to this House, for whoever is able to make his way to it; because of His saying: ﴿And for Allah is a duty upon the people: the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran 97]. Or "hajj al-bayt" is a seven-canonical reading.

If it is called the Mother of the Cities, why? Because it gathers all the cities, and "cities" here means towns, since the qarya in common usage is a small town. Linguistically, however, qarya applies even to a great city, as Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you—We destroyed them﴾ [Muhammad 13].

His words ﴿and those around it﴾: the author says the intended meaning of "those around it" is "all people." This explanation, though its meaning is correct, because the Prophet's message reached all people and whoever has not been reached will be reached, nevertheless the apparent wording is contrary to it, because what is around a thing is what is near it. Thereupon a difficulty remains, since the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, was sent to all people. But it may be said: there is no difficulty. It is like His saying: ﴿He it is who has sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2], and he was sent to all creation; for this reason He said: ﴿And to others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 3].

On this basis we say: the intended warning is the direct warning, and the direct warning from the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, was only to the Mother of the Cities and those around it. For this reason Syria, Iraq, and Egypt were not conquered in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family, rather only the Arabian Peninsula. Accordingly, the intended meaning of His words ﴿you warn﴾ is the warning that took place during his lifetime, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, for it included only the Mother of the Cities and those around it.

His words ﴿the Mother of the Cities and those around it﴾: is the intended meaning here the warning of the city itself, or the warning of its people? The people, without doubt, and no one finds this difficult. This is what led Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, to say that there is no metaphor (majaz) in the Qur'an or in any other Arabic speech, because when a word indicates its specific meaning, it is not considered a metaphor. Here we say: the intended meaning is not that the Messenger warns the houses and markets of Makkah, but that he warns its people.

It remains to ask: where is the second object of ﴿yundhir﴾ (warns)? Because ﴿andhara﴾ takes two objects, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire flaming﴾ [al-Layl 14]. The kaf is the first object, and ﴿fire﴾ is the second object. We say: the second object is omitted and is to be estimated by what suits it. Here it is possible to estimate it with His words: ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾. ﴿The Day of Gathering﴾ is the evidence: ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾. So you now find in the noble verse: in the first clause an object was omitted, and in the second clause an object was omitted; but in the first clause the second object was omitted, and in the second clause the first object was omitted. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. So the second object in His words ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾ is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Day of Gathering." We may estimate it differently, but as long as there is before us something that indicates it, it is preferable.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And warn of the Day of Gathering﴾. He said: (and warn the people). This is the omitted first object. ﴿The Day of Gathering﴾ is the second object, i.e., you warn them of the day on which people are gathered, and that is the Day of Resurrection, on which all creation is gathered. This is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection: the Day of Gathering, just as it is called the Day of Resurrection, because it includes this meaning and that.

His words ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾: he says (on which creation is gathered), because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud 103].

(﴿There is no doubt﴾ means "no suspicion") ﴿in it...﴾ and so on. His words ﴿There is no doubt﴾: "doubt" (rayb) is suspicion, but Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Interpreting rayb as shakk is a close approximation, not an exact equivalence, because rayb suggests unease in the soul, and the meaning is that there is in it no doubt and no unease."

His words ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: ﴿la﴾ is negating. Is the intended negation a prohibition, so the meaning is "do not doubt it," or is the intended negation its literal meaning?

We say: its literal meaning is intended, because if its meaning is negation, the description of this day is the absence of doubt. On this basis, whoever doubts it has doubted an existing fact. But if we made the negation mean prohibition, we would have taken the speech away from its apparent meaning. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that the prohibition may be obeyed by people or may not be obeyed, but the negation here is clearer: first, because it corresponds to the apparent wording, since the apparent wording is negation; second, because it gives that this day is described by the absence of doubt in it, so whoever doubts it is contrary to reality.

(﴿There is no doubt in it: a party﴾ of them ﴿in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾, in Hellfire.) The word ﴿a party﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and the second ﴿a party﴾ is also a subject. Whoever among you knows grammar will say: there is a difficulty here. What is the difficulty?

* A student: The beginning with an indefinite noun.
* The Shaykh: And beginning with an indefinite noun is not permissible. Why? Because the subject (mubtada') is that about which a judgment is made. If you say "Zayd is standing," you have made a judgment about Zayd as standing, and that about which judgment is made must be definite and known. If it is indefinite, what benefit is there in judging it? So the grammarians' statement that beginning with an indefinite noun is not permissible has this as its rationale, since the subject is judged, and the judged must be a known definite. Here, a sentence begins with an indefinite noun. The grammarians say that what justifies beginning with an indefinite noun in this verse is division (taqsim), and division is meaningful: "a party in Paradise," i.e., one kind of people is in Paradise, and one kind in the Blaze. So division permits beginning with an indefinite noun. From this is the poet's verse:

*One day against us and one day for us,*
*and one day we are grieved and one day we are gladdened.*

This is a subject that is indefinite, but it contains division, so the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun here is division. ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura 7]: which of them is more numerous? The party in the Blaze is more numerous, as occurs in the authentic hadith that Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection calls out, saying: "O Adam." He says: "At Your service and Your pleasure." He says: "Bring forth from your progeny the group for the Fire." He said: "O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?" He said: "Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine are in the Fire, and one is in Paradise."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him. The wording of al-Bukhari: "Allah says: O Adam. He says: At Your service. He is called out with a loud voice: Allah commands you to bring forth from your progeny a group to the Fire." The hadith.]] The rest of the thousand are in the Fire. So which is more numerous? The people of the Fire are far more numerous than the people of Paradise. May Allah save us and you from the Fire. The Companions were alarmed by this and said: "O Messenger of Allah, which of us is that one?" He said to them: "Rejoice, for you are among two peoples; they have never been present with anything without multiplying it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3169) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, and its wording: "Indeed you are with two creations, which have never been with anything without multiplying it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj." The hadith.]] They are of the children of Adam, as the Qur'an indicates, so from you there is one and from them a thousand. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, rejoiced at this.

The point is that Allah said "a party and a party," with the two parties differing greatly. This shows that the word firq (party) in the language applies to both few and many. ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾. What is Paradise? Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared for the believers and the God-fearing, a dwelling in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The kinds of bliss in this Paradise, may Allah make us and you of its people, are present in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. As for al-Sa'ir, may Allah protect us, it is the Fire by which bodies are kindled, and in it are kinds of torment and punishment such that its people wish they would die and it would not happen to them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed you will remain." (77) We had brought you the truth, but most of you were averse to the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf 77-78]. ﴿And a party in the Blaze﴾.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one nation﴾ [al-Shura 8], i.e., upon one religion, which is Islam. Yes, if Allah had willed to make the people one nation, He would have made them one nation upon error or upon guidance; that is, if He willed this or that, because the entire matter is in His hand, the Mighty and Majestic.

His words ﴿He would have made them one nation﴾ mean one group upon one religion. His words "which is Islam" may be disputed, because the verse is unrestricted and contains nothing indicating that it is Islam or other than Islam, since His words ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy; and the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾ [al-Shura 8] mention both matters. So we say: the verse admits both meanings together: if Allah had willed, He would have made them one nation, i.e., upon Islam or upon disbelief, but He, the Mighty and Majestic, in His wisdom made them divided: ﴿He it is who created you; then among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun 2].

He said: ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 8]. His words ﴿whom He wills﴾: ﴿whom﴾ is a general relative pronoun, but we must know that this generality is restricted to those in whom Allah knows goodness. It is He who admits them into His mercy, because every act that Allah attributes to His will must be for a wisdom, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For whoever among you wills to take a straight path (28). And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir 28-29]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30].

So ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 8] refers to those in whom Allah knows goodness, so that His admitting them into mercy accords with wisdom.

His words ﴿into His mercy﴾: is the intended mercy here the mercy which is His attribute, or the mercy which is His creation? The second, because the mercy which is His attribute is not entered by people; rather they enter the mercy which is His creation, and that is Paradise. This is shown by the words of the Blessed and Exalted in the sacred hadith addressed to Paradise: "You are My mercy; through you I show mercy to whom I will."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] He said to it: "You are My mercy."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verses 7–8 (part 2 of 3):

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) ﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and it is not conjoined (ma'tufah) to ﴿مَنْ﴾, because that would corrupt both the meaning and the wording.

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) The author here interprets ﴿الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ as "the disbelievers," because Allah, blessed and exalted is He, described the disbelievers with wrongdoing (ẓulm), saying: ﴿وَالْكَافِرُونَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:254, "And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers"]. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, also said: ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَلَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إِيمَانَهُمْ بِظُلْمٍ﴾ [al-An'am 6:82, "Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing"]. The Prophet ﷺ explained it as shirk (associating partners with Allah) and said: "Have you not heard the saying of the righteous servant: 'Indeed, shirk is a great wrongdoing'?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4776), Muslim (124/197), and Ahmad (3589), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) ﴿مَا لَهُمْ مِنْ وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ﴾ [They have no protector or helper]. ﴿مَا﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿وَلِيٍّ﴾ is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar) to which the redundant preposition (harf al-jarr al-za'id) has been attached for emphasis.

(﴿مَا لَهُمْ مِنْ وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ﴾ who would ward off the punishment from them) That is: there is no protector who would take charge of them and bear for them, and no helper who would repel (the punishment) from them. Thus there is no one to console them in the time of calamity, nor anyone to repel it from them when it befalls them.

* This noble verse contains benefits, among them: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ قُرْآنًا﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "And thus We revealed to you an Qur'an"]. The way it is the speech of Allah: is this Qur'an speech or a created thing? It is speech. And since it is speech and Allah has attributed it to Himself, we know that it is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic. Is it created? No. Why? For two reasons. The first: it is an attribute (wasf) of Him, and all of Allah's attributes are uncreated, because an attribute follows the essence; the Creator is Allah, and His attributes are uncreated.
Second: if we said it is created, the command and prohibition would be voided. For if we say it is created, it becomes a created thing in a specific form, just as the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains and the rivers are created in a specific shape. So, for example, ﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ [al-An'am 6:72, "Establish the prayer"] would not be a command, why? Because it was created as a drawing, created in this form. Now, for instance, if you wrote in the Qur'an: ﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ and you say: this is not speech, but a created thing, it would not convey a command. The same applies to reports: a verse that is entirely a report about something, if you say the Qur'an is created, it becomes merely a pattern, and not speech. That is why Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The claim that the Qur'an is created invalidates the Shari'ah, because there would be in it no command and no prohibition." They are only shapes created in this form.
﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾: if you look at it now, you find it is a script in which some parts differ from others; ﴿أَقِيمُوا﴾ has a shape, and ﴿الصَّلَاةَ﴾ has a shape. So if we say these are things Allah created in this shape, it would be neither a command nor a prohibition. Therefore the verse indicates that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, attributed it to Himself.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the pride of the Arabs, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and it is for all nations.

* And among its benefits: the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, in sending down the Qur'an in the language understood by the one to whom it was sent. This is like His saying: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ﴾ [Ibrahim 14:4, "And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, so that he might make clear to them"].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the emphasis on knowing the Arabic language. The reason: if the Qur'an is in Arabic, and we are addressed by it and obligated to act upon it, then this cannot be reached except by learning the Arabic language.

* Among the benefits of the verse: an indication that all people ought to speak the Arabic language, because all people are required to have Islam as their religion. If it is required that their religion be Islam, it follows that they must learn the language of Islam. That is why we see that when Islam was at the height of its honor and strength, people entered the religion of Allah and learned the Arabic language, and among the Persians and the Romans were imams in religion and imams in Arabic. The Qamus al-Muhit, the reference of people in the language now and before now, whose author is it? al-Fayruzabadi. Was he from Quraysh or from Banu Hashim? No, neither; he was Persian, and yet he is a reference for the Arabic language.
Al-Bukhari, the imam of the hadith scholars, that is, the imam of those who transmitted the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace be upon him, was he Arab or non-Arab? Non-Arab. Because in the Islamic conquests dominance belonged to the Muslims who spoke Arabic, so people learned Arabic out of necessity, since understanding the religion is not possible except through the Arabic language. What is the state of people today? On the contrary, now the Arab tries to learn non-Arab languages. Because Islam, with great regret, has been abandoned and humiliated through the sins of its people, and they were among the most humiliated nations, if I do not say: the most humiliated of nations.
I say: the most humiliated of nations, and I do not care, because the Muslims have great wealth, great minerals, and wide, spacious lands, such that if we measure it against their condition, we find that they are the most humiliated of nations. Who would have such wealth and yet fall behind to this degree? A handful of Jews play with their minds night and day, and if I said: groups of Christians play with them... If they had honor, they would be the ones who dominate the people and fight them until the religion is entirely for Allah. But when they were humiliated, their language was humiliated. Now you find the shops in the lands of the Arabs, in our cities and our villages, filled with signs in non-Arabic languages; sometimes you find the shops as if you were in the market of London, unless Allah wills otherwise. All of this is from humiliation.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, which is derived from His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ ["that you may warn"], because the lam here is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and whenever you find the lam of causation in the Qur'an, it indicates the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic. Then we know that everything Allah does or legislates is for a wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: restricting oneself to one of the two aspects of the message when wisdom requires it. Its basis: He said: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "that you may warn the Mother of Towns and those around it"], and did not mention glad tidings, although Allah in many places mentions both warning and glad tidings: ﴿لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ الْمُتَّقِينَ وَتُنْذِرَ بِهِ قَوْمًا لُدًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:97, "that you may give glad tidings to the righteous and warn with it a people obstinate in opposition"]. That is because the context concerns Quraysh, and Quraysh, as you know, are stubborn transgressors, so it was fitting to mention warning without mentioning glad tidings. For if you see a person who is transgressing, do you try to set him straight first with glad tidings or first with warning? With warning first. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that it places everything in its proper place.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: that the Prophet ﷺ is obligated to warn the Mother of Towns as a primary obligation, because of His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى﴾, while warning others is a secondary obligation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the Prophet ﷺ will not reach those to whom he was sent directly, but rather warns those around him, because of His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾. I mentioned this benefit to you a little while ago; we have mentioned it in the book of tafsir.

* There is also another benefit: that the Qur'an in the Arabic language can only be used to warn ﴿أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾, who are Arabs. As for Persians, Romans, Copts and those like them, they do not benefit from the Qur'an except after they know the Arabic language and understand the meanings of the Qur'an. Perhaps this, and Allah knows best, is also among the wisdoms behind His saying: ﴿وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: frightening people with the Day of Resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿وَتُنْذِرَ يَوْمَ الْجَمْعِ﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "and warn of the Day of Gathering"].

* And among its benefits: that the Day of Resurrection is certain to occur, because of His saying: ﴿لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ [there is no doubt about it].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that on that Day people will be divided into two groups: a group in Paradise and a group in the blaze. The people of Paradise head toward the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) to reach the higher place, Paradise. As for the people of the Fire, they do not ascend the Sirat, because there is no hope that they will be saved; rather, they are driven to Hell as a waterless herd (wirdan), that is, in the greatest thirst. The Fire appears to them like a mirage; they think it is water, so they hasten toward it. When they reach it, they find the reverse of what they expected, so they stop. But they are pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push, and it is said to them: ﴿هَذِهِ النَّارُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ [al-Tur 52:14, "This is the Fire which you used to deny"], ﴿اصْلَوْهَا فَاصْبِرُوا أَوْ لَا تَصْبِرُوا﴾ [al-Tur 52:16, "Burn in it, so endure it or do not endure it"].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ [al-Shura 42:8, "Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community"].

* And among its benefits: the refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination). Do you know who the Qadariyyah are? The Qadariyyah are those who say that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has no connection to the act of the servant. They say: the servant is independent; Allah has no will in it. Their extremists deny Allah's knowledge of the servant's conditions except what has already occurred; they say: Allah does not know what the servant will do, but when he does it, He knows it. These people are undoubtedly disbelievers, because they denied the knowledge of Allah. Their moderate ones deny the will and the creation: this is the position their opinion settled on. They say: Allah has no will in the act of the servant, and He is not the creator of the act of the servant. The servant is free; he speaks and remains silent, acts and abstains, sleeps and wakes, independently, with no will of Allah in it. For this reason they have been called the Magians of this Muslim community, because by this belief they make for the created things two creators: the actions of the servants are created by the servants, and the actions of Allah are created by Allah. Therefore they are called the Magians of the Islamic community.
The noble verse refutes them. The basis of the refutation: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ [al-Shura 42:8]. This is like His saying in Surah Hud: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ رَبُّكَ لَجَعَلَ النَّاسَ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً وَلَا يَزَالُونَ مُخْتَلِفِينَ (١١٨) إِلَّا مَنْ رَحِمَ رَبُّكَ وَلِذَلِكَ خَلَقَهُمْ﴾ [Hud 11:118–119, "And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them"].
In it is a refutation of the Qadariyyah, and in it is an argument for the Jabriyyah (those who deny human choice), because Allah said: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾. So they became divided by the will of Allah, and what Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. This is evidence that man has no choice, and that his act is by the will of Allah. It is said: this is what those in whose hearts is deviation cling to, because those in whose hearts is deviation follow the ambiguous (mutashabih) and leave the clear (muhkam). They take the ambiguous in verses like this one and say: this is evidence that the act of the servant is by the will of Allah, and no one can change the will of Allah.
We say: Glory be to Allah! You have looked at the evidences with one blind eye, and the remaining eye has haze or dimness on it; it is not good. So they looked with one blind eye and a quarter or more. There are explicit verses attributing action to the human being himself, and that it is by the will of the human being. Does Allah not say: ﴿فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِنْ وَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29, "So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve"]? Does Allah, blessed and exalted is He, not say: ﴿لِمَنْ شَاءَ مِنْكُمْ أَنْ يَسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [al-Takwir 81:28, "for whoever among you wills to be upright"]? And the verses on this are many.
Does a person not sense within himself that he does an act with no one compelling him? You come to the mosque with no one forcing you; you enter the mosque with no one forcing you; you leave the mosque with no one forcing you. This is a tangible thing. So what is the meaning of our act being by the will of Allah?
We say: the meaning of our act being by the will of Allah is that whatever we do, Allah has willed it, and His will for it precedes our will; but we do not know of Allah's will except after the thing occurs, so we know that Allah has willed it. Is this clear or not clear? That is: I now will to speak with you, and I will to move my hand. Is that not so? Did Allah will that I speak and that I move my hand? Yes. How did you know? By its occurrence. Because I know with certainty that nothing can be in the dominion of Allah that He does not will, and I am in the dominion of Allah, and the heavens and the earth are all in the dominion of Allah. So it is not possible that there be in His dominion what He does not will. But I do not know the will of Allah except after the thing occurs. That is why some scholars said: "Divine decree (qadar) is a hidden secret," which the servants do not know, because they know it only after it has occurred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, exalted is He, bestows His favor upon whomever He wills of His servants, admitting them into His mercy, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَكِنْ يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [al-Shura 42:8, "But He admits whom He wills into His mercy"].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that there is nothing in Paradise that causes distress. What is its basis? His saying: ﴿فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [in His mercy]. Mercy entails the attainment of what is desired and deliverance from what is feared. That is why the people of Paradise are proclaimed: "Indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill, that you will be young and never grow old, and that you will live and never die"[[Recorded by Muslim (2837/22) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A caller will call out: Indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill, and indeed for you is that you will live and never die, and indeed for you is that you will be young and never grow old, and indeed for you is that you will be blessed and never be miserable."]]. Also we say: "And that they will be cheerful and never grieve." All complete bliss belongs to the people of Paradise, and there is in it no disturbance, no fear of sickness, and no fear of death. Do they not even sleep, out of anxiety and pain? Answer.
No, by Allah, they do not sleep out of joy and happiness, so that all their time is absorbed in joy and happiness. Their not sleeping is a sign of the perfection of their life, because we need sleep only to restore the fatigue that came before and to renew the strength that follows. Is that not so? That is why whenever a person becomes tired he needs sleep, and when he sleeps he rises energetic. So we need sleep in this worldly life because our life is deficient, but in the Hereafter there is no deficiency. They are always in happiness. O Allah, make us among them! That is why He said: ﴿يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾; there is nothing in mercy that causes sorrow or distress; rather, all of it is good.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the disbelievers are wrongdoers, indeed they are the greatest of wrongdoers. The greatest sin is disbelief, that you set up a rival to Allah while He is the one who created you. So the most wrongful of wrongdoers are the disbelievers. If we believe this, and it is obligatory for us to believe it, do we hope for good from the disbelievers when they are the greatest of wrongdoers? No, by Allah; we never hope for any good from them for Islam, because they are the greatest of wrongdoers. That is why you must implant in your heart hatred for the disbelievers and for disbelief. You must make it a settled, hidden disposition: to hate every disbeliever and every disbelief.
And if a person has qualities of disbelief and qualities of faith? The just and equitable course is that I love him for what faith he has, and I hate him for what disbelief he has. A person may have a quality of faith and a quality of disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There are two qualities among people which are disbelief in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead."[[Recorded by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] These two do not take a person out of faith.
So pay attention to this: the disbelievers are the greatest of wrongdoers, and whoever is the greatest of wrongdoers, it is not possible to hope from him for any good or justice. Know that if he acts justly, it is only to seize an opportunity, so that instead of justice he takes injustice many times over. Now, we know that the Jews are among the people most eager for wealth, and yet we find them spending, but they spend a qirsh in order to take a dinar. Never think that they spend anything except to gain more than it. This is well known: ﴿وَلَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ عَلَى حَيَاةٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:96, "And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life"].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wrongdoers will find neither a helper nor a protector. No helper will push away or lift the punishment, and no protector will console them and ease their calamities. They have none of this. This shows that they will be in severe regret, because they hope for no benefit. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you wronged, that you are in the punishment together﴾ [az-Zukhruf 39].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. The negation is more emphatic and better suits the context. We have said: we interpret the verse as having both meanings when?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, and there is no preponderant meaning. Notice this qualification, because if you do not say "and there is no preponderant meaning," the people of ta'til (the Mu'tattila, who deny Allah's attributes) will come to you and say, "What we said is possible." No, you must understand this. Yes, indeed, but Allah negated it in terms of what actually occurs.
* Student: In other countries, for example, there are scholars who are deeply learned in some sciences, but who are, for example, Mu'tazili (followers of the Mu'tazila) or Ash'ari (followers of al-Ash'ari). During the lesson, for example, they may teach their school of thought. So, if a student of knowledge knows the truth on this issue, should he debate his teacher about it, especially when the teacher is elderly and it may be hard for him to retract his opinion?
* Shaykh: Undoubtedly, first: those who call to bid'ah (innovation in religion), avoid them, and provision is from Allah. Even if they are scholars of grammar and rhetoric, there is no good in them, these who call to it. As for those who do not call to their innovation and conceal it, there is no harm in sitting with them in what is beneficial. But if you see them deviating from the right path, it is obligatory for you to warn them. However, do not warn them in front of the students, because a person may be seized by pride in sin, especially if he sees himself as outstanding in one of the sciences. If a student of knowledge answers him in front of people, be assured that he will swell up, become greater than the mountain, and will not return. But it is possible for you to write him a letter that makes the truth clear to him, if you cannot debate him directly. If he is a caller (to innovation), do not go near him at all, and warn against him, because he is to be feared. Then, if people see that you, so-and-so, and so-and-so refer to him, they will imagine that he is upon the truth. Do you understand? We ask Allah the Exalted to gather us and you in His mercy, and to grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 7–8 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you﴾. The kaf (ك) here is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), and it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq). For this reason the author estimated it with his words: "like that revelation" (mithl dhalika al-iyha'). The first: He said: ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾ [al-Shura 3], and did not specify what is revealed. Here He said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Qur'an﴾ [al-Shura 7], so it specified the revealed thing. Therefore there is here a detail after a generality. Where is the generality? ﴿He reveals to you﴾, because it did not specify what is revealed. And here ﴿We have revealed to you a Qur'an﴾, so it is a detail after a generality. It is not hidden from us that detail after generality is one of the great rhetorical styles of the language, because when a thing is stated in general terms, the soul remains looking forward, longing and eager for its details. When it comes detailed, it arrives like water on dry land. Water on dry land, what does it do? You drink it immediately. Likewise, when detail follows generality, it arrives at a heart that is wholly eager for the detail.

﴿And thus﴾, i.e., like this revelation, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾. The address is to the Messenger, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, through whom? Through Jibril. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down (193) upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 193-194]. ﴿We have revealed to you a Qur'an in Arabic, that you may warn﴾ [al-Shura 7]. ﴿Qur'an﴾ means either "that which is recited" (maqru') or "one who recites" (qari'). As for the word itself, it is a verbal noun (masdar): qur'an is the masdar of qara'a, like ghufran is the masdar of ghafara and shukran is the masdar of shukr.

So qur'an is a masdar, but is it in the sense of the active participle, or the passive participle, or both together?

We have a principle that was mentioned earlier: if a verse or a hadith admits two meanings equally, with no contradiction between them, it must be understood as both together. So qur'an means both "one who recites" and "that which is recited." How can qur'an mean "one who recites" (qari')? Qari' means "one who gathers" (jami'), and from this the village (qarya) is named, because it gathers people. So qur'an means "one who gathers." Undoubtedly the Qur'an gathers the sciences of the first and the last and every beneficial knowledge and righteous deed.

His words ﴿Arabic﴾ mean: in the tongue of the Arabs. Does the Arabness here refer to Arab lineage (nasab) or Arab language (lisan)?
* Students: The language.
* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning is Arabness of language, but the reality is that Arabness of language originally derives from Arabness of lineage. Even if someone who is not Arab speaks the Arabic language, its origin is Arabness of lineage. For this reason, those people of Persia and Rome, we say they are Arabs in language, not Arabs in lineage. Do they then share in the praise of the Arabs? The answer: No, it does not extend to them, because the praise of the Arabs is only for Arab lineage. As for the description of being Arab by language, it does not deserve this praise. Therefore, if we were asked: Who are the most noble of people in lineage? Answer.
* Students: The Arabs.
* The Shaykh: Arabs by language, or Arabs by lineage?
* Students: Lineage.
* The Shaykh: Arabs by lineage.

We have explained earlier that Allah the Exalted gave a generality and then a detail: at the beginning He said ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾. Here He said ﴿And thus We have revealed to you﴾, and He attributed the revelation to Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, because the matter is extremely important, and what is revealed is the noblest speech.

﴿Qur'an﴾: We said that qur'an is a masdar like al-ghufran and al-shukran. Is it in the sense of the active participle or the passive participle? That is, does it mean that it is one who recites, or that it is that which is recited? We mentioned that both are permissible. As for its being one who recites, it is because it gathers all perfections in speech. From it comes "al-qarya" (the village), because it gathers people. As for its meaning as a passive participle, it is because it is recited and read. Both are suitable descriptions of the Qur'an and neither negates the other. On this basis it is understood as both meanings together, as is the rule in tafsir and in the Prophetic hadith: when a word may have two meanings with no preponderance of one over the other and no contradiction between them, it is obligatory to understand both.

﴿A Qur'an in Arabic﴾, i.e., in the language of the Arabs. Does the intended language of the Arabs refer to pronunciation or lineage? The original is lineage, because the language of the Arabs spread after the Islamic conquests; otherwise it was only in the Arabian Peninsula.

Then He said: ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾. The lam is for causation. What is the caused thing? His words ﴿We have revealed﴾. On this basis the lam is connected to His words ﴿We have revealed﴾. ﴿That you may warn﴾. The author said: (to warn ﴿the Mother of the Cities and those around it﴾, i.e., the people of Makkah and all other people).

His words ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾: the Mother of the Cities is Makkah, and it was so named because it gathers the cities, since all cities turn to it. Undoubtedly all Muslims turn toward the Mother of the Cities, because the Ka'bah is there. It also gathers the cities in the sense that all Muslims are obliged to perform Hajj to this House, for whoever is able to make his way to it; because of His saying: ﴿And for Allah is a duty upon the people: the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it﴾ [Al 'Imran 97]. Or "hajj al-bayt" is a seven-canonical reading.

If it is called the Mother of the Cities, why? Because it gathers all the cities, and "cities" here means towns, since the qarya in common usage is a small town. Linguistically, however, qarya applies even to a great city, as Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has expelled you—We destroyed them﴾ [Muhammad 13].

His words ﴿and those around it﴾: the author says the intended meaning of "those around it" is "all people." This explanation, though its meaning is correct, because the Prophet's message reached all people and whoever has not been reached will be reached, nevertheless the apparent wording is contrary to it, because what is around a thing is what is near it. Thereupon a difficulty remains, since the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, was sent to all people. But it may be said: there is no difficulty. It is like His saying: ﴿He it is who has sent among the unlettered a messenger from among themselves﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 2], and he was sent to all creation; for this reason He said: ﴿And to others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 3].

On this basis we say: the intended warning is the direct warning, and the direct warning from the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, was only to the Mother of the Cities and those around it. For this reason Syria, Iraq, and Egypt were not conquered in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him and his family, rather only the Arabian Peninsula. Accordingly, the intended meaning of His words ﴿you warn﴾ is the warning that took place during his lifetime, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, for it included only the Mother of the Cities and those around it.

His words ﴿the Mother of the Cities and those around it﴾: is the intended meaning here the warning of the city itself, or the warning of its people? The people, without doubt, and no one finds this difficult. This is what led Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, to say that there is no metaphor (majaz) in the Qur'an or in any other Arabic speech, because when a word indicates its specific meaning, it is not considered a metaphor. Here we say: the intended meaning is not that the Messenger warns the houses and markets of Makkah, but that he warns its people.

It remains to ask: where is the second object of ﴿yundhir﴾ (warns)? Because ﴿andhara﴾ takes two objects, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire flaming﴾ [al-Layl 14]. The kaf is the first object, and ﴿fire﴾ is the second object. We say: the second object is omitted and is to be estimated by what suits it. Here it is possible to estimate it with His words: ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾. ﴿The Day of Gathering﴾ is the evidence: ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾. So you now find in the noble verse: in the first clause an object was omitted, and in the second clause an object was omitted; but in the first clause the second object was omitted, and in the second clause the first object was omitted. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an. So the second object in His words ﴿That you may warn the Mother of the Cities﴾ is omitted, and its estimate is: "the Day of Gathering." We may estimate it differently, but as long as there is before us something that indicates it, it is preferable.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And warn of the Day of Gathering﴾. He said: (and warn the people). This is the omitted first object. ﴿The Day of Gathering﴾ is the second object, i.e., you warn them of the day on which people are gathered, and that is the Day of Resurrection, on which all creation is gathered. This is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection: the Day of Gathering, just as it is called the Day of Resurrection, because it includes this meaning and that.

His words ﴿the Day of Gathering﴾: he says (on which creation is gathered), because of the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day witnessed﴾ [Hud 103].

(﴿There is no doubt﴾ means "no suspicion") ﴿in it...﴾ and so on. His words ﴿There is no doubt﴾: "doubt" (rayb) is suspicion, but Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Interpreting rayb as shakk is a close approximation, not an exact equivalence, because rayb suggests unease in the soul, and the meaning is that there is in it no doubt and no unease."

His words ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾: ﴿la﴾ is negating. Is the intended negation a prohibition, so the meaning is "do not doubt it," or is the intended negation its literal meaning?

We say: its literal meaning is intended, because if its meaning is negation, the description of this day is the absence of doubt. On this basis, whoever doubts it has doubted an existing fact. But if we made the negation mean prohibition, we would have taken the speech away from its apparent meaning. This is one aspect. Another aspect is that the prohibition may be obeyed by people or may not be obeyed, but the negation here is clearer: first, because it corresponds to the apparent wording, since the apparent wording is negation; second, because it gives that this day is described by the absence of doubt in it, so whoever doubts it is contrary to reality.

(﴿There is no doubt in it: a party﴾ of them ﴿in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾, in Hellfire.) The word ﴿a party﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and the second ﴿a party﴾ is also a subject. Whoever among you knows grammar will say: there is a difficulty here. What is the difficulty?

* A student: The beginning with an indefinite noun.
* The Shaykh: And beginning with an indefinite noun is not permissible. Why? Because the subject (mubtada') is that about which a judgment is made. If you say "Zayd is standing," you have made a judgment about Zayd as standing, and that about which judgment is made must be definite and known. If it is indefinite, what benefit is there in judging it? So the grammarians' statement that beginning with an indefinite noun is not permissible has this as its rationale, since the subject is judged, and the judged must be a known definite. Here, a sentence begins with an indefinite noun. The grammarians say that what justifies beginning with an indefinite noun in this verse is division (taqsim), and division is meaningful: "a party in Paradise," i.e., one kind of people is in Paradise, and one kind in the Blaze. So division permits beginning with an indefinite noun. From this is the poet's verse:

*One day against us and one day for us,*
*and one day we are grieved and one day we are gladdened.*

This is a subject that is indefinite, but it contains division, so the justification for beginning with an indefinite noun here is division. ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura 7]: which of them is more numerous? The party in the Blaze is more numerous, as occurs in the authentic hadith that Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection calls out, saying: "O Adam." He says: "At Your service and Your pleasure." He says: "Bring forth from your progeny the group for the Fire." He said: "O Lord, what is the group for the Fire?" He said: "Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine are in the Fire, and one is in Paradise."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him. The wording of al-Bukhari: "Allah says: O Adam. He says: At Your service. He is called out with a loud voice: Allah commands you to bring forth from your progeny a group to the Fire." The hadith.]] The rest of the thousand are in the Fire. So which is more numerous? The people of the Fire are far more numerous than the people of Paradise. May Allah save us and you from the Fire. The Companions were alarmed by this and said: "O Messenger of Allah, which of us is that one?" He said to them: "Rejoice, for you are among two peoples; they have never been present with anything without multiplying it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj."[[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3169) from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, and its wording: "Indeed you are with two creations, which have never been with anything without multiplying it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj." The hadith.]] They are of the children of Adam, as the Qur'an indicates, so from you there is one and from them a thousand. The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, rejoiced at this.

The point is that Allah said "a party and a party," with the two parties differing greatly. This shows that the word firq (party) in the language applies to both few and many. ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾. What is Paradise? Paradise is the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared for the believers and the God-fearing, a dwelling in which is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. The kinds of bliss in this Paradise, may Allah make us and you of its people, are present in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. As for al-Sa'ir, may Allah protect us, it is the Fire by which bodies are kindled, and in it are kinds of torment and punishment such that its people wish they would die and it would not happen to them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us." He will say, "Indeed you will remain." (77) We had brought you the truth, but most of you were averse to the truth﴾ [al-Zukhruf 77-78]. ﴿And a party in the Blaze﴾.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one nation﴾ [al-Shura 8], i.e., upon one religion, which is Islam. Yes, if Allah had willed to make the people one nation, He would have made them one nation upon error or upon guidance; that is, if He willed this or that, because the entire matter is in His hand, the Mighty and Majestic.

His words ﴿He would have made them one nation﴾ mean one group upon one religion. His words "which is Islam" may be disputed, because the verse is unrestricted and contains nothing indicating that it is Islam or other than Islam, since His words ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy; and the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾ [al-Shura 8] mention both matters. So we say: the verse admits both meanings together: if Allah had willed, He would have made them one nation, i.e., upon Islam or upon disbelief, but He, the Mighty and Majestic, in His wisdom made them divided: ﴿He it is who created you; then among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ [al-Taghabun 2].

He said: ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 8]. His words ﴿whom He wills﴾: ﴿whom﴾ is a general relative pronoun, but we must know that this generality is restricted to those in whom Allah knows goodness. It is He who admits them into His mercy, because every act that Allah attributes to His will must be for a wisdom, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For whoever among you wills to take a straight path (28). And you do not will except that Allah wills, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Takwir 28-29]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30].

So ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 8] refers to those in whom Allah knows goodness, so that His admitting them into mercy accords with wisdom.

His words ﴿into His mercy﴾: is the intended mercy here the mercy which is His attribute, or the mercy which is His creation? The second, because the mercy which is His attribute is not entered by people; rather they enter the mercy which is His creation, and that is Paradise. This is shown by the words of the Blessed and Exalted in the sacred hadith addressed to Paradise: "You are My mercy; through you I show mercy to whom I will."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] He said to it: "You are My mercy."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verses 7–8 (part 2 of 3):

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) ﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and it is not conjoined (ma'tufah) to ﴿مَنْ﴾, because that would corrupt both the meaning and the wording.

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) The author here interprets ﴿الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ as "the disbelievers," because Allah, blessed and exalted is He, described the disbelievers with wrongdoing (ẓulm), saying: ﴿وَالْكَافِرُونَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:254, "And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers"]. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, also said: ﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَلَمْ يَلْبِسُوا إِيمَانَهُمْ بِظُلْمٍ﴾ [al-An'am 6:82, "Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing"]. The Prophet ﷺ explained it as shirk (associating partners with Allah) and said: "Have you not heard the saying of the righteous servant: 'Indeed, shirk is a great wrongdoing'?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4776), Muslim (124/197), and Ahmad (3589), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

(﴿وَالظَّالِمُونَ﴾ the disbelievers) ﴿مَا لَهُمْ مِنْ وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ﴾ [They have no protector or helper]. ﴿مَا﴾ is a negation particle, ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿وَلِيٍّ﴾ is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar) to which the redundant preposition (harf al-jarr al-za'id) has been attached for emphasis.

(﴿مَا لَهُمْ مِنْ وَلِيٍّ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ﴾ who would ward off the punishment from them) That is: there is no protector who would take charge of them and bear for them, and no helper who would repel (the punishment) from them. Thus there is no one to console them in the time of calamity, nor anyone to repel it from them when it befalls them.

* This noble verse contains benefits, among them: that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, as in His saying: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ أَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْكَ قُرْآنًا﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "And thus We revealed to you an Qur'an"]. The way it is the speech of Allah: is this Qur'an speech or a created thing? It is speech. And since it is speech and Allah has attributed it to Himself, we know that it is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic. Is it created? No. Why? For two reasons. The first: it is an attribute (wasf) of Him, and all of Allah's attributes are uncreated, because an attribute follows the essence; the Creator is Allah, and His attributes are uncreated.
Second: if we said it is created, the command and prohibition would be voided. For if we say it is created, it becomes a created thing in a specific form, just as the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains and the rivers are created in a specific shape. So, for example, ﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ [al-An'am 6:72, "Establish the prayer"] would not be a command, why? Because it was created as a drawing, created in this form. Now, for instance, if you wrote in the Qur'an: ﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾ and you say: this is not speech, but a created thing, it would not convey a command. The same applies to reports: a verse that is entirely a report about something, if you say the Qur'an is created, it becomes merely a pattern, and not speech. That is why Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The claim that the Qur'an is created invalidates the Shari'ah, because there would be in it no command and no prohibition." They are only shapes created in this form.
﴿أَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ﴾: if you look at it now, you find it is a script in which some parts differ from others; ﴿أَقِيمُوا﴾ has a shape, and ﴿الصَّلَاةَ﴾ has a shape. So if we say these are things Allah created in this shape, it would be neither a command nor a prohibition. Therefore the verse indicates that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, attributed it to Himself.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the pride of the Arabs, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and it is for all nations.

* And among its benefits: the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, in sending down the Qur'an in the language understood by the one to whom it was sent. This is like His saying: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ﴾ [Ibrahim 14:4, "And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, so that he might make clear to them"].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the emphasis on knowing the Arabic language. The reason: if the Qur'an is in Arabic, and we are addressed by it and obligated to act upon it, then this cannot be reached except by learning the Arabic language.

* Among the benefits of the verse: an indication that all people ought to speak the Arabic language, because all people are required to have Islam as their religion. If it is required that their religion be Islam, it follows that they must learn the language of Islam. That is why we see that when Islam was at the height of its honor and strength, people entered the religion of Allah and learned the Arabic language, and among the Persians and the Romans were imams in religion and imams in Arabic. The Qamus al-Muhit, the reference of people in the language now and before now, whose author is it? al-Fayruzabadi. Was he from Quraysh or from Banu Hashim? No, neither; he was Persian, and yet he is a reference for the Arabic language.
Al-Bukhari, the imam of the hadith scholars, that is, the imam of those who transmitted the Sunnah of the Messenger, peace be upon him, was he Arab or non-Arab? Non-Arab. Because in the Islamic conquests dominance belonged to the Muslims who spoke Arabic, so people learned Arabic out of necessity, since understanding the religion is not possible except through the Arabic language. What is the state of people today? On the contrary, now the Arab tries to learn non-Arab languages. Because Islam, with great regret, has been abandoned and humiliated through the sins of its people, and they were among the most humiliated nations, if I do not say: the most humiliated of nations.
I say: the most humiliated of nations, and I do not care, because the Muslims have great wealth, great minerals, and wide, spacious lands, such that if we measure it against their condition, we find that they are the most humiliated of nations. Who would have such wealth and yet fall behind to this degree? A handful of Jews play with their minds night and day, and if I said: groups of Christians play with them... If they had honor, they would be the ones who dominate the people and fight them until the religion is entirely for Allah. But when they were humiliated, their language was humiliated. Now you find the shops in the lands of the Arabs, in our cities and our villages, filled with signs in non-Arabic languages; sometimes you find the shops as if you were in the market of London, unless Allah wills otherwise. All of this is from humiliation.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom, which is derived from His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ﴾ ["that you may warn"], because the lam here is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), and whenever you find the lam of causation in the Qur'an, it indicates the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic. Then we know that everything Allah does or legislates is for a wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: restricting oneself to one of the two aspects of the message when wisdom requires it. Its basis: He said: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "that you may warn the Mother of Towns and those around it"], and did not mention glad tidings, although Allah in many places mentions both warning and glad tidings: ﴿لِتُبَشِّرَ بِهِ الْمُتَّقِينَ وَتُنْذِرَ بِهِ قَوْمًا لُدًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:97, "that you may give glad tidings to the righteous and warn with it a people obstinate in opposition"]. That is because the context concerns Quraysh, and Quraysh, as you know, are stubborn transgressors, so it was fitting to mention warning without mentioning glad tidings. For if you see a person who is transgressing, do you try to set him straight first with glad tidings or first with warning? With warning first. This is from the eloquence of the Qur'an, that it places everything in its proper place.

* Among the benefits of these noble verses: that the Prophet ﷺ is obligated to warn the Mother of Towns as a primary obligation, because of His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى﴾, while warning others is a secondary obligation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that the Prophet ﷺ will not reach those to whom he was sent directly, but rather warns those around him, because of His saying: ﴿لِتُنْذِرَ أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾. I mentioned this benefit to you a little while ago; we have mentioned it in the book of tafsir.

* There is also another benefit: that the Qur'an in the Arabic language can only be used to warn ﴿أُمَّ الْقُرَى وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾, who are Arabs. As for Persians, Romans, Copts and those like them, they do not benefit from the Qur'an except after they know the Arabic language and understand the meanings of the Qur'an. Perhaps this, and Allah knows best, is also among the wisdoms behind His saying: ﴿وَمَنْ حَوْلَهَا﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: frightening people with the Day of Resurrection, because of His saying: ﴿وَتُنْذِرَ يَوْمَ الْجَمْعِ﴾ [al-Shura 42:7, "and warn of the Day of Gathering"].

* And among its benefits: that the Day of Resurrection is certain to occur, because of His saying: ﴿لَا رَيْبَ فِيهِ﴾ [there is no doubt about it].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that on that Day people will be divided into two groups: a group in Paradise and a group in the blaze. The people of Paradise head toward the Sirat (the bridge over Hell) to reach the higher place, Paradise. As for the people of the Fire, they do not ascend the Sirat, because there is no hope that they will be saved; rather, they are driven to Hell as a waterless herd (wirdan), that is, in the greatest thirst. The Fire appears to them like a mirage; they think it is water, so they hasten toward it. When they reach it, they find the reverse of what they expected, so they stop. But they are pushed toward the Fire of Hell with a violent push, and it is said to them: ﴿هَذِهِ النَّارُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ [al-Tur 52:14, "This is the Fire which you used to deny"], ﴿اصْلَوْهَا فَاصْبِرُوا أَوْ لَا تَصْبِرُوا﴾ [al-Tur 52:16, "Burn in it, so endure it or do not endure it"].
