* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ [al-Shura 42:8, "Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community"].

* And among its benefits: the refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination). Do you know who the Qadariyyah are? The Qadariyyah are those who say that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has no connection to the act of the servant. They say: the servant is independent; Allah has no will in it. Their extremists deny Allah's knowledge of the servant's conditions except what has already occurred; they say: Allah does not know what the servant will do, but when he does it, He knows it. These people are undoubtedly disbelievers, because they denied the knowledge of Allah. Their moderate ones deny the will and the creation: this is the position their opinion settled on. They say: Allah has no will in the act of the servant, and He is not the creator of the act of the servant. The servant is free; he speaks and remains silent, acts and abstains, sleeps and wakes, independently, with no will of Allah in it. For this reason they have been called the Magians of this Muslim community, because by this belief they make for the created things two creators: the actions of the servants are created by the servants, and the actions of Allah are created by Allah. Therefore they are called the Magians of the Islamic community.
The noble verse refutes them. The basis of the refutation: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾ [al-Shura 42:8]. This is like His saying in Surah Hud: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ رَبُّكَ لَجَعَلَ النَّاسَ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً وَلَا يَزَالُونَ مُخْتَلِفِينَ (١١٨) إِلَّا مَنْ رَحِمَ رَبُّكَ وَلِذَلِكَ خَلَقَهُمْ﴾ [Hud 11:118–119, "And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will continue to differ, except those upon whom your Lord has mercy; and for that He created them"].
In it is a refutation of the Qadariyyah, and in it is an argument for the Jabriyyah (those who deny human choice), because Allah said: ﴿وَلَوْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَجَعَلَهُمْ أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً﴾. So they became divided by the will of Allah, and what Allah wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. This is evidence that man has no choice, and that his act is by the will of Allah. It is said: this is what those in whose hearts is deviation cling to, because those in whose hearts is deviation follow the ambiguous (mutashabih) and leave the clear (muhkam). They take the ambiguous in verses like this one and say: this is evidence that the act of the servant is by the will of Allah, and no one can change the will of Allah.
We say: Glory be to Allah! You have looked at the evidences with one blind eye, and the remaining eye has haze or dimness on it; it is not good. So they looked with one blind eye and a quarter or more. There are explicit verses attributing action to the human being himself, and that it is by the will of the human being. Does Allah not say: ﴿فَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيُؤْمِنْ وَمَنْ شَاءَ فَلْيَكْفُرْ﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29, "So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve"]? Does Allah, blessed and exalted is He, not say: ﴿لِمَنْ شَاءَ مِنْكُمْ أَنْ يَسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [al-Takwir 81:28, "for whoever among you wills to be upright"]? And the verses on this are many.
Does a person not sense within himself that he does an act with no one compelling him? You come to the mosque with no one forcing you; you enter the mosque with no one forcing you; you leave the mosque with no one forcing you. This is a tangible thing. So what is the meaning of our act being by the will of Allah?
We say: the meaning of our act being by the will of Allah is that whatever we do, Allah has willed it, and His will for it precedes our will; but we do not know of Allah's will except after the thing occurs, so we know that Allah has willed it. Is this clear or not clear? That is: I now will to speak with you, and I will to move my hand. Is that not so? Did Allah will that I speak and that I move my hand? Yes. How did you know? By its occurrence. Because I know with certainty that nothing can be in the dominion of Allah that He does not will, and I am in the dominion of Allah, and the heavens and the earth are all in the dominion of Allah. So it is not possible that there be in His dominion what He does not will. But I do not know the will of Allah except after the thing occurs. That is why some scholars said: "Divine decree (qadar) is a hidden secret," which the servants do not know, because they know it only after it has occurred.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, exalted is He, bestows His favor upon whomever He wills of His servants, admitting them into His mercy, because of His saying: ﴿وَلَكِنْ يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [al-Shura 42:8, "But He admits whom He wills into His mercy"].

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that there is nothing in Paradise that causes distress. What is its basis? His saying: ﴿فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾ [in His mercy]. Mercy entails the attainment of what is desired and deliverance from what is feared. That is why the people of Paradise are proclaimed: "Indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill, that you will be young and never grow old, and that you will live and never die"[[Recorded by Muslim (2837/22) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "A caller will call out: Indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill, and indeed for you is that you will live and never die, and indeed for you is that you will be young and never grow old, and indeed for you is that you will be blessed and never be miserable."]]. Also we say: "And that they will be cheerful and never grieve." All complete bliss belongs to the people of Paradise, and there is in it no disturbance, no fear of sickness, and no fear of death. Do they not even sleep, out of anxiety and pain? Answer.
No, by Allah, they do not sleep out of joy and happiness, so that all their time is absorbed in joy and happiness. Their not sleeping is a sign of the perfection of their life, because we need sleep only to restore the fatigue that came before and to renew the strength that follows. Is that not so? That is why whenever a person becomes tired he needs sleep, and when he sleeps he rises energetic. So we need sleep in this worldly life because our life is deficient, but in the Hereafter there is no deficiency. They are always in happiness. O Allah, make us among them! That is why He said: ﴿يُدْخِلُ مَنْ يَشَاءُ فِي رَحْمَتِهِ﴾; there is nothing in mercy that causes sorrow or distress; rather, all of it is good.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the disbelievers are wrongdoers, indeed they are the greatest of wrongdoers. The greatest sin is disbelief, that you set up a rival to Allah while He is the one who created you. So the most wrongful of wrongdoers are the disbelievers. If we believe this, and it is obligatory for us to believe it, do we hope for good from the disbelievers when they are the greatest of wrongdoers? No, by Allah; we never hope for any good from them for Islam, because they are the greatest of wrongdoers. That is why you must implant in your heart hatred for the disbelievers and for disbelief. You must make it a settled, hidden disposition: to hate every disbeliever and every disbelief.
And if a person has qualities of disbelief and qualities of faith? The just and equitable course is that I love him for what faith he has, and I hate him for what disbelief he has. A person may have a quality of faith and a quality of disbelief. The Prophet ﷺ said: "There are two qualities among people which are disbelief in them: slandering lineage and wailing over the dead."[[Recorded by Muslim (67/121) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] These two do not take a person out of faith.
So pay attention to this: the disbelievers are the greatest of wrongdoers, and whoever is the greatest of wrongdoers, it is not possible to hope from him for any good or justice. Know that if he acts justly, it is only to seize an opportunity, so that instead of justice he takes injustice many times over. Now, we know that the Jews are among the people most eager for wealth, and yet we find them spending, but they spend a qirsh in order to take a dinar. Never think that they spend anything except to gain more than it. This is well known: ﴿وَلَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ أَحْرَصَ النَّاسِ عَلَى حَيَاةٍ﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:96, "And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life"].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wrongdoers will find neither a helper nor a protector. No helper will push away or lift the punishment, and no protector will console them and ease their calamities. They have none of this. This shows that they will be in severe regret, because they hope for no benefit. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you wronged, that you are in the punishment together﴾ [az-Zukhruf 39].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. The negation is more emphatic and better suits the context. We have said: we interpret the verse as having both meanings when?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, and there is no preponderant meaning. Notice this qualification, because if you do not say "and there is no preponderant meaning," the people of ta'til (the Mu'tattila, who deny Allah's attributes) will come to you and say, "What we said is possible." No, you must understand this. Yes, indeed, but Allah negated it in terms of what actually occurs.
* Student: In other countries, for example, there are scholars who are deeply learned in some sciences, but who are, for example, Mu'tazili (followers of the Mu'tazila) or Ash'ari (followers of al-Ash'ari). During the lesson, for example, they may teach their school of thought. So, if a student of knowledge knows the truth on this issue, should he debate his teacher about it, especially when the teacher is elderly and it may be hard for him to retract his opinion?
* Shaykh: Undoubtedly, first: those who call to bid'ah (innovation in religion), avoid them, and provision is from Allah. Even if they are scholars of grammar and rhetoric, there is no good in them, these who call to it. As for those who do not call to their innovation and conceal it, there is no harm in sitting with them in what is beneficial. But if you see them deviating from the right path, it is obligatory for you to warn them. However, do not warn them in front of the students, because a person may be seized by pride in sin, especially if he sees himself as outstanding in one of the sciences. If a student of knowledge answers him in front of people, be assured that he will swell up, become greater than the mountain, and will not return. But it is possible for you to write him a letter that makes the truth clear to him, if you cannot debate him directly. If he is a caller (to innovation), do not go near him at all, and warn against him, because he is to be feared. Then, if people see that you, so-and-so, and so-and-so refer to him, they will imagine that he is upon the truth. Do you understand? We ask Allah the Exalted to gather us and you in His mercy, and to grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 9–10 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ (Am) here is munqati'ah (disjunctive), and munqati'ah am carries the meaning of bal (rather, but) and the interrogative hamzah.

There is also am muttasilah (conjunctive), which occurs between two opposing things and carries the meaning of aw (or). An example is: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. This am is called muttasilah because it lies between two opposing things and because it carries the meaning of aw (or). ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. In other speech besides the Qur'an, if aw were placed in place of am, the sentence would be sound.

So we say: am is either munqati'ah or muttasilah. The difference between them: am muttasilah carries the meaning of aw, while am munqati'ah carries the meaning of bal and the hamzah of interrogation.

Second: am muttasilah occurs between two opposing things, whereas am munqati'ah is otherwise.

Here the Exalted says: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ There are no two opposing things in it. Therefore it is munqati'ah, meaning bal and the hamzah. ﴿Or have they taken﴾: the pronoun refers to the polytheists. ﴿besides Him﴾: the pronoun refers to the Lord, the Exalted.

﴿Protectors﴾: the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (i.e., the idols). This is an indication from him that the first object of ﴿taken﴾ is omitted, and the estimate is: "Or have they taken besides Him the idols as protectors?", because (ittakhadha) takes two objects, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa' 125]. In this verse, ﴿Or have they taken besides Him protectors?﴾, only one object is before us. We say: the first object is omitted, and the estimate is: "Or have they taken the idols as protectors?"

﴿Protectors﴾ means helpers, whom they seek help from, seek victory through, befriend, and draw near to as if they were a lord.

The author-commentator said: "(Am) is munqati'ah with the meaning of bal, which is for transition, and the hamzah is for denial; i.e., those taken as protectors are not [protectors]." That is: these people took as protectors the idols. The idols are some trees, some stones, and some created cosmic things like the sun and the moon, and some human creations. None of these benefits its worshipper. That is why, when the polytheists fall into distress, whom do they call upon? They call upon Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shades, they call upon Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾ [Luqman 32]. So the idols do not benefit, and they themselves acknowledge this, saying: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 3].

(﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, i.e., the Helper of the believers; and the fa' is merely for conjunction.) The fa' in His saying ﴿So Allah﴾: it is not a response to a condition, but is merely for conjunction. ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾. Pay attention to the grammatical analysis of this sentence: (Allah) is the subject, (Huwa) is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and (al-Wali) is the predicate of the subject.

Know that the pronoun of separation is a particle, not a noun. This is one point. It has three benefits:

The first benefit: restriction (al-hasr).

The second benefit: separating the predicate from the adjective. For example, if you say: "Fulan al-karim" (Fulan the generous), (Fulan) is the subject and (al-karim) is the predicate, but it may also be that (Fulan) is the subject, (al-karim) is its adjective, and the predicate is omitted: "Fulan al-karim is present." But if you say "Fulan huwa al-karim" (Fulan is the generous one), it becomes certain that (al-karim) is the predicate and not an adjective. For this reason they call it the pronoun of separation, because it separates, i.e., distinguishes, between the predicate and the adjective. It has no place in the grammatical analysis. Therefore we say: (Allah) is the subject, (al-Wali) is its predicate, and (Huwa) is a pronoun of separation with no grammatical place. Thus it conveys restriction, emphasis, and distinction between the predicate and the adjective.

We add to this with an example: "Muhammad al-Rasul." It may be that (al-Rasul) is an adjective of (Muhammad), and the estimate is: "Muhammad the Messenger is truthful." If you bring in (huwa) and say: "Muhammad huwa al-Rasul," it becomes certain that (al-Rasul) is the predicate. This is one point.

Also, (huwa al-Rasul) conveys restriction, meaning not anyone else. There is no doubt that Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah, peace and blessings be upon him, is the Messenger of this Ummah, and there is no other messenger.

The third benefit: emphasis. ("huwa al-Rasul"). These are the benefits of the pronoun of separation. As for its grammatical analysis, it has no place in it, because it is a particle.

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾. His saying ﴿He is the Protector﴾: the author says: "(i.e., the Helper of the believers)." In this there is room for consideration, because the author has now restricted wilayah to the special wilayah, whereas the correct view is that it is general: He is the Protector of every person in both the general wilayah and the special wilayah. The general wilayah belongs to everyone, for none manages the affairs of creation except Allah the Exalted. The special wilayah is the wilayah of support and aid. Accordingly, the author's restriction to the special wilayah, may Allah have mercy on him, is open to consideration. So He is the Protector of every person by both the general and the special wilayah.

The difference between the general and special wilayah: the general wilayah includes everyone, so Allah is the protector of each person who manages his affairs, even the disbelievers have Allah as their protector. The special wilayah entails support and aid, and among it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut; they bring them out of light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah 257].

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾: does this sentence contain restriction or not? It contains restriction. What is its method? The pronoun of separation.

﴿And He gives life to the dead﴾: nothing else can give life to the dead, because giving life is making a thing alive after it was dead, and no one is capable of this except Allah. Indeed, when Allah the Exalted wills to cause someone to die, no one can prevent death, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] has reached the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see, then why, if you are not to be judged, do you not return it, if you should be truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–87]. That is: "Why do you not bring it back, if you are truthful?" Is the answer possible or not? It is not possible. So Allah gives life to the dead and causes the living to die, the Exalted.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: over all things. Any non-existent thing, Allah is capable of bringing it into existence; any existent thing, Allah is capable of annihilating it. Every thing, Allah the Exalted is capable of it. The opposite of power is incapacity, and for this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is never to be impeded by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾ [Fatir 44].

﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾: (ma) is a conditional particle, and ﴿differ﴾ is the conditional verb, and ﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾ is the response of the condition. In His saying ﴿And whatever you differ over﴾: whatever dispute occurs among people, its referral is to Allah the Exalted, whether it concerns religious or worldly matters, and whether it is with believers or with disbelievers. Whatever it is, its ruling belongs to Allah the Exalted; no one is referred to a ruling except Allah.

The commentator says: (﴿And whatever you differ over﴾ with the disbelievers ﴿over it﴾). The correct view is that it is more general: whatever you differ over, O people, with the disbelievers or among yourselves, O Muslims, ﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾.

As for His saying ﴿anything﴾, the commentator says: "(from religion and other than it)." Yes indeed: "(from religion)": religion is everything a person worships Allah with; "and other than it" is what is not such. Its ruling is with Allah alone, meaning its referral of ruling is to Allah. For this reason he said: "(﴿Its ruling﴾ is referred ﴿to Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, He will judge between you)." The correct view is that it is referred to Allah in this world and the Hereafter. This is shown by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59].

* It is derived from this verse that there is no reference point in man-made laws, and that laws contrary to the ruling of Allah are void. That is so, because law is from the making of humans, and humans do not have comprehensive knowledge, neither in the present nor in the future. They have not encompassed the world with knowledge. At most, the one who drafted the legal article knows only the apparent conditions of his people. Does he know all people and that this ruling suits them? No. This is a deficiency.

Second: even if he knew the conditions of people in general, can he know the condition of every individual? People differ even regarding a single ruling. Consider a rich man and a poor man: the rich man owes zakat, while the poor man does not owe zakat; it is permissible to give zakat to the poor man, but not to the rich. The incapable and the capable: the capable prays standing, and the incapable prays seated. Does the one who drafted this law know people's conditions such that the law suits every condition of people? No. This is another deficiency.

Third: does the drafter of the law perceive people's conditions in the future or not? He does not perceive them. It is known that rulings differ according to differing conditions. For this reason we find that the Islamic Shari'ah differs from the Christian Shari'ah, and the Christian Shari'ah differs from the Jewish Shari'ah. Behold, 'Isa says: ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 50]. The Islamic religion also came differing in many subsidiary matters from the religions before it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48].

Therefore law is deficient in every respect. If it is deficient in every respect, can this deficient thing be the reference in disputes? It cannot.

As for the one who refers to law, is he a disbeliever? This requires detail. If a person finds no way to take his right except through law, this is not disbelief, nor even prohibited. If you are in a country that rules by law and you have a dispute with a person, and you cannot resort to a Shari'ah ruling, there is no harm in your litigating under the law. If it rules in your favor, this means it is like a police force for you. Had we said otherwise, people's rights would be lost. The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this meaning in his book al-Turuq al-Hukmiyyah.

However, if you litigate under the law while you know that it rules with injustice, is it permissible to litigate before it or not? It is not permissible, there is no ambiguity in this, because some people may not deserve something by the Shari'ah ruling, but by the law they would deserve it, so he says: "I will litigate to take my right according to the law." What do we say? We say: this is haram and not permissible.

Example: what they call bank interest. Is bank interest haram or halal in the Shari'ah ruling? It is haram. This man knows it is haram in the Shari'ah, but says: "I want to litigate under the law, because the law will enable me to obtain it." Is it permissible? It is not permissible, because this is consuming wealth falsely.

So, litigating before the taghut, which is whatever contradicts the Shari'ah ruling: if it is to extract a right and not in the belief that what it rules is the truth (note the difference), that is to extract a right and not in the belief that what it rules is right, then it is permissible, as if you made them police who extract your right from the one who wronged you. But if it is in the belief that what is in the law is right while it contradicts the Shari'ah, then it is haram. This is regarding litigation under the law.

Now regarding the drafting of law: the one who drafts the law either knows that it contradicts the Shari'ah but believes that it is more beneficial to creation than the Shari'ah of the Lord of creation. This is without doubt a disbeliever, a disbelief that removes one from the religion, because he denies the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], and denies His saying the Exalted: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8]. Because he has now written a book in place of the Book of Allah, and it is clear he is a disbeliever: he has replaced the religion of Allah with another, and replaced the ruling of Allah with another.

But if he does not know that it contradicts the Shari'ah, and he made it by interpretation (ta'wil) if he is from among the people of ijtihad, or by misguidance (tadlil) if he is not from among the people of ijtihad, then he does not become a disbeliever. Such as one who believes that the matter of 'inah is permissible and drafts it as law. The matter of 'inah is known among you: that a person sells something on deferred payment and buys it back in cash for less. He says, for example: "Article such-and-such: if a person sells something on deferred payment and buys it back for less, the contract is valid." This article contradicts the Shari'ah, but he does not know that it contradicts the Shari'ah, or he interpreted that it is permissible based on the form of the transaction. This does not make him a disbeliever.

It may also be that drafting a law that contradicts the Shari'ah is from misguidance rather than interpretation, such as when the ruler is an unlettered ignoramus but some scholars of the state misled him, and he said: "This is no harm, because the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world'" [Narrated by Muslim (2363/141) with his chain from the hadith of 'A'ishah and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by people pollinating palms and said: "If you did not do this, it would be good." He said: so it came out as shees (poor dates), and he passed by them and said: "What is the matter with your palms?" They said: "We said such and such." He said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world."], and we know that this is good for us in this world based on his supposition. This person does not become a disbeliever.

So now, one who drafts a law that contradicts the Shari'ah, believing it is superior to the Shari'ah and more beneficial to creation, is without doubt a disbeliever. We have no doubt about this, but on two conditions: that he knows it contradicts the Shari'ah, and that he believes it is more beneficial to creation or equal to the Shari'ah. Even whoever believes it is equal is a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], and says: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8].

As for one who drafts it contrary to the Shari'ah through interpretation or misguidance, he does not become a disbeliever, because in his view he has not contradicted the Shari'ah, so he does not become a disbeliever by this.

Summary now: when people differ over something, to whom do they refer? To Allah: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾.

If someone says: From where do we know the ruling of Allah?

We say: from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is explained by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa' 59].

Now we understand that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, fell short in interpreting the verse in his saying: ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, where he restricted it to the believers with the special wilayah. He also fell short here ("﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, He will judge between you"). This too is a shortcoming, and the correct view is that its ruling is with Allah in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied﴾: (dhalikum) and (dhalik) occur often for us, so why does the kaf vary from one place to another? The answer is that the kaf follows the addressee, and the demonstrative follows the thing pointed to.

Here is a test for you: the kaf is according to the addressee, and the demonstrative is according to the thing pointed to. Point to a masculine singular thing, addressing a masculine singular.

* Student: dhalika.
* Shaykh: (dhalika) is correct. Point to two things, addressing two.
* Student: dhalikan.
* Shaykh: dhanikuma. (dhan) is the thing pointed to, the addressee is (kuma): dhanikuma. Point to a feminine thing, addressing a masculine.
* Student: (dhalika).
* Shaykh: No, you cannot now make the woman masculine.
* Student: (tilka).
* Shaykh: (tilka) is correct, yes, (tilka), because the demonstrative for the feminine is with the ta' (tilka). Point to a feminine thing, addressing two feminine.
* Student: (tilkuma).
* Shaykh: (tilkuma), good, excellent. So, praise be to Allah, we have understood; there is no need to absorb all the examples. The demonstrative follows the thing pointed to, the kaf follows the addressee.

Here, ﴿Dhalikumu Allahu rabbi﴾: the demonstrative (dhalika) agrees with what it refers to. You are pointing at the Name "Allah," which is singular, while the address is to a group. ﴿Dhalikumu Allahu rabbi﴾: ﴿dhalikum﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Allahu﴾ is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), and ﴿rabbi﴾ is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ must declare to these people that Allah is his Lord, and that he has no lord besides Him. We say "and that he has no lord besides Him" because both parts of the sentence are definite, and when both parts of a nominal sentence are definite, it indicates exclusivity (hasr).

If someone asks: with what is the word ﴿'alayhi﴾ connected? We say it is connected to ﴿tawakkaltu﴾. With what is ﴿ilayhi﴾ connected? We say it is connected to ﴿uneebu﴾. So the governing word is placed after the governed word in ﴿'alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ and in ﴿ilayhi uneebu﴾. The rule among the rhetoricians is that when something that should be postponed is placed first, this indicates exclusivity. So ﴿'alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ is equivalent to: "I place my trust only in Him," and ﴿ilayhi uneebu﴾ is equivalent to: "I turn to none but Him."

﴿'Alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ means: I entrust my affair to Allah with complete entrustment. Trust in Allah is not like trust in people. Trusting a person means that you appoint him to buy something for you; this is a specific entrustment, and also an entrustment in which you believe you are the one in charge of the matter. In other words, if you wished, you could dismiss him and cancel the agency. But your trust in Allah is an entrustment to Allah in everything, and you cannot cancel that agency; even if you were to cancel it, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is still the Guardian over you.

From this we learn the difference between one who says, "I trusted so-and-so," meaning "I appointed him as my agent," and "I trust in Allah." Is "I trust in Allah" like "I appointed so-and-so as agent"? No, never. Even though the two expressions may coincide in wording, their meanings differ greatly. Notice, brothers: "I trusted so-and-so" means I entrusted my affair to him, and the matter is in my hands; if I wish, I can dismiss him. But "I trust in Allah" means I have entrusted my affair to Him, relying on Him, may He be exalted, to facilitate and ease my affair. Therefore we do not say that whoever relies on a person to buy something has committed shirk with Allah. We do not say this, because there is a great difference between my trust in the person whom I have appointed to buy a need and my trust in Allah. My trust in Allah is entrustment and seeking help; but with a person it is not so: appointing or relying on him in an agency is in reality a form of employment. For this reason, whenever you wish, you may say, "I no longer rely on him," and dismiss him. But with regard to trust in Allah, it is not like that.

So what is trust in Allah? We say: it is entrusting the matter to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with complete entrustment. Some say: it is sincere reliance upon Allah in bringing benefits and warding off harms, together with confidence in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is explained in this way.

Does trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mean abandoning the means (asbab)? No. For this reason, if a man were told, "Marry so that children may come to you," and he said, "I am relying on Allah," would that be acceptable? It would not be acceptable, because children do not grow from the roof. Take the means and then trust. There is a proverb: "Tie it (the camel) and trust." Do not release the camel and say, "I trust in Allah"; if you release the camel, it goes wherever it wishes. Even if you say, "I trust in Allah," take the means. If a person is told, "O so-and-so, seek provision: sell, buy, do the things through which wealth is obtained," and he says, "Not at all, I trust in Allah," is he truthful? This is the trust of the negligent. If you are sincere in trusting Allah, then take the means, but do not depend on the means; make the means a means, and the Planner is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Wa-ilayhi uneebu﴾: I return to Allah, the Exalted, in my acts of worship and in all my circumstances.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community﴾ [Ash-Shura 8]. In this verse there are benefits. Among them: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who deny divine decree (qadar) and say that a person is independent in his actions.

As you know, as you studied or as some of you studied in creed ('aqidah), people divided regarding the acts of the servant into three categories. One group says that the servant has no choice, no will, and no volition, and that he performs voluntary acts just as he performs compelled acts. These are the Jabriyyah, and the Jahmiyyah are Jabriyyah regarding the acts of the servant. Thus a person's voluntary movements, such as standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping and waking, are compelled upon him. In these movements he is like a sick person who shivers from fever without his choice. These people are astray, because by their own principle, if Allah punishes the disobedient person, He would be unjust to him, since he does not choose. They hold that injustice with regard to Allah is impossible, because injustice is a doer's disposal of what is not his property, and Allah has the dominion of the heavens and the earth; therefore injustice is impossible for Him in their view. This is one group.

Another group says: the person is independent in his acts, doing whatever he wills, and Allah has no connection to his actions. These are the Qadariyyah, whom the Prophet ﷺ called "the Magians of this Ummah"[[Abu Dawud (4691) narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Qadariyyah are the Magians of this Ummah; if they fall ill, do not visit them, and if they die, do not attend their funerals."]], because they say that cosmic events have two creators: the acts of the servants are created by them, and the events of the universe are created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Thus they made two creators for events, just as the Magians made two creators for events. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ called them the Magians of this Ummah.

According to their view, there would exist in Allah's dominion something He does not will. Since the heavens and the earth belong to Allah, if the actions of the servants occur without the will and volition of Allah, then something occurs in His dominion that He does not will. These people are astray and in error, because how can Allah be the Creator of the servant while we say the servant is independent of Allah, with no involvement of Allah in it at all?

The people of the Sunnah and the community say: a person acts by his own choice and will, and the Qur'an indicates this: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its striving while he is a believer—those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated﴾ [Al-Isra 19]; ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment, We will pay them in it their deeds﴾ [Hud 15]; ﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]. They say: the person has will and choice, and he distinguishes between voluntary and compelled acts, without doubt. A person stands, sits, eats, drinks, sleeps and wakes, and he does not feel that anyone compels him to it. Yet this act and this will are created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. How are they created by Allah? Because the person himself is created by Allah, so his wills within himself and his acts in his limbs are created; for the attributes of the created and the acts of the created are created, just as the attributes of the Creator are uncreated. For this reason we say the Qur'an is uncreated, because it is the speech of Allah.

Thus the people of the Sunnah and the community, and praise be to Allah, were guided by Allah to the truth, and they were a middle path between extremes.

The noble verse ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community﴾ refutes whom? The Qadariyyah who say that a person is independent in his acts. According to their view, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, cannot guide all people or lead them all astray.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is part of Allah's wisdom, the Mighty and Majestic, that people divide into believer and disbeliever, from His saying: ﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾; for the effect of mercy cannot appear unless people are divided into those who receive mercy and those who do not. So it is part of Allah's wisdom that people differ. We know that if people did not differ, a believer would not be distinguished from a disbeliever; if people did not differ, there would be no jihad, and no enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, and there would be no purpose in creating Paradise and Hellfire, and so on.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of mercy for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying: ﴿in His mercy﴾. Know that mercy is of two kinds: created and uncreated. The uncreated is the mercy of Allah which is His attribute, because all of Allah's attributes are uncreated. The created is the thing separate from Allah that results from the effects of His mercy which is His attribute. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for those whose faces will be white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide forever﴾ [Al 'Imran 107]. Is this created or uncreated? Created. "Fi" indicates place, and the mercy of Allah which is His attribute cannot be a container for those who believed. Therefore ﴿fa-fi rahmati Allah﴾ means the created mercy. What is the created mercy of Allah? It is Paradise, based on the saying of Allah to Paradise: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah radiya Allahu 'anhu.]].

﴿Wa-rabbuka al-Ghafuru dhu al-rahmah﴾ [Al-Kahf 58]: is the intended meaning of "mercy" here the attribute or the created? The attribute.

So mercy is one of Allah's attributes. It is strange that some people who claim to glorify Allah say that Allah cannot be described as merciful! We ask Allah not to make our hearts swerve. They say: Allah cannot be described with mercy, because mercy is an emotion and a state of being moved, as when you show mercy to a child or to an orphan, and Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that. Then what do we do with the countless verses that affirm Allah's mercy? They say: interpret mercy as bestowal of favour, and so they interpret it as created mercy; or interpret mercy as the will to bestow favour, and so they interpret it as will. These are the Ash'irah, because they affirm will as an attribute of Allah.

Glory be to Allah! Their argument in this is: will is indicated by reason, but mercy is not indicated by reason; rather reason indicates the opposite. We say to them: what is the reason that indicates will? They say: the reason that indicates will is specification (takhsis), the specification of created things. A camel has a specific form, a sheep has a specific form, the children of Adam have specific forms; that He makes the camel in this attribute, the sheep in this attribute, and the children of Adam in this attribute indicates will.

Now, as for mercy, there are rational proofs for mercy that are more indicative than the indication of specification for will. All the blessings in the universe, what do they indicate? They indicate mercy. This is why the common person, when the sky rains, says: "We have been given rain by the grace and mercy of Allah." So the indication of these things for mercy is stronger than the indication of specification for will. Therefore we believe that Allah has mercy.

If they say that mercy is a state of being moved and a state of being broken, we say: this applies to the mercy of creatures; but the mercy of the Creator is befitting to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, with no brokenness, no deficiency, and no defect in it.

Have you seen anger? Anger is an emotion that occurs in a person until he loses his nerves and behaves like a madman; it may even lead him to break his property, beat his children, divorce his wife, and perhaps throw himself into the water. Anger is an ember that Satan throws into a person's heart until his blood boils. Do we say that the anger of Allah is like the anger of a person? Never, far from it. The anger of Allah is an attribute befitting Him, indicating the perfection of His sovereignty and His power to take vengeance, but it can never result in bad conduct, unlike the anger of the creature.

The point is: there are people who denied the mercy of Allah, and how did they interpret mercy? By one of two things: either bestowal of favour, or the will to bestow favour. This is undoubtedly from their misguidance and innovation, and from their returning matters of the unseen to what their deficient minds dictate. The truth is that these minds are not minds but illusions. We know with certainty that what the Sharia has brought can never contradict clear reason; authentic transmitted texts never contradict clear reason. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, wrote a multi-volume work on the agreement of clear reason with authentic transmission, called Dar' Ta'arud al-'Aql wa'l-Naql (The Refutation of the Contradiction between Reason and Transmission).

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the evil end of injustice, from His saying: ﴿And the wrongdoers have no protector or helper﴾; even their allies in this world will not benefit them in the Hereafter; they have no ally to support them, and no helper to repel harm from them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: those who stand by justice have a helper and a protector, derived from the reverse implication: if the wrongdoer has no protector or helper, then whoever stands by justice has a protector and a helper.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the rebuke of those who take protectors besides Allah, because (am) here means (bal) and the interrogative hamzah of rebuke.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: these people sought something from other than its proper place, from His saying: ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾; He is the one who should be taken as Protector, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of protection for Allah, from His saying: ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾. Is it general or specific? Al-Jalalayn took it as specific, saying "the protector of the believers." The correct view is that in this verse it is general: Allah is the protector of everyone. Allah, the Exalted, is the protector of the disbelievers too: He provides for them, grants them well-being, averts evil from them, and takes care of them, as He says: ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fail. Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [Al-An'am 61-62]. But we say: protection is of two kinds, general and specific, as we explained in the tafsir.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: there is no protection for anyone apart from Allah. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿He﴾, because "huwa" is a separating pronoun (damir fasl) that indicates exclusivity.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the demonstration of Allah's power over a matter that no one claims, and whoever claims it is refuted by reality, from His saying: ﴿and He gives life to the dead﴾. No one claims this sentence at all, and whoever claims it is a liar.

If someone says: Is it not the case that a man who deserves execution is brought, and the ruler orders that he not be killed; is that not giving life?

The answer: it cannot be giving life, but rather preserving a life, because life already existed. He did not place life in him so that it would remain; rather he preserved an existing life.

If someone says: What do you say about the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Because of that, We prescribed for the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all mankind; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved all mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 32]? ﴿Whoever saves it, it is as if he had saved all mankind﴾, thus affirming the act of giving life to a human?

The answer: he gives them life by preserving their lives; that is, whoever lifts killing from a person and defends a person who is about to be killed, it is as if he had given life to all mankind. Otherwise, it is well known that no one can breathe the spirit into a dead person.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's power, blessed and exalted, from His saying: ﴿and He is over all things Competent﴾.

* Among its benefits: the encouragement (I mean, encouraging a person) to supplicate to Allah for whatever he wishes, so long as he does not transgress in supplication. Brother, pay attention: this is an educational lesson, that you may supplicate to Allah for anything except what Allah has forbidden you to supplicate for; from His saying: ﴿and He is over all things Competent﴾. When you supplicate to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for anything, do not despair; do not say, "This is impossible." Only what is transgression and aggression is not permitted.

This opens for a person the door of hope and of supplicating to Allah and turning to Him. If you have a critically ill patient whom you have given up on, and you say, "By Allah, I cannot supplicate to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because the man has reached a dangerous state," this is without doubt a mistake, because Allah is over all things Competent. So supplicate to Allah.

A person whose means have run out, who sought provision through buying and selling and suffered losses, or applied for a job and was not successful, and so on, says: "Then that's it, there is no point in my supplicating." What do we say to him? We say: this is a mistake and an error. Supplicate to Allah, for Allah is ﴿Competent over all things﴾. How many a person has been prepared for by those who washed him, bought his shroud, brought his bier near, and his companions made ready to escort him, and then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, granted him health, because Allah is ﴿Competent over all things﴾.

So when you believe that Allah is ﴿Competent over all things﴾, do not consider anything beyond the power of Allah. Ask of Him for everything, as long as it is not sinful or a severing of kinship ties, and do not despair. This is why He said: ﴿And He is Competent over all things﴾. This sentence, as I have told you, indicates that a person should not despair of the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and should supplicate to Allah, Exalted, for whatever he wishes, as long as it is not sinful or a severing of kinship ties.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾, and so on to the end. In this verse there are the following benefits:

* First: Disagreement among people must occur, and this is the reality. That is, it is not possible to remove disagreement among people; they must differ. The causes of disagreement are many. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) mentioned them in his book *Raf' al-Malam 'an al-A'immah al-A'lam* (Removing Blame from the Imams), which is a concise and beneficial book. We have summarized it and added some material to it, and we have mentioned practical examples of the principles he stated (may Allah have mercy on him) in our small treatise entitled *Ikhtilaf al-'Ulama' wa Mawqifuna Minhu* (The Disagreement of the Scholars and Our Stance Towards It), or something of this meaning, and it is beneficial.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: when disagreement arises, it is obligatory to return to the judgment of Allah, because of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿so its ruling is with Allah﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: its ruling is with Allah in this world and in the Hereafter, due to the generality of His saying: ﴿so its ruling is with Allah﴾. As for those who restricted this to the Hereafter, they are mistaken. Even in matters of this world we return to the judgment of Allah, as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should be believing in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [An-Nisa 59].

* Among its benefits: the prohibition of referring to man-made laws (al-qawanin al-wad'iyyah) when disagreement arises, because of His saying: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾, not with anyone else.

If someone says: Do you not say that the statement of a Companion is a proof (hujjah)?

The answer: Yes, though there is some disagreement on this. The matter is not one of consensus (ijma'). But on the view that the statements of the Companions who were jurists are proofs, we say: Yes, we hold that, but we rely on the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): «Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly-guided, rightly-directed Caliphs after me» [Narrated by Abu Dawud (96), and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, with this wording (246), from the hadith of al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah (may Allah be pleased with him)]. This is because the correct view is that "the rightly-guided Caliphs" is attached to attributes, not to specific individuals. That is, the rightly-guided Caliphs are not just the four; rather, everyone who succeeded the Prophet (ﷺ) in his community in knowledge, call, and teaching is a rightly-guided caliph. The most rightly-guided of those who succeeded the Prophet (ﷺ) are the Companions, in returning to the judgment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the Prophet (ﷺ) declared sincerity and monotheism, because of His saying: ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾; that is, that One to whose judgment one returns is Allah, my Lord.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is from the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) to rely upon Allah alone, because of His saying: ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾. But where did we take the word "alone" (wahdah) from? From the restriction (hasr) whose method is placing before what should be placed after.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse as well: it is from the guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ) to turn in repentance to Allah alone, because of His saying: ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾. And if this is from the guidance of the Messenger (ﷺ), it is obligatory upon us to follow it, because of the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and who remembers Allah often﴾ [Al-Ahzab 21].

* Student: Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And had Allah willed, He would have made you one nation﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 48], (...) is it transgression in supplication for a person to ask for the guidance of all people, believers and disbelievers alike?

* Shaykh: No, it is not transgression, because the people of your time, what do they represent compared to all of mankind? A few. So it is not transgression in supplication.

* Student: Regarding the sorcerer, and that he (...)?

* Shaykh: Does the sorcerer give life and cause death?

* Student: How does one respond to him?

* Shaykh: We say: He neither gives life nor causes death.

* Student: It is imagination (takhyil), in other words.

* Shaykh: That is, if he made people imagine that the dead person moved, then in reality he did not move. This is why, if someone came who did not perceive the sorcery by which he covered the eyes of the people, he would perceive the dead person not moving.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Did we say here: a real attribute?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, the affirmation of mercy for Allah. Then we divided it ourselves. We did not divide it on the basis of this verse; we divided mercy in general.

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾. What is the meaning of the verse? Disagreement in matters of religion is referred to Allah. So in matters of religion and of worldly affairs alike, its ruling is with Allah, Exalted. Good.

Can it be derived from this that judging by man-made laws is prohibited?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: If these laws contradict the Shari'ah, then it is prohibited to refer to them.

Good. If a person is compelled to seek judgment under man-made laws?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, seeking judgment as such. That is, if his aim is to obtain his right, this is permissible. But if his aim is to submit to them in the sense that their ruling is the one that takes effect, this is not permissible. Good.

On the first aspect, what is the basis for permissibility?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: That is, it is as if he has made them like the police (al-shurtah) who recover his right for him, not as if they were judges, but that he reaches his right through them. Good.

Regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾, is there a restriction in it or not?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: What is its method?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Placing before what should be placed after. This explanation by the more general principle is better, because placing before what should be placed after indicates restriction. Good.

What is the meaning of tawakkul (reliance)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Entrusting the matter to Allah, Exalted, with complete entrustment, while recognizing that you are in need of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Good.

What is the difference between relying upon Allah and relying upon a person?

* Student: (...).

* Another student: (...).

* Shaykh: Correct. Relying upon a person means using him for a need you rely upon him for, and in that case you believe that you are above him. This is why, if you wished, you could cancel the agency. But relying upon Allah means depending upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, entrusting the matter to Him, on the basis that He is the Doer who does as He wills.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 9–10 (part 1 of 3):

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ (Am) here is munqati'ah (disjunctive), and munqati'ah am carries the meaning of bal (rather, but) and the interrogative hamzah.

There is also am muttasilah (conjunctive), which occurs between two opposing things and carries the meaning of aw (or). An example is: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun 6]. This am is called muttasilah because it lies between two opposing things and because it carries the meaning of aw (or). ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾. In other speech besides the Qur'an, if aw were placed in place of am, the sentence would be sound.

So we say: am is either munqati'ah or muttasilah. The difference between them: am muttasilah carries the meaning of aw, while am munqati'ah carries the meaning of bal and the hamzah of interrogation.

Second: am muttasilah occurs between two opposing things, whereas am munqati'ah is otherwise.

Here the Exalted says: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ There are no two opposing things in it. Therefore it is munqati'ah, meaning bal and the hamzah. ﴿Or have they taken﴾: the pronoun refers to the polytheists. ﴿besides Him﴾: the pronoun refers to the Lord, the Exalted.

﴿Protectors﴾: the commentator, may Allah have mercy on him, says: (i.e., the idols). This is an indication from him that the first object of ﴿taken﴾ is omitted, and the estimate is: "Or have they taken besides Him the idols as protectors?", because (ittakhadha) takes two objects, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend﴾ [al-Nisa' 125]. In this verse, ﴿Or have they taken besides Him protectors?﴾, only one object is before us. We say: the first object is omitted, and the estimate is: "Or have they taken the idols as protectors?"

﴿Protectors﴾ means helpers, whom they seek help from, seek victory through, befriend, and draw near to as if they were a lord.

The author-commentator said: "(Am) is munqati'ah with the meaning of bal, which is for transition, and the hamzah is for denial; i.e., those taken as protectors are not [protectors]." That is: these people took as protectors the idols. The idols are some trees, some stones, and some created cosmic things like the sun and the moon, and some human creations. None of these benefits its worshipper. That is why, when the polytheists fall into distress, whom do they call upon? They call upon Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when a wave covers them like shades, they call upon Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾ [Luqman 32]. So the idols do not benefit, and they themselves acknowledge this, saying: ﴿We do not worship them except that they bring us near to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar 3].

(﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, i.e., the Helper of the believers; and the fa' is merely for conjunction.) The fa' in His saying ﴿So Allah﴾: it is not a response to a condition, but is merely for conjunction. ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾. Pay attention to the grammatical analysis of this sentence: (Allah) is the subject, (Huwa) is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and (al-Wali) is the predicate of the subject.

Know that the pronoun of separation is a particle, not a noun. This is one point. It has three benefits:

The first benefit: restriction (al-hasr).

The second benefit: separating the predicate from the adjective. For example, if you say: "Fulan al-karim" (Fulan the generous), (Fulan) is the subject and (al-karim) is the predicate, but it may also be that (Fulan) is the subject, (al-karim) is its adjective, and the predicate is omitted: "Fulan al-karim is present." But if you say "Fulan huwa al-karim" (Fulan is the generous one), it becomes certain that (al-karim) is the predicate and not an adjective. For this reason they call it the pronoun of separation, because it separates, i.e., distinguishes, between the predicate and the adjective. It has no place in the grammatical analysis. Therefore we say: (Allah) is the subject, (al-Wali) is its predicate, and (Huwa) is a pronoun of separation with no grammatical place. Thus it conveys restriction, emphasis, and distinction between the predicate and the adjective.

We add to this with an example: "Muhammad al-Rasul." It may be that (al-Rasul) is an adjective of (Muhammad), and the estimate is: "Muhammad the Messenger is truthful." If you bring in (huwa) and say: "Muhammad huwa al-Rasul," it becomes certain that (al-Rasul) is the predicate. This is one point.

Also, (huwa al-Rasul) conveys restriction, meaning not anyone else. There is no doubt that Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah, peace and blessings be upon him, is the Messenger of this Ummah, and there is no other messenger.

The third benefit: emphasis. ("huwa al-Rasul"). These are the benefits of the pronoun of separation. As for its grammatical analysis, it has no place in it, because it is a particle.

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾. His saying ﴿He is the Protector﴾: the author says: "(i.e., the Helper of the believers)." In this there is room for consideration, because the author has now restricted wilayah to the special wilayah, whereas the correct view is that it is general: He is the Protector of every person in both the general wilayah and the special wilayah. The general wilayah belongs to everyone, for none manages the affairs of creation except Allah the Exalted. The special wilayah is the wilayah of support and aid. Accordingly, the author's restriction to the special wilayah, may Allah have mercy on him, is open to consideration. So He is the Protector of every person by both the general and the special wilayah.

The difference between the general and special wilayah: the general wilayah includes everyone, so Allah is the protector of each person who manages his affairs, even the disbelievers have Allah as their protector. The special wilayah entails support and aid, and among it is His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut; they bring them out of light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah 257].

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾: does this sentence contain restriction or not? It contains restriction. What is its method? The pronoun of separation.

﴿And He gives life to the dead﴾: nothing else can give life to the dead, because giving life is making a thing alive after it was dead, and no one is capable of this except Allah. Indeed, when Allah the Exalted wills to cause someone to die, no one can prevent death, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Then why, when it [the soul] has reached the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see, then why, if you are not to be judged, do you not return it, if you should be truthful?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 83–87]. That is: "Why do you not bring it back, if you are truthful?" Is the answer possible or not? It is not possible. So Allah gives life to the dead and causes the living to die, the Exalted.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: over all things. Any non-existent thing, Allah is capable of bringing it into existence; any existent thing, Allah is capable of annihilating it. Every thing, Allah the Exalted is capable of it. The opposite of power is incapacity, and for this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah is never to be impeded by anything in the heavens or on the earth. Indeed, He is ever Knowing, Competent﴾ [Fatir 44].

﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾: (ma) is a conditional particle, and ﴿differ﴾ is the conditional verb, and ﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾ is the response of the condition. In His saying ﴿And whatever you differ over﴾: whatever dispute occurs among people, its referral is to Allah the Exalted, whether it concerns religious or worldly matters, and whether it is with believers or with disbelievers. Whatever it is, its ruling belongs to Allah the Exalted; no one is referred to a ruling except Allah.

The commentator says: (﴿And whatever you differ over﴾ with the disbelievers ﴿over it﴾). The correct view is that it is more general: whatever you differ over, O people, with the disbelievers or among yourselves, O Muslims, ﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾.

As for His saying ﴿anything﴾, the commentator says: "(from religion and other than it)." Yes indeed: "(from religion)": religion is everything a person worships Allah with; "and other than it" is what is not such. Its ruling is with Allah alone, meaning its referral of ruling is to Allah. For this reason he said: "(﴿Its ruling﴾ is referred ﴿to Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, He will judge between you)." The correct view is that it is referred to Allah in this world and the Hereafter. This is shown by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa' 59].

* It is derived from this verse that there is no reference point in man-made laws, and that laws contrary to the ruling of Allah are void. That is so, because law is from the making of humans, and humans do not have comprehensive knowledge, neither in the present nor in the future. They have not encompassed the world with knowledge. At most, the one who drafted the legal article knows only the apparent conditions of his people. Does he know all people and that this ruling suits them? No. This is a deficiency.

Second: even if he knew the conditions of people in general, can he know the condition of every individual? People differ even regarding a single ruling. Consider a rich man and a poor man: the rich man owes zakat, while the poor man does not owe zakat; it is permissible to give zakat to the poor man, but not to the rich. The incapable and the capable: the capable prays standing, and the incapable prays seated. Does the one who drafted this law know people's conditions such that the law suits every condition of people? No. This is another deficiency.

Third: does the drafter of the law perceive people's conditions in the future or not? He does not perceive them. It is known that rulings differ according to differing conditions. For this reason we find that the Islamic Shari'ah differs from the Christian Shari'ah, and the Christian Shari'ah differs from the Jewish Shari'ah. Behold, 'Isa says: ﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾ [Al 'Imran 50]. The Islamic religion also came differing in many subsidiary matters from the religions before it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48].

Therefore law is deficient in every respect. If it is deficient in every respect, can this deficient thing be the reference in disputes? It cannot.

As for the one who refers to law, is he a disbeliever? This requires detail. If a person finds no way to take his right except through law, this is not disbelief, nor even prohibited. If you are in a country that rules by law and you have a dispute with a person, and you cannot resort to a Shari'ah ruling, there is no harm in your litigating under the law. If it rules in your favor, this means it is like a police force for you. Had we said otherwise, people's rights would be lost. The scholar Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, pointed to this meaning in his book al-Turuq al-Hukmiyyah.

However, if you litigate under the law while you know that it rules with injustice, is it permissible to litigate before it or not? It is not permissible, there is no ambiguity in this, because some people may not deserve something by the Shari'ah ruling, but by the law they would deserve it, so he says: "I will litigate to take my right according to the law." What do we say? We say: this is haram and not permissible.

Example: what they call bank interest. Is bank interest haram or halal in the Shari'ah ruling? It is haram. This man knows it is haram in the Shari'ah, but says: "I want to litigate under the law, because the law will enable me to obtain it." Is it permissible? It is not permissible, because this is consuming wealth falsely.

So, litigating before the taghut, which is whatever contradicts the Shari'ah ruling: if it is to extract a right and not in the belief that what it rules is the truth (note the difference), that is to extract a right and not in the belief that what it rules is right, then it is permissible, as if you made them police who extract your right from the one who wronged you. But if it is in the belief that what is in the law is right while it contradicts the Shari'ah, then it is haram. This is regarding litigation under the law.

Now regarding the drafting of law: the one who drafts the law either knows that it contradicts the Shari'ah but believes that it is more beneficial to creation than the Shari'ah of the Lord of creation. This is without doubt a disbeliever, a disbelief that removes one from the religion, because he denies the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment for a people who are certain?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], and denies His saying the Exalted: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8]. Because he has now written a book in place of the Book of Allah, and it is clear he is a disbeliever: he has replaced the religion of Allah with another, and replaced the ruling of Allah with another.

But if he does not know that it contradicts the Shari'ah, and he made it by interpretation (ta'wil) if he is from among the people of ijtihad, or by misguidance (tadlil) if he is not from among the people of ijtihad, then he does not become a disbeliever. Such as one who believes that the matter of 'inah is permissible and drafts it as law. The matter of 'inah is known among you: that a person sells something on deferred payment and buys it back in cash for less. He says, for example: "Article such-and-such: if a person sells something on deferred payment and buys it back for less, the contract is valid." This article contradicts the Shari'ah, but he does not know that it contradicts the Shari'ah, or he interpreted that it is permissible based on the form of the transaction. This does not make him a disbeliever.

It may also be that drafting a law that contradicts the Shari'ah is from misguidance rather than interpretation, such as when the ruler is an unlettered ignoramus but some scholars of the state misled him, and he said: "This is no harm, because the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world'" [Narrated by Muslim (2363/141) with his chain from the hadith of 'A'ishah and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ passed by people pollinating palms and said: "If you did not do this, it would be good." He said: so it came out as shees (poor dates), and he passed by them and said: "What is the matter with your palms?" They said: "We said such and such." He said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world."], and we know that this is good for us in this world based on his supposition. This person does not become a disbeliever.

So now, one who drafts a law that contradicts the Shari'ah, believing it is superior to the Shari'ah and more beneficial to creation, is without doubt a disbeliever. We have no doubt about this, but on two conditions: that he knows it contradicts the Shari'ah, and that he believes it is more beneficial to creation or equal to the Shari'ah. Even whoever believes it is equal is a disbeliever, because Allah says: ﴿And who is better than Allah in judgment?﴾ [al-Ma'idah 50], and says: ﴿Is not Allah the most just of judges?﴾ [al-Tin 8].

As for one who drafts it contrary to the Shari'ah through interpretation or misguidance, he does not become a disbeliever, because in his view he has not contradicted the Shari'ah, so he does not become a disbeliever by this.

Summary now: when people differ over something, to whom do they refer? To Allah: ﴿And whatever you differ over, its ruling is with Allah﴾.

If someone says: From where do we know the ruling of Allah?

We say: from the Qur'an and the Sunnah. This is explained by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And if you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you should believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa' 59].

Now we understand that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, fell short in interpreting the verse in his saying: ﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾, where he restricted it to the believers with the special wilayah. He also fell short here ("﴿its ruling is with Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, He will judge between you"). This too is a shortcoming, and the correct view is that its ruling is with Allah in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied﴾: (dhalikum) and (dhalik) occur often for us, so why does the kaf vary from one place to another? The answer is that the kaf follows the addressee, and the demonstrative follows the thing pointed to.

Here is a test for you: the kaf is according to the addressee, and the demonstrative is according to the thing pointed to. Point to a masculine singular thing, addressing a masculine singular.

* Student: dhalika.
* Shaykh: (dhalika) is correct. Point to two things, addressing two.
* Student: dhalikan.
* Shaykh: dhanikuma. (dhan) is the thing pointed to, the addressee is (kuma): dhanikuma. Point to a feminine thing, addressing a masculine.
* Student: (dhalika).
* Shaykh: No, you cannot now make the woman masculine.
* Student: (tilka).
* Shaykh: (tilka) is correct, yes, (tilka), because the demonstrative for the feminine is with the ta' (tilka). Point to a feminine thing, addressing two feminine.
* Student: (tilkuma).
* Shaykh: (tilkuma), good, excellent. So, praise be to Allah, we have understood; there is no need to absorb all the examples. The demonstrative follows the thing pointed to, the kaf follows the addressee.

Here, ﴿Dhalikumu Allahu rabbi﴾: the demonstrative (dhalika) agrees with what it refers to. You are pointing at the Name "Allah," which is singular, while the address is to a group. ﴿Dhalikumu Allahu rabbi﴾: ﴿dhalikum﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿Allahu﴾ is an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan), and ﴿rabbi﴾ is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is that the Messenger ﷺ must declare to these people that Allah is his Lord, and that he has no lord besides Him. We say "and that he has no lord besides Him" because both parts of the sentence are definite, and when both parts of a nominal sentence are definite, it indicates exclusivity (hasr).

If someone asks: with what is the word ﴿'alayhi﴾ connected? We say it is connected to ﴿tawakkaltu﴾. With what is ﴿ilayhi﴾ connected? We say it is connected to ﴿uneebu﴾. So the governing word is placed after the governed word in ﴿'alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ and in ﴿ilayhi uneebu﴾. The rule among the rhetoricians is that when something that should be postponed is placed first, this indicates exclusivity. So ﴿'alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ is equivalent to: "I place my trust only in Him," and ﴿ilayhi uneebu﴾ is equivalent to: "I turn to none but Him."

﴿'Alayhi tawakkaltu﴾ means: I entrust my affair to Allah with complete entrustment. Trust in Allah is not like trust in people. Trusting a person means that you appoint him to buy something for you; this is a specific entrustment, and also an entrustment in which you believe you are the one in charge of the matter. In other words, if you wished, you could dismiss him and cancel the agency. But your trust in Allah is an entrustment to Allah in everything, and you cannot cancel that agency; even if you were to cancel it, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is still the Guardian over you.

From this we learn the difference between one who says, "I trusted so-and-so," meaning "I appointed him as my agent," and "I trust in Allah." Is "I trust in Allah" like "I appointed so-and-so as agent"? No, never. Even though the two expressions may coincide in wording, their meanings differ greatly. Notice, brothers: "I trusted so-and-so" means I entrusted my affair to him, and the matter is in my hands; if I wish, I can dismiss him. But "I trust in Allah" means I have entrusted my affair to Him, relying on Him, may He be exalted, to facilitate and ease my affair. Therefore we do not say that whoever relies on a person to buy something has committed shirk with Allah. We do not say this, because there is a great difference between my trust in the person whom I have appointed to buy a need and my trust in Allah. My trust in Allah is entrustment and seeking help; but with a person it is not so: appointing or relying on him in an agency is in reality a form of employment. For this reason, whenever you wish, you may say, "I no longer rely on him," and dismiss him. But with regard to trust in Allah, it is not like that.

So what is trust in Allah? We say: it is entrusting the matter to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with complete entrustment. Some say: it is sincere reliance upon Allah in bringing benefits and warding off harms, together with confidence in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is explained in this way.

Does trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mean abandoning the means (asbab)? No. For this reason, if a man were told, "Marry so that children may come to you," and he said, "I am relying on Allah," would that be acceptable? It would not be acceptable, because children do not grow from the roof. Take the means and then trust. There is a proverb: "Tie it (the camel) and trust." Do not release the camel and say, "I trust in Allah"; if you release the camel, it goes wherever it wishes. Even if you say, "I trust in Allah," take the means. If a person is told, "O so-and-so, seek provision: sell, buy, do the things through which wealth is obtained," and he says, "Not at all, I trust in Allah," is he truthful? This is the trust of the negligent. If you are sincere in trusting Allah, then take the means, but do not depend on the means; make the means a means, and the Planner is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Wa-ilayhi uneebu﴾: I return to Allah, the Exalted, in my acts of worship and in all my circumstances.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made them one community﴾ [Ash-Shura 8]. In this verse there are benefits. Among them: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, who deny divine decree (qadar) and say that a person is independent in his actions.

As you know, as you studied or as some of you studied in creed ('aqidah), people divided regarding the acts of the servant into three categories. One group says that the servant has no choice, no will, and no volition, and that he performs voluntary acts just as he performs compelled acts. These are the Jabriyyah, and the Jahmiyyah are Jabriyyah regarding the acts of the servant. Thus a person's voluntary movements, such as standing, sitting, eating, drinking, sleeping and waking, are compelled upon him. In these movements he is like a sick person who shivers from fever without his choice. These people are astray, because by their own principle, if Allah punishes the disobedient person, He would be unjust to him, since he does not choose. They hold that injustice with regard to Allah is impossible, because injustice is a doer's disposal of what is not his property, and Allah has the dominion of the heavens and the earth; therefore injustice is impossible for Him in their view. This is one group.

Another group says: the person is independent in his acts, doing whatever he wills, and Allah has no connection to his actions. These are the Qadariyyah, whom the Prophet ﷺ called "the Magians of this Ummah"[[Abu Dawud (4691) narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The Qadariyyah are the Magians of this Ummah; if they fall ill, do not visit them, and if they die, do not attend their funerals."]], because they say that cosmic events have two creators: the acts of the servants are created by them, and the events of the universe are created by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.
