This is known from the study of grammar, because verbs of the heart either govern, or are suspended, or are cancelled. If they are cancelled, their governing is lost both in position and in wording; if they are suspended, their governing remains in position but not in wording; if they govern, they govern both in wording and in position.

* In this noble verse there are benefits:

* Among them: the warning of the drowning of ships, from His saying ﴿or He destroys them﴾. You have already learned that winds with respect to ships divide into three kinds: a suitable gentle wind, a violent wind that destroys and drowns, and a still wind that leaves the ship motionless on the surface of the water. So one of its benefits: the warning of ships being drowned because of sins.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the warning against sins and that they are a cause of punishments, from His saying ﴿for what they have earned﴾.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, glorified and exalted, pardons many misdeeds and does not punish for them, from His saying ﴿and pardons much﴾, meaning that even with the drowning of ships, Allah, blessed and exalted, pardons much.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the warning to those disobedient ones that there is no escape for them from Allah the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying ﴿and those who dispute concerning Our signs﴾.

* Among them: the blame of disputing to refute truth, derived from His saying ﴿and those who dispute﴾. As for disputing to establish truth, it is obligatory, when a person is skilled and proficient in it. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And argue with them in a way that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 125], and He, exalted, said: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best, except for those of them who have wronged﴾ [al-'Ankabut 46].

Disputing to establish truth and refute falsehood is obligatory, but on condition that the person has knowledge of what he disputes with. If he has no knowledge, then it is obligatory that he not dispute, because if he disputes to establish truth without knowledge, the matter may be reversed against him: he will be presented with doubts he cannot repel, and then he will be silenced. The silencing of one who argues for the truth does not harm only himself, but harms himself and the truth for whose establishment he argues.

Is disputing acquired by natural disposition or by practice? The answer: by both. Allah, glorified and exalted, may give a person strength of argument, a quick mind, and swift response, and this is from Allah the Mighty and Majestic; or a person may be weak in this respect by his natural make-up, but through disputation he becomes trained.

For this reason some scholars, when they wished to clarify and establish a question, would posit an opponent to themselves: they would raise an objection against themselves and then answer it, then another objection and answer it, until they became trained in disputation.

It is reported that a commoner was debated by a Christian, who said to him: "You Muslims are oppressors." He said: "Why?" The Christian said: "Because you permit marrying our women but do not permit us to marry yours." When this objection is put to a person who does not know disputation, he says: "Yes, that is true." Then the commoner said: "We believe in your Prophet and you do not believe in ours. Believe in our Prophet and we will marry your women." Is this a sound argument or not? It is sound without doubt. If it is sound from a commoner, this is evidence that disputation can be natural and can come by practice and training.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that there is no escape for one who opposes Allah and His Messenger from the punishment of Allah, from His saying ﴿and those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no place of escape﴾. It is known that ya'lamu takes two objects; where are its two objects? The clause ﴿ma lahum min mahis﴾ — what is it called? It is called ta'liq (suspension), and we mentioned to you that "zanna" and its sisters may be operative, suspended, or cancelled.

His saying ﴿and those who dispute concerning Our signs﴾: is this praise or blame? Blame. Now how can it be blame when Allah commanded disputing with the People of the Book? Thus we say: disputing to manifest and clarify the truth is commanded, while disputing in the opposite direction, to refute truth and manifest falsehood, is the one under threat. Done.

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And among His signs are the ships, sailing in the sea like mountains﴾ [al-Shura 32]. (Min) is for partitive meaning (tab'id), and His signs are His indicators that point to His mercy, power and wisdom. ﴿Al-Jawari﴾ is a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), but it is inflected with a dhamma estimated on the elided yaa' for lightness. The original of al-jawar is al-jawari with a yaa', the plural of jariyah, and al-jariyah is the ship, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 11]. Among the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic are these ships ﴿in the sea﴾, on the water, ﴿like mountains﴾, meaning (like mountains in size). These great ships, loaded with wealth, people and animals, are among the signs of Allah: that they should be in this roiling sea, moving upon the water, cleaving the surging of the water with what they carry of provisions. There is no doubt that they are among the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Allah, blessed and exalted, warned their riders with the following: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind so that they remain motionless upon its surface﴾ [al-Shura 33]. This is the lightest punishment: He stills the wind so that they remain motionless upon its back. Why? Because ships in the past only moved according to the winds, since they moved by means of a long sail that the winds strike, so they advance. When the winds calm, they stop. Hence He said: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind so that they remain﴾, i.e., the ships, ﴿motionless upon its surface﴾, i.e., upon the surface of the sea, and then the benefits are disrupted, and perhaps a violent wind comes and smashes the ship and drowns it.

So the conditions are then three: either gentle winds by which the ship sails as it should, or violent winds that drown the ship, or stillness. What happens with stillness? They stand motionless on the surface of the water. So He, glorified and exalted, explains that among His signs is the movement of these ships.

﴿If He wills, He stills the wind so that they remain﴾ [become] ﴿motionless﴾, fixed, not running, ﴿upon its surface﴾ — i.e., the surface of the sea. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾ [from His signs].

Then He said: ﴿signs﴾ (plural), because partitive means a part of a thing. If the thing is a thousand, its part may be two hundred or three hundred; if the thing is two, the part is one. Ships are countless, hence He said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, considering the many ships that run upon the sea. We may also say that, considering a single ship, what its passengers observe at sea are great signs indicating the perfection of Allah's power. Thus those who go out to sea to catch fish tell us of wonders they witness about the fish, its varieties, and the differences in their forms, sizes and shapes, which are among the greatest signs of Allah.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one﴾. Sabbar is an intensive form: one who is greatly patient. Shakur: one who is greatly grateful. What is the connection between patience and gratitude?

Its aspect is clear: if these ships travel as they should, the duty of the person is gratitude; if they travel otherwise, his duty is patience. Both the patient and the grateful will see in these ships of the signs of Allah the Mighty and Majestic what makes them certain that Allah, glorified and exalted, is capable of all things, that He is merciful to His servants, and other things that they will see.

He (the author) said: (It is the believer who is patient in hardship and grateful in ease). It may be said: the believer and the disbeliever. But the disbeliever is patient and does not give thanks; the believer is patient and grateful, patient in the place of patience and grateful in the place of gratitude. The disbeliever is patient in the place of patience and endures, but he does not give thanks in the place of thanks; rather he only grows in arrogance and insolence.

(﴿Or He destroys them﴾ is conjoined to "He stills", i.e., He drowns them by the violence of the wind together with their people.) This is a third division: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind﴾, or if He wills ﴿He destroys them﴾, i.e., drowns them ﴿for what they have earned﴾, i.e., because of their earning. What is the earning that leads to punishment? Sins, either by abandoning obligations or by committing prohibited acts. ﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned, and pardons much﴾.

As for His saying ﴿and pardons much﴾: it is not conjoined to "He stills", because that would corrupt the meaning, since the meaning would be: if He wills, He stills, or destroys, or pardons much, and this is invalid. Rather the meaning is: He destroys them for what they have earned, and "He pardons" is a resumptive clause (jumlah isti'nafiyyah), but the waw was dropped for lightness. The meaning is that Allah, exalted, pardons many sins and does not punish for them ((﴿and pardons much﴾ of them, so He does not drown their people)).

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿So whatever you have been given is [but] the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾, meaning: whatever you have been given of the adornments of this world, ﴿it is [only] the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾.

On "﴿fa-mata'u﴾": the fa' here is connective, linking to the response of the conditional, which is His saying ﴿fa-ma uwititum min shay'in﴾, because (ma) here is conditional, and (min shay') is its explanation. The clause (fa-mata'u) is the response of the conditional. On this basis we say: (mata') is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the estimated meaning is: "it is the enjoyment of the worldly life."

He said: (It is enjoyed therein, then it passes away). ﴿But what is with Allah is better and more lasting for those who believe﴾, to the end of the verse. Here (ma) is a relative pronoun meaning (that which), and (khayr) is the predicate of the subject. ﴿And more lasting﴾: Allah has described it with two extremely important attributes. The first: that it is better; the second: that it is more lasting. This is because whatever is in this world is a fleeting, troubled enjoyment; not a week passes without you finding some disturbance in it, in line with the saying of the poet:

"One day for us and one day against us, and one day we are grieved and one day we are gladdened."

As for the Hereafter, it is pure good with no evil in it. Also, it is more lasting, meaning more enduring: the enjoyment of this world is small and passes quickly, unlike what is with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿For those who believe﴾: believe in what? In everything that must be believed in. Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about faith, and he said to him: "Faith is that you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the divine decree, both its good and its evil."[[Narrated by Muslim (8/1), from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.]] So, they believe in what must be believed in; this phrase is inclusive of everything. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾: the fronting of the object is for the purpose of restriction and emphasis upon it.

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾: the Lord is the Creator, the Owner, the Manager. ﴿They rely﴾: meaning they depend upon and entrust their affairs to Him, blessed and exalted. Some have defined tawakkul as: sincere reliance upon Allah in bringing benefits and warding off harms, along with trust in Allah, blessed and exalted. ("Sincere reliance upon Allah"): meaning that you rely upon Allah with sincere reliance, not turning to anyone else. ("In bringing benefits and warding off harms"), add ("along with trust in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic"): meaning you rely upon Him, the Mighty and Majestic, while being certain that He is sufficient for you and will help you.

Reliance upon Allah is half of the religion, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah 5], since a person cannot perform the duties of Islam except through reliance upon Allah and depending on Him. Look at His saying: ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾, and at His saying: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him﴾ [Hud 123]; you will find that Allah, exalted is He, divided the religion into two parts: worship and seeking help.

﴿So whatever you have been given is [but] the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾. ﴿Whatever you have been given﴾: the address. The commentator says: (It is addressed to believers and others) ﴿of anything﴾: of the furnishings of this world, ﴿it is [only] the enjoyment of the worldly life. But what is with Allah is better and more lasting﴾. As for His saying ﴿whatever you have been given of anything﴾, (min) here is extra, for the purpose of indicating generality: i.e., whatever you are given of worldly matters, it is the enjoyment of the worldly life.

As for his saying: (The address is to believers and others), it is correct, since this is addressed to both the believer and the disbeliever. The believer enjoys in this world, but they enjoy as livestock enjoys, and the Fire is their abode. The believer enjoys the world, but if he performs deeds for the Hereafter, his bounty becomes in this world and in the Hereafter.

(﴿So whatever you have been given of anything is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾: one enjoys it therein, then it passes away). This is the reality: the enjoyment of the worldly life passes away or is taken from him. That is, either this or that. Suppose a person remains wealthy, physically healthy and secure in his residence; is it not possible that this could be taken from him? Yes. Then it becomes an enjoyment that has passed away. If it does not pass from him, he passes from it. Who has been granted enjoyment forever? No one. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We did not grant any human before you eternity. So if you die, will they be eternal?﴾ [al-Anbiya' 34]. ﴿But what is with Allah is better and more lasting﴾: (ma) here is a relative noun, the subject, and (khayr) is its predicate. ﴿But what is with Allah is better and more lasting﴾: better than the enjoyment of this world in its essence, its kind, and all its pleasures. ﴿And more lasting﴾: i.e., more enduring, because the enjoyment of this world passes away. The bounty of the Hereafter combines the two attributes: it is better, and it is more lasting. Thus, with respect to its type, kind and categories, it is better; and with respect to its duration, it is more lasting. A person wants nothing from bounty but this; he wants only the most perfect and the most lasting, so that it does not pass from him. But for whom? ﴿For those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾.

Know that such an expression has come in three ways. The first: that the person is addressed directly, and it is said to him: the Hereafter is better for you.

The second: that it comes qualified with desirable, sought-after attributes.

The third: that it comes unrestricted.

Listen to the saying of Allah the Mighty and Majestic to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]﴾ [al-Duha 4]. So now we affirm that the Hereafter is better for the Prophet ﷺ than the first life; this is restricted to a specific person. The qualified one with attributes is like the verse we have here, and like His saying: ﴿And the home of the Hereafter is best for those who fear Allah﴾ [Yusuf 109]; this is qualified with attributes.

The third is unrestricted, like His saying: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la 16-17]. However, this unrestricted expression is interpreted in light of the restricted one, or it is said that this refers to its description and not to who attains it. In general terms, the Hereafter is better and more lasting; in detail, it is explained in each place according to its context.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So whatever you have been given...﴾ to the end.

* In this verse there are benefits, among them: encouragement to renounce the world and that it is passing.

* Among its benefits: warning the disbelievers that what they are in of bounty is nothing compared to the bounty of the Hereafter.

Historians mention that Ibn Hajar, may Allah have mercy on him, author of Fath al-Bari, was chief judge in Egypt. One day he passed by a Jewish oil-seller, who was working with oil, whose clothes were all dirty, whose vessels were soiled, and who was in great hardship. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, may Allah have mercy on him, while he was chief judge, passed by in a carriage pulled by horses or mules, in pomp. The Jew stopped him and said: "What do you say about the words of your Prophet: 'The world is a prison for the believer and a paradise for the disbeliever'?[[Narrated by Muslim (2956/1) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] How does this agree with our present state? You are a believer and in this bounty, and the Jew is a Jew in this hardship and toil; how does this agree?" Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar answered him immediately, saying: "What I am in of bounty, compared to the bounty of the Hereafter, is a prison, because the Hereafter is good, and this is nothing; and what you are in of hardship, compared to the torment of the Fire, is a paradise." The Jew said: "I testify that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." He embraced Islam immediately, because this entered his mind and that what the Messenger said is true. Whatever the world is, compared to the Hereafter it is a prison; it is nothing. Yet however narrow the world may be, compared to the Fire it is a paradise.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that this life of ours is "dunya," from "dunuww" meaning nearness, or from "dana'a" meaning baseness and worthlessness; it includes both meanings. It is near, because it precedes the Hereafter, from the moment a person is born and is in it; and it is base, i.e., worthless, compared to what? Compared to the Hereafter. So "dunya" is the feminine of "adna," and it is either from nearness or from baseness and worthlessness, and in it is the belittling of the world.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that what is with Allah is better than the whole world, by His saying: ﴿But what is with Allah is better and more lasting﴾. So the verse contains encouragement to renounce the world and encouragement toward the Hereafter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: praise of those who combine faith and reliance: ﴿For those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾.

* Among its benefits: that reliance is an act of worship which must be devoted to Allah alone. The proof: the fronting of the object, which is evidence of the obligation of devoting it to Allah. As for the proof that it is worship: Allah mentioned it in a context of praise, and there is no praise except for worship.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the virtue of combining these mentioned attributes, since each one is a praiseworthy attribute beyond doubt, but their combination is more perfect. Do you see that if you describe a person as generous and say "So-and-so is generous," is that not praise? Now, if you say "brave," generosity is added to bravery, and the combination of two attributes produces a third, which is his combining of attributes. Likewise we say about all multiple attributes: their combination increases the praise of the one described by them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of relying upon Allah, by His saying ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾, where the object is fronted.

If someone says: Is it permissible to rely upon another person in what he is capable of? The answer: Yes, but this reliance should not be made into full entrusting in which the heart is attached. There is a difference between my saying: "O so-and-so, I have appointed you to buy such-and-such for me," where I depend on him but do not entrust the matter to him entirely; rather, when I say "O so-and-so, buy such-and-such for me," do I consider myself above him or below him? Above him, because I am now the one who holds the matter, commanding and forbidding him. But the reliance which is absolute entrusting belongs only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If someone raises this objection to us, we say: the answer is easy: delegating something does not indicate absolute entrusting; relying on something does not attach the heart to the one relied upon himself, unlike reliance upon Allah. Thus the difference becomes clear. And it is said of a person who appoints another that he does not lack in reliance, as evidence that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, appointed: "He appointed 'Ali ibn Abi Talib during the Farewell Pilgrimage to sacrifice the remainder of his offering on his behalf."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1716) and Muslim (1317/348) from the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]

He appointed 'Urwah ibn al-Ja'd to buy a sacrificial animal for him. Listen to the story: the Prophet ﷺ gave him a dinar and said: "Buy a sacrificial animal with it for me." He bought two sheep for one dinar, then sold one of them for a dinar, and returned to the Prophet ﷺ with what? With a sheep and a dinar. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, did not lose anything: the dinar he had given him was returned to him, and the sheep he wanted was obtained. "The Prophet ﷺ prayed for blessing in his trade, so he never bought anything without profiting from it, even if he bought dust, he would profit from it."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3384) from the hadith of 'Urwah ibn al-Ja'd.]] By the blessing of the prayer of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

Scholars derived from this story the permissibility of disposing of another's property for the sake of benefit, since 'Urwah acted: he bought two sheep while he was commanded with one sheep, and he sold one though he was not commanded to sell. But this is for the benefit of the other, although it is still conditional upon his approval. So if the one who acted were told by his owner, "I do not accept this action," it would be annulled. If we knew that a man wanted to sell his house and had put it up for sale, and a person came and offered a large sum for it, offering twice its value, and another man came forward and sold it without being appointed, is it permissible or not? It is permissible, because I know the man is determined to sell the house, and if he is determined to sell it, the sale would be at the market price. When a person offers more than the market value, say twice, and someone without appointment steps forward and sells it, the sale is valid, because this is disposal on behalf of another in a way he would like. But if the owner of the house says, "I do not allow this," then the sale is annulled. Then another problem arises, with whom? With the buyer. The buyer says: "I have bought, and I don't care about you or your companion; I bought." The principal says: "I did not agree." The agent says: "I agree." So what is the solution? The solution: if the agent informed the buyer that he is an agent and that the house belongs to so-and-so, and then so-and-so, the principal, says: "I do not accept this sale," it is cancelled; otherwise the sale stands and the agent bears what the principal requires. And Allah is the Granter of success.

* Student: Why did He use the expression "walī" together with "naṣīr," when the walī is the naṣīr?

* Shaykh: No. The walī is one who manages affairs, and he may not be able to repel harm; he manages their affairs but may not be able to defend them. The naṣīr is able to defend. So they have no walī who brings good, nor naṣīr who repels evil.

* Student: May Allah be good to you. The words ﴿So for what your hands have earned﴾: what is the reconciliation between this and the trial of the believer (...)?

* Shaykh: The answer is that this is for those who are struck, so it shows them that this is because of what their hands earned, that perhaps they will repent and return to Allah. As for affliction without sin, this is for raising of ranks, because affliction is met by patience; patience must be exercised upon it. Patience is a high rank that only those granted success attain. It cannot be said of one never touched by harm that he is patient. For this reason the trial of the prophets was multiplied over the trials of others, even in illness: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "was feverish as two of us are feverish."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5648) and Muslim (2571/45) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]] And he was tested in death, peace and blessings be upon him, so that the end of his life would be at the highest levels of patience. As for when this is said of the sinners, the meaning is that they should stop their sins.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: No, this is not a punishment from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "Khizy" means humiliation: that these dominating arrogant ones will see their affair return to humiliation, and in the Hereafter they will be punished.

* Student: Shaykh, ﴿they argue concerning Our signs﴾: is the intended meaning here the legislative signs or the cosmic signs?

* Shaykh: Both the cosmic and the legislative. Arguing about the cosmic signs is saying: "Why does Allah decree such-and-such?" and "Why does Allah, for example, bring wars and strife upon the Muslim people?" and the like. Regarding the legislative signs, it is clear: one says, "Why did Allah obligate such-and-such? Why did He forbid such-and-such?" and the like.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, the intended meaning is contentious disputation aimed at overcoming the other, but disputation aimed at establishing the truth is obligatory. Even His saying in the Hajj, ﴿there is no obscenity, nor wrongdoing, nor quarreling﴾ [al-Baqarah 197]: that is the quarreling that is meant to contend with fools or is without benefit. As for establishing the truth, it is indispensable.

* Student: Is it obligatory in (...)?

* Shaykh: Yes, it is obligatory for one who argues to establish the truth that his intention be the elevation of the word of Allah.

* Student: If some showing-off mixes with it, does this invalidate it?

* Shaykh: It invalidates it. But a person must repel showing-off, or intend by it to prevail over this enemy who argues with falsehood; this is not objectionable.

* Student: Did we say that His saying ﴿min shay'in﴾ is extra?

* Shaykh: No, we moved away from that. We said: ﴿fa-ma uwititum min shay'in﴾ — we said at first it is explanatory, but it became clear that (ma) is not negating; rather it is extra for generality of negation, i.e., whatever thing you have been given, it is the enjoyment of the worldly life.

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, regarding His saying, glorified and exalted: ﴿and He spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura 28], you explained for us that His mercy is the rain?

* Shaykh: The author explained it.

* Student: So is it said that it is a time of supplication, supplication when rain falls because it is mercy?

* Shaykh: We mentioned that the author's statement is deficient; the intended meaning of spreading mercy is the effects that result from rain. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to encompass us and you with His mercy, and to grant us and you success in what He loves and approves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 37:

The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm) and the abominations﴾ [ash-Shura 37]. He stated explicitly that it is conjoined to what precedes it (ma'tuf 'alayhi), lest one who is doubtful suppose that the waw here is for resumption (isti'naf). On this basis, it is conjunction of attributes ('atf al-sifat), not conjunction of entities ('atf al-a'yan). Thus, "those who answered their Lord" are "those who believed and upon their Lord they rely."

Is there a parallel to this, i.e., the conjunction of attributes to a single described entity?

The answer: Many. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High (1), who created and proportioned (2), and who destined and guided (3), and who brought forth the pasture﴾ [al-A'la 1-4]. His saying "and who destined and guided" is not something other than the first, but rather it is the first, so this is from the category of conjunction of attributes, not entities.

If you say: "Zayd, 'Amr, Bakr and Khalid came," this is conjunction of entities, because the second is other than the first. And if you say: "Zayd the virtuous, the generous and the brave came," this is conjunction of attributes, because the second is the first, but the attribute differs.

So conjunction is of two kinds: conjunction of entities and conjunction of attributes. In the verses before us: ﴿those who avoid the major sins of wrongdoing and the abominations﴾ [ash-Shura 37], this is conjunction of attributes, because those who avoid the major sins of wrongdoing and the abominations are those who believed and upon their Lord they rely.

﴿kaba'ir al-ithm wa'l-fawahish﴾: kaba'ir is the plural of kabirah (major sin). So what is the kabirah? The answer: whatever the Shari'ah has declared to be a major sin is a major sin, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Bakrah: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents." He had been reclining, then he sat up and said: "Beware, and false speech, beware, and false testimony" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5977) and Muslim (88/144) from the hadith of Anas]. Here it is explicitly stated to be a major sin. As for what the Shari'ah has not explicitly stated, the scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, have differed concerning the definition of the major sin. The closest to correct is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, chose, when he said: The major sin is that for which a specific punishment is prescribed, meaning that which is singled out with a specific punishment.

This is because the prohibited matters divide into two categories:

One category in which there is a prohibition, or forbiddance, or the like, but no punishment is mentioned for it; and another category in which a punishment is mentioned. So he says: whatever has a specific punishment mentioned for it is a major sin.

If a curse is prescribed for a sin, as in his saying: "Allah curses the one who curses his parents" [Muslim (1978/44) from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib], what is it? A major sin, because a specific punishment is prescribed for it, namely the curse. If wrath (sakhat) is prescribed for it, it is a major sin, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the woman whose husband spends the night angry with her: "Verily Allah is angry with her" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5194) and Muslim (1436/120) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, with similar wording]. This is a major sin. If it is said: "He is not of us who tears garments, slaps cheeks, and calls with the call of the Jahiliyyah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1294) and Muslim (103/165) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud], then it is a major sin. What is prescribed for it? Disassociation from it: "He is not of us." "Whoever cheats is not of us" [Muslim (102) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], likewise a major sin, because a specific punishment is prescribed for it. "He does not believe whose neighbour is not safe from his evil" [Muslim (46/73) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah] is a major sin, because the negation of faith is prescribed for it.

So is the major sin limited or enumerated? Limited: it is known by definition, not by counting. And the best of what has been said about it is what Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, chose: that the major sin is that for which a specific punishment is prescribed.

As for His saying: ﴿wa'l-fawahish﴾, in the accusative, it is conjoined to kaba'ir, meaning: and they avoid the abominations. He said: (They are the matters that entail the prescribed penalties (hudud), conjunction of part to whole). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, explained the fawahish as those matters which entail a hadd, so let us enumerate them: Fornication (zina) is an abomination, and by the text of the Qur'an: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is ever an abomination﴾ [al-Isra' 32].

Marriage to those within the prohibited degrees (dhawat al-mahram) is an abomination, by the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already occurred; indeed, it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way﴾ [an-Nisa' 22]. Now consider: which is greater, marrying those within the prohibited degrees or fornication? The former, because Allah said of it: ﴿it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way﴾. Of fornication He said: ﴿indeed, it was an abomination and hatred and an evil way﴾. Therefore the more correct view is that if a person commits fornication with his mahram, he must be stoned, whether he is married (muhsan) or not.

Now, is theft an abomination or not? It is an abomination; the author said: everything that has a hadd is an abomination.

Highway robbery (qat' at-tariq) is an abomination, because it carries a hadd.

Is wine-drinking an abomination? Does it carry a hadd? The correct view is that the punishment for wine is not a hadd but a ta'zir (discretionary punishment), yet it is not less than forty. The evidence that it is a punishment is that the drinker in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him, was brought and the people struck him: whoever struck with his hand, whoever with his garment, and whoever with his sandal, without a fixed limit. Then Abu Bakr made it forty, then Umar made it forty, then wine-drinking increased and Umar increased it to eighty after consulting the Companions. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I think you should make it like the lightest of the hadd penalties." What is the lightest of the hadd penalties? The hadd for qadhf (false accusation) is eighty. So Umar made it eighty, and this is like a consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that the punishment of the wine-drinker is not a hadd. For if it were a hadd, could anyone add to it? No. And so, if fornication became widespread among people, we would not exceed one hundred lashes.

Moreover, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "Make it like the lightest of the hadd penalties," which indicates it is not a hadd, otherwise it would not be correct to say "like the lightest of the hadd penalties." Also, if he is repeatedly flogged, in the fourth instance he is killed according to many scholars, because of what has come in the Sunan: "If he drinks, flog him; then if he drinks, flog him; then if he drinks, flog him; then if he drinks a fourth time, kill him." This hadith is sahih, and the people of the outward meaning (ahl al-zahir) adopted it, but most scholars say he is not killed even if he drinks a thousand times and is flogged a thousand times. Shaykh al-Islam chose a middle position and said: if people do not desist without killing, he is killed, so that wine-drinking does not multiply; but if people desist without killing, he is not killed.

The main point: the author, may Allah have mercy on him, holds that the fawahish are those matters entailing the hadd. He said: (and it is conjunction of part to whole), because the abominations are part of the major sins of wrongdoing. This occurs often: conjunction of part to whole, and sometimes conjunction of whole to part. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr 4] is conjunction of part to whole. If you say: "Honour Zayd and the students," and he is among them, this is conjunction of whole to part. Singling out some individuals by making them conjoined or the one conjoined to indicates care and concern for them.

﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾ [ash-Shura 37]. (ma) here is superfluous (za'idah) in terms of i'rab, while in meaning it is for emphasis. I say:

O seeker, take this benefit: (ma) after (idha) is superfluous.
Will you accept it, or not accept it? That is: whenever (ma) comes after (idha), it is superfluous, as in this verse: ﴿And when they are angered﴾, meaning: and when they are angered. And like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when they come to it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them﴾ [Fussilat 20], meaning: until when they come to it. So take this benefit. And (ma) is among the most broad of particles in meaning, for it has ten or more meanings, gathered in the saying of the poet:

Its carriers are ten, if you wish to count them, so guard a sound line free from poetic defect. You will understand the condition of conjunction, so marvel at its denial and its ... [the text of the verse as cited]

Quickly:
("you will understand") refers to interrogative (ma).
("condition") refers to conditional (ma).
("conjunction") refers to relative (ma).
("marvel") refers to exclamatory (ma), as in saying: "How good is Zayd!"
("its denial") refers to indefinite (ma), either described or describing.
("kaff") refers to the restrictive (ma) that attaches to inna, like: ﴿Indeed, Allah is but one God﴾ [an-Nisa' 171].
("denial") refers to negative (ma).
("increase") refers to superfluous (ma).
("magnification") refers to magnifying (ma), like: ﴿The Inevitable Reality (1) what is the Inevitable Reality﴾ [al-Haqqah 1-2], and ﴿The Striking Calamity (1) what is the Striking Calamity﴾ [al-Qari'ah 1-2].
("verbal noun") refers to the verbal (ma), like: "What you did pleases me," i.e., your doing pleases me.

These are ten meanings of (ma).

﴿when they are angered, they forgive﴾: meaning, when anger overtakes them, they master themselves and forgive whoever angered them. The commentator said the meaning of (yaghfirun) is (they overlook), and we add something else: concealment, meaning they overlook the one who wronged them and conceal it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: that among the attributes of those who believed and upon their Lord rely is their avoidance of the major sins of wrongdoing and the abominations, and their distance from them, because (ijtanaba) means one is on one side and another on the other side, which conveys their distance from major sins and abominations.

* Among its benefits: minor sins do not diminish the perfection of faith. Why? Because they are forgiven when major sins are avoided, as Allah, blessed and exalted, said in Surat an-Najm: ﴿except for the minor faults (al-lamam)﴾ [an-Najm 32], meaning, except minor sins, which do no harm. And the Prophet (ﷺ) informed that "the five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations for what is between them, if the major sins are avoided" [Muslim (233/16) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

But if someone asks: does persistence in minor sins turn them into major sins?

The answer: Yes, this is well known among the scholars: persistence in a minor sin is a major sin. But they do not say that the minor sin becomes a major sin; they say that a person's persistence in disobedience indicates his contempt for the Shari'ah of Allah and his indifference to it, and therefore persistence becomes a major sin, not that the minor sin transforms into a major one, but because persistence indicates contempt for the Shari'ah of Allah, it becomes a major sin on account of that contempt.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among the attributes of those who believed and upon their Lord rely is that when they are angered, they forgive. The Prophet (ﷺ) described anger as a live coal that Satan casts into a person's heart, so that his blood boils and his veins swell. As for the theologians, they say: anger is the boiling of the blood of the heart out of love for revenge. What the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned is better: that it is "a live coal cast by Satan" [al-Tirmidhi (2191), Ahmad (11143), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (8754) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri]. Therefore you find a man, when angry, acts in a bad manner that he himself does not praise once his anger has subsided.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person should, when angry, restrain his rage. One of the Companions asked the Prophet (ﷺ) to advise him, and he said: "Do not become angry," and he repeated it several times, and he said: "Do not become angry" [al-Bukhari (6116) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿And those who avoid the major sins of wrongdoing and the abominations, and when they are angered, they forgive﴾ [ash-Shura 37]. What is the difference between the major sins of wrongdoing and the abominations?

* Student: What is below that.

* The Shaykh: What is below that, but they are above the minor sins. Those for which a hadd is prescribed, what are they?

* Student: Highway robbery.

* The Shaykh: Highway robbery.

* Student: Fornication.

* The Shaykh: Fornication.

* Student: Theft.

* The Shaykh: Theft.

* Student: Qadhf.

* The Shaykh: Qadhf. Now, is wine-drinking a hadd or a ta'zir? The correct view is that it is a ta'zir, but a ta'zir not less than forty lashes. What is the evidence that it is a ta'zir and not a hadd, although the majority of scholars hold it is a hadd? That when people's drinking of wine increased in the time of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, he consulted the Companions, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: make it eighty, like the lightest of the hadd penalties. This is a clear proof, nearly a consensus of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, under the leadership of the rightly-guided Caliph Umar, that it is not a hadd, for two reasons: first, he said: make it like the lightest of the hadd penalties; second, if it were a hadd, it would not be permissible for Umar or anyone else to add to it.

The saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾. What is the i'rab of (ma)?

* Student: A relative noun.

* The Shaykh: A relative noun? No, that is wrong.

* Student: Superfluous.

* The Shaykh: (Ma) is superfluous. Recite for me the rajaz verse mentioned about it.

* Student:

O seeker, take this benefit: (ma) after (idha) is superfluous.

* The Shaykh: You have understood. Whenever (ma) comes after (idha), it is superfluous. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿until, when they come to it, their hearing and their sight testify against them﴾ [Fussilat 20].
﴿And when they are angered, they forgive﴾.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And those who answer their Lord⌉ The waw is a conjunction particle. Does "alladhina" (those who) stand in apposition to what preceded it, by way of referring to the same persons, or is it a description? It is a description: ﴿And those who answer their Lord﴾. The commentator (al-Mufassir) said: (They responded to Him in what He called them to, of tawhid and worship). "Istajabu li-rabbihim" means "ajabuhu" (they answered Him). We have already mentioned examples of istajaba meaning ajaba.

His saying "(of tawhid and worship)" is an acceptable explanation. Yet if he, may Allah have mercy on him, had said: ﴿istajabu li-rabbihim﴾, meaning they answered Him in all that He called them to, of doing the commands and abstaining from the prohibitions, it would have been clearer and more comprehensive. ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ is conjoined to (istajabu), so it falls within the relative clause (silat al-mawsul).

﴿Establish the prayer﴾: The author said: (They maintained it), and this is open to question. Rather, the meaning of ﴿aqamu al-salat﴾ is that they performed it upright, in the manner that was required of them, because there is a difference between establishing the prayer (iqamat al-salat) and persisting in the prayer (idamat al-salat). Certainly persistence is part of establishing it, without doubt, but establishing is not the same as persisting. So "establishing" means bringing the prayer in its proper, upright form, in the manner required: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾. His saying ﴿al-salat﴾ includes both the obligatory and the voluntary prayer.

﴿And their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾: "Amruhum" means their matter, and what is meant is the general affair, not a private matter: the general affair that concerns everyone, which they consult about, and "consulting about it" means exchanging opinions, whether to advance or hold back, whether to change or leave things as they are. The point is that consultation (mushawara) is the exchange of opinions in order to reach a result acceptable to all.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ (they consult one another about it and do not hasten). ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾: "min" here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and it may be for kind (lil-jins). If it is partitive, the praise is for the one who spends part of his wealth; if we say it is for kind, the praise is for the one who spends all or part of his wealth. Which is preferable: that we say partitive or kind? Kind is preferable, to include the little, the much and the whole.

﴿And from what We have provided them﴾: he said: (We gave them). ﴿They spend﴾ in obedience to Allah.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the characteristics of the believers who rely upon Allah is that they respond to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; that is, they answer Him in what He has asked of them. Its meaning is hastening and not delaying, because delay in carrying out an obligation is a deficiency in responding. I will give you an example: a man ordered his son to bring him something, and the son delayed and remained an hour or two, then brought it. Would it be said that the son complied in full compliance? No. Full compliance is through prompt action, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿those who answer their Lord﴾ [al-Shura 38].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the emphasis on establishing the prayer. The reason is that Allah specified it after the general statement, since His saying ﴿istajabu li-rabbihim﴾ [al-Shura 38] includes the prayer and other things. When He said ﴿and establish the prayer﴾ He singled it out by name, and this is evidence of its importance. It is indeed right, by Allah, that it be given attention, because there is no act of worship more closely connecting you with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than the prayer. Is that not so? A person gives charity but does not feel the connection between himself and his Lord; he fasts, he performs Hajj, but the true, legislated prayer is that a person feels he is in a connection between himself and Allah. For this reason it is called salat, because it is a connection (silah) between the human being and Allah. "When a person says: Praise be to Allah, Allah says: My servant has praised Me" [Narrated by Muslim (395/38) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and so is this dialogue. Then he feels that when he bows there is above him a Lord whom he exalts, and when he prostrates he places his most noble limb upon the place of the feet. For this reason the attention to the prayer is such that He said: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾.

Where was the prayer made obligatory? The prayer was made obligatory on the night of the Mi'raj, from Allah to the Messenger, directly or through an intermediary? Without an intermediary. This shows its importance and the attention given to it. Then it was made obligatory as fifty prayers, and Allah lightened it for the servants, making it five prayers, yet in reality it is fifty prayers. That means that when you pray one obligatory prayer, it is as though you prayed ten. This is not because a good deed is rewarded tenfold, since that applies to all good deeds; rather, it is as though you prayed the Dhuhr, for example, ten times: you pray and give salam, pray and give salam, until you reach ten. By this the difference between it and the other acts of worship becomes evident: the reward of a good deed is ten times its like, but this one is as though you had actually prayed fifty prayers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: observing social circumstances, and that general matters must be subjected to consultation; because of His saying: ﴿and their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura 38].

Does the verse indicate that when a person wishes to do an act specific to himself, he must consult? No, it does not indicate this, but consultation is legislated. If something becomes unclear to you, you have two things: istikhara and consultation. But for a general matter, consultation is necessary. An exception is made when the matter becomes clear to the ruler (waliyy al-amr); then there is no need to consult about it. That is, if the benefit becomes clear to the amir, the leader or the king regarding something he wants, there is no need for consultation, because consultation is resorted to when? When there is confusion and hesitation. But when the benefit is evident, there is no need to consult, why? Because consultation at that point only increases the matter in confusion and chaos, since people are not of one opinion. If you want a matter to be torn apart, place it before ten; and if you want it to dissolve entirely, place it before twenty. People must differ.

So is ﴿and their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura 38] general in its scope, or is an exception made from it? An exception is made: whatever its benefit has become evident to the ruler, there is no need for him to consult. The practice of the righteous predecessors supports this exception. Here is 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who was among the most attentive of the caliphs to his subjects: he did not consult when the benefit was clear to him, but consulted only when the matter was unclear to him. If you counted what he consulted about, it would not reach more than tens or fewer, and he remained ten years in the caliphate. This practice of the rightly guided caliphs restricts His saying: ﴿and their affair is by consultation among themselves﴾ [al-Shura 38]. So what is excepted?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: So there is no need for consultation, because consultation in such a case is harmful to carrying out and proceeding with the matter.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the characteristics of those who believe and rely upon their Lord is spending wealth in obedience to Allah; by His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [al-Shura 38].

Is a person required to spend all his wealth? This depends on "min": whether it is partitive or for kind. If we say partitive, the praise is for the one who spends part of his wealth; if we say for kind, meaning that they spend from this kind which Allah has provided them, it becomes general. The detail is the foundation, if Allah wills. If a person does not reduce his spending on the obligations toward his family at all, there is no harm in his spending all his wealth, such as when a person has one hundred riyals that he does not need for spending on his family and has nothing else; we say here: spend all the wealth, then earn for spending on your family, as Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, did. But if he needs the wealth for the obligatory spending on his family and he is weak in earning, then here we say: do not spend all your wealth; keep back some of your wealth, for it is better for you.

* A student: The consultation (...) the benefit may appear to him in something when there is no benefit in it.

* The Shaykh: He is trustworthy; the principle is that he is trustworthy. If he wishes to betray, he prevents consultation even if he needs it.

* The student: Good, Shaykh, if his betrayal becomes evident (...) it has become clear to him that (...).

* The Shaykh: We do not concern ourselves with him in this matter, because if we said that the ruler must consult in everything, it would be a problem and the situation could not be set right. It would mean that if he writes to the police, "Imprison so-and-so, because he did wrong," we would say: come on, gather the people and consult.

* The student: There are specific people.

* The Shaykh: That is not the point. Specific by their persons; it does not mean that everyone is to be summoned. Consultation has come; do we say that every matter concerning the public must be consulted upon? That is impossible. As I have just said, we showed you that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the caliphs who consulted most, yet his consultations can nearly be counted. This is necessary, otherwise the matter could not be set right.

* A student: May Allah be good to you, Shaykh. If a person is confused about something, does he begin with istikhara or with istishara?

* The Shaykh: A good question. If a person is confused about something, does he begin with istikhara or istishara? We say he begins with istikhara, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: "When one of you intends a matter, let him pray two rak'ahs" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6382) from the hadith of Jabir]. "Hamma" means that concern for it befalls him and he hesitates and doubts. His intention is not that every matter you intend means praying two rak'ahs. "When one of you intends a matter": if a person intends to have lunch, does he pray two rak'ahs to seek guidance? No. So "when one of you intends a matter" means when the matter weighs on him and nothing has become clear to him, then let him pray two rak'ahs. We say: begin first with istikhara, for two reasons:

First: it is the apparent meaning of the hadith.

Second: that you return to Allah is better than that you return to the opinions of people. So we begin with istikhara before istishara.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those who, when tyranny afflicts them, defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura 39]. The "و" (wa) is a conjunction particle, and what is conjoined here is taken in terms of attributes: meaning, among their attributes is that when someone oppresses them, they defend themselves. ﴿When tyranny afflicts them﴾ means aggression from someone against them. ﴿They defend themselves﴾: defend themselves against whom? Themselves. They do not show themselves in the guise of the weak and humiliated; rather, they defend their own selves. Defending oneself in a position of dignity is a required matter, whereas in a position of humility, that is something else, which will come, God willing, in the future.

He says: (﴿They defend themselves﴾ is a category). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that those who believe and rely upon their Lord are two categories. However, the correct view is that all of this is a description of one described subject, and there are no categories. Accordingly, we say: among the attributes of those who believe and rely upon their Lord is that they defend themselves when wronged (i.e., they retaliate against those who wronged them with the same kind of wrong), without transgression. Moreover, His saying ﴿they defend themselves﴾ does not necessarily mean that they take their rights to the full extent; rather, when they defend themselves, they may pardon, and if they pardon while being able to retaliate, that is more perfect.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that among the attributes of those who believe and rely upon their Lord is that they do not accept humiliation or shrinking from taking their rights; by His saying: ﴿those who, when tyranny afflicts them, defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura 39]. Does defending oneself necessarily entail exacting retribution, or having the upper hand, whether by retaliation, by pardon, or otherwise? The apparent view is the second, because it is more general; for whoever pardons from a position of power and dignity is undoubtedly one who defends himself, and whoever takes his right is one who defends himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that these people defend themselves only when aggression against them is established; as for mere suspicion, they do not act upon it. This is derived from His saying: ﴿when tyranny afflicts them﴾. So if they suspect someone of wronging them, they do not move; but when aggression actually afflicts them, then they defend themselves.

* Among the benefits in this verse: that whoever defends himself when aggression afflicts him is obligated not to exceed the limit in exacting his right.

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ (The second is called an evil because it resembles the first in form, and this is clear in cases of retaliation for wounds. Some of them said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he replies, "May Allah disgrace you.").

His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. This is in reality a principle: a person may avenge himself for an evil done to him with its like, and no more, for if he exceeds it he has wronged. Excess may be in quantity, in quality, or in kind. So if he retaliates against the one who wronged him by striking him three times when he had wronged him with two, that is excess in quantity; if he is struck lightly and retaliates with a heavy blow, that is excess in quality; if he is attacked with a weak whip and retaliates with a larger whip, that is excess in kind. The point is that the requital must be with the same evil by which he was harmed, and no more. If he exceeds, he is a wrongdoer, and for this it is said: "This for this, and the one who begins is the greater wrongdoer."

The author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him: (The second is called an evil because it resembles the first in form) is clearly open to objection. Retaliation is an evil, but it is not an evil with respect to the one who carries it out; rather it is an evil with respect to the one against whom it is carried out, who is grieved, pained, and whose standing is diminished if he considered himself above his opponent. So it is evil not in terms of the agent but in terms of the one retaliated against. As for his saying that it resembles the first, it cannot be applied as "evil" merely because of resemblance or mere similarity: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

In fact, this is a principle for all retaliation. Consider: if someone tears your garment, may you tear his garment? The apparent meaning of the verse is yes. But if your garment is poor and worth ten, and his garment is good and worth a hundred, should you tear his garment or not? If you tear it and it loses a tenth of its value, how much is that? It loses a tenth. For instance, this garment is worth ten riyals; the aggressor tore it with a tear that lowers its value by a tenth. A tenth of ten is how much? One.

His garment is worth a hundred, and you tore it with a tear equal to a tenth; how much does it lose?
* Students: Ten.
* Shaykh: Ten. Now you have taken ten in return for one. Shall we say the consideration is the meaning: when he tore your garment he humiliated you, and if you retaliate and tear his garment you humiliate him, since he was the aggressor, so we tear his garment even if it is more expensive? Or shall we say: we tear his garment if it is equal to the first or close to it, and otherwise not? Yes. Because the one whose garment is worth ten has his standing broken just as the one whose garment is worth a hundred does; the aim is to humiliate the aggressor and break his standing. On this basis we say: whoever tears your garment, tear his garment.

And is the consideration the area or the proportion? Here is a short man... or did you not understand the question? Here is a short man who tore his garment by the length of a span. That span equals, say, a tenth of his garment, and the other is very tall and tore his garment by the length of a span. Is that equal in proportion to the first? It is not equal. So we now ask: is the consideration the area or the proportion? Justice requires that the consideration be proportion. If the short man's garment has a half-area of one cubit torn, and the tall man's garment is torn by an area of one cubit, but he is twice the height of the first, is that sufficient or not? It is not sufficient. We say: tear until the proportion is reached; if it is a tenth, then a tenth. Because this is the true justice: the aggressor spoiled a tenth of the victim's garment, so let him spoil a tenth of his garment, even though he is the aggressor. This applies exactly to the saying of Allah: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

A man said to someone in anger: "You are a donkey." Should he say to him: "You are the donkey"?
* A student: He should not say it.
* Shaykh: No, he may say it. How should he not say it? But should he say: "You are a donkey and your father is a donkey"?
Answer: No, that is aggression. But he may say: "You are a donkey."

If he says to him, "May Allah curse you," should he say, "Rather, may He curse you"? You have the Book of Allah: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. He may say this. Therefore, if a person curses someone who did not deserve it, where does the curse go? It returns to the first, and he is punished with what he did.

Listen to the author's words: (and this is clear in cases of retaliation for wounds). This is clear: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]. Retaliation for wounds applies to every organ that is independent in itself, and every wound that reaches bone. Retaliation applies there: every independent organ such as the eye, the finger, and the like. If a man cuts off your little finger, you cut off his little finger; this is clear. Or a wound that reaches bone: if he wounds his head until the skull bone is exposed, is retaliation applied or not? If he wounds his leg until the bone is exposed, retaliation applies, even if the layer of flesh over the bone in the offender is thicker. Retaliation applies until it reaches the bone. If the wound does not reach the bone, as when he wounds his thigh in a way that does not reach the bone, is retaliation applied to him?

The jurists say: retaliation is not applied, because retaliation cannot be controlled precisely; it is only controlled when it reaches the bone. But in view of the progress of medicine, we say: if it is possible to apply retaliation, it is applied.

If he cuts off his hand from mid-forearm, is retaliation applied or not?

The jurists say: retaliation is not applied, for lack of precision. But if it is at the joint, as when he cuts off the hand at its joint, retaliation is applied. The sound view in the first case, when he cuts off the hand from mid-forearm, is that if retaliation is possible, it is applied. In our age, is it possible or not? It is possible to within a hair's breadth or less than a hair. If it is not possible, and the injured person says: "Cut off his hand, and I will forgo what is cut off beyond it," or the injured person says: "Cut the offender's hand, and I forgo the excess," is retaliation applied or not? The sound view is that it is applied: the offender's hand is cut off, and if the injured person waives the excess, it is dropped.

If the injured person says: "I want you to cut his hand and I take the compensation for the excess," he may do so, because Allah says: ﴿And wounds carry retaliation﴾ [al-Ma'ida 45], and here He says: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]. This is clear in cases of retaliation for wounds, which is every independent organ or a wound that reaches bone. The rest is a matter of disagreement. Some of them, meaning some scholars, said: if he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," he replies, "May Allah disgrace you," based on His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40].

If he says, "May Allah curse your father," what do you say? Do you say to him, "May Allah curse your father"? No. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah curses the one who curses his parents." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, does a man curse his parents?" He said: "Yes: he insults the father of a man, so he insults his father, and he insults his mother, so he insults his mother."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (5973) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]] What does this indicate?
* Students: That it is impermissible.
* Shaykh: It is impermissible. How is it impermissible? We say: the Messenger's statement ﷺ here explains the reality, not the legal ruling. The custom in insulting among people is that when a man insults another's father, he insults his father. This is something you know; if you do not know it, learn it: go to the markets and observe the insults between people. If he insults his father, he insults his father. Is that clear or not? So the Messenger's statement is an explanation of reality, and explaining reality does not confer legal permissibility. The proof that explaining reality does not confer permissibility is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you," meaning the Jews and Christians.[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (7320) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] Are we to follow the Jews and Christians? No; that was stated to explain reality.

Likewise, he informed that a woman travels from such-and-such a place to such-and-such a place alone; this is to explain reality, not to state a legal ruling.

If someone asks: what led you to make his saying ﷺ, "He insults the father of a man, so he insults his father, and he insults his mother, so he insults his mother,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5973) and Muslim (90/146) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As.]] to be an explanation of reality and not a legal ruling?

I say: what led me to this is that it is not permissible to aggress against anyone who has not aggressed. This is wrongdoing: how would I insult his father? This is undoubtedly wrongdoing, and the Law does not permit wrongdoing. But if someone says: when a person's parents are cursed, the one whose parents were cursed will not be content unless the parents of the other are cursed, since cursing parents humiliates the child and he wants to console himself, we say: praise be to Allah; there is no necessity. If your parents are cursed, curse him yourself, and this is even more humiliating.

The conclusion is: if he curses your father and mother, do not curse his father and mother, for they have done nothing wrong. As for the hadith, you know the answer: it explains reality, not the legal ruling. But you may turn the insult and curse onto the doer himself, not onto his parents.

(...) A questioner asks: does the killer get killed with the same means he used to kill, or with the sword?

The answer: he is killed with the same means he used, because "the Prophet ﷺ crushed the head of the Jew between two stones, because he had crushed the head of a girl between two stones."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2413) and Muslim (1672/15) from the hadith of Anas.]] And the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqara 194]. However, the scholars excepted the case where the means is itself forbidden in essence; then retaliation is not applied. They said: if a man sodomized a small child, knowing that this act would kill him, and the child died because of it, do we subject that man to the same? No, we do not; some scholars said: we do not do that, and this is known, because sodomy is forbidden in its essence. But we insert a stick into his rectum until he dies. This has a point of view, but in my opinion there is an objection to it, because the stick is more painful than sodomy, so retaliation is not possible.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]. On what did the author base the second evil? On its resemblance to the first in wording, yes, by way of parallelism. Now, is his statement correct or not?
* A student: It is not correct.
* Shaykh: It is not correct. How so?
* The student: The correct view is that the resemblance is in harm, because the one retaliated against is harmed; when he is retaliated against, it grieves him.
* Shaykh: So then it is an evil with respect to whom? With respect to the one retaliated against. And keeping the wording on its apparent meaning is better than distorting it without evidence.

Allah says: ﴿But whoever forgoes and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ [al-Shura 40]. (Whoever) here is conditional; the verb of the condition is (forgoes), and the coordinated clause ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾ is the response of the condition. Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿whoever forgoes﴾, that is: does not take him to account for the sin, meaning for the one who wronged him; ﴿and makes reconciliation﴾, he says: (the affection between him and the one forgiven). ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾, that is, Allah will certainly reward him.

His saying: ﴿whoever forgoes﴾. The author said: (against the one who wronged him). This is clear: forgoing means not calling him to account. ﴿and makes reconciliation﴾, he says: (the affection between him and the one who wronged him). This is a very limited explanation. Rather, the meaning is: he made reconciliation in his forgoing, that is, his forgoing became something including reform.

We said this because what we mentioned is more general and more beneficial for the meaning.

So the author takes ﴿makes reconciliation﴾ as restricted to restoring affection between him and the one who wronged him, whereas the correct view is that the meaning is: he made reconciliation in his forgoing, that is, his forgoing was a reform.

As for ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾, the author says: (that is, Allah will certainly reward him). "Reward" here means recompense. Allah called the recompense a reward because it is in return for an act, like the wage of a laborer when he does his work. It also hints that this reward is obligatory, just as paying a laborer his wage is obligatory. The author's statement, "that is, Allah will certainly reward him," derives the meaning "certainly" from the nominal form of the sentence, because a nominal sentence conveys establishment and continuity.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: ﴿And the recompense for an evil﴾ shows that retaliation must be carried out with justice, so that the recompense for an evil is an evil like it. It is not permitted to exceed in retaliation, whether verbal or physical. Consider: if a man insults you with two descriptions and you insult him with three, what do you say? Is it permitted or not? Because Allah says specifically: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40].

If a man cut off a person's hand and asked for retaliation, and the offender said: "I want to put anesthetic in my hand so I do not feel the pain," and the injured person said: "No," whose word is accepted? The word of the injured person, because the offender brought two harms: the pain and the loss of the organ. Retaliation is not complete unless both of these occur to the offender.

If a thief is sentenced to hand amputation and asks that his hand be anesthetized, is this permitted or not? It is permitted, because the aim with respect to the thief is to destroy the transgressing hand, and that is achieved; there is no retaliation here, so we cannot say the like must be matched with the like.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the confirmation that retaliation must be just, from His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura 40]; He confirmed it with His saying: ﴿like it﴾. If the injured person wants to take part of his right, is that permitted or not? The verse says: ﴿like it﴾.
* A student: ﴿But whoever forgoes and makes reconciliation﴾.
* Shaykh: We have not reached "forgoes and makes reconciliation." The meaning is: if we want justice, this is it; and if a person forgoes his own right, there is no harm, just as there is no blame on him if he forgoes entirely.
* Among the benefits of His saying: ﴿But whoever forgoes and makes reconciliation﴾ to the end, is the encouragement of forgiveness when it is reform. If it is not reform, then taking the firm course is better. The evidence for this is that Allah said: ﴿But whoever forgoes and makes reconciliation﴾.

From this follows an important issue: if the offender is known for evil and corruption and he attacks a person, do we say that it is better to forgive him?
The answer: no, we do not say that; rather, we stipulate that it must be reform. If this evil man, known for wickedness, harms a person, do we say to the injured person: forgive him, and your reward is with Allah? No, we do not say this; because if we forgive this wicked man in this particular case, he will do the same or worse afterward, since he took forgiveness as encouragement, and he would be expected to be forgiven for every act. If the offender is wicked and known for corruption and harms someone, do we say it is better for you to forgive him or to take your right? We have mentioned that in this case it is better to take your right, because if you forgive this wicked man, who is disposed to evil, now, he will go on the next day and do something worse. We must know that the unrestricted verse of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿And that you forgive is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Baqara 237] is restricted by this verse; indeed, every text that encourages forgiveness is restricted by this verse.

So forgiveness must be reform. Pay attention to this.

If someone strikes a person while driving a car, and the person dies, is it better for the heirs of the slain to forgo the blood money or to take the blood money?

There is detail: if this man is known for recklessness and carelessness, and as some foolish people say: "the blood money is on the tablet" (i.e., the blood money is set by the license plate or the car's insurance), then he should not be forgiven. But if he is a man of honor, and we know this happened to him as the common people say, "a lapse of attention," then it is better to forgive him. This verse is the criterion for praiseworthy and unpraiseworthy forgiveness.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the grace of Allah, blessed and exalted, toward His servants, in that He made it obligatory upon Himself to reward the one who forgives. From where is this taken? ﴿his reward is with Allah﴾. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, guaranteed the forgiving person a reward, but on the condition that it be reform.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 40 (part 2 of 2):

He said: (﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Shura 40], meaning: those who initiate wrongdoing, so that His punishment is incurred upon them.) His words, ﴿Indeed, He does not love﴾: the pronoun refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. ﴿He does not love the wrongdoers﴾ means the transgressors, whether they wrong themselves or wrong others. The one who commits sins is not beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the one who transgresses against the servants of Allah is not beloved to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for the author's statement, may Allah have mercy on him, (meaning: those who initiate wrongdoing), it is open to question. The verse is general, encompassing those who initiate wrongdoing and those who wrong in retaliation. The meaning is that the one who initiates wrongdoing is not beloved to Allah, and likewise the one who exceeds the limit in his right is not beloved to Allah. Therefore, leaving the verse on its general application is better, meaning: He does not love wrongdoers, whether by initiating wrongdoing or by retaliating.

* Student: He mentioned His words, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. Some scholars have stated that it is permissible for one whose property has been misappropriated by another to take an equivalent of it without the other's knowledge, citing the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement to Hind, the wife of Abu Sufyan, that she may take from his wealth what suffices her and her children.

* The Shaykh: The question says: some scholars have derived from the words of the Most High, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, that if a person denies you some property, you may take from his wealth an amount equal to what he denied, without his knowledge?

We say: Yes, this is the apparent meaning of the verse: if he took from your property and you are able to recover it from his property, then this is permitted for you. However, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you» [Abu Dawud (3534), al-Tirmidhi (1264), al-Darimi (2639)]. If this door were opened, affairs would be chaotic, each person taking from the property of another and saying, "He denied my property." This does not work out in practice. As for the case of Hind, its reason is clear: everyone knows that this is his wife and that he is obligated to provide maintenance. So if she took from his wealth without his knowledge and said, "He does not provide for me," people would not object, because the cause is evident. Similarly, if a guest stays with someone and is not offered hospitality, and he is able to take from that person's wealth an amount equal to his hospitality, then he may do so, because the cause is evident. In this way, the evidences are reconciled.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged — those, there is no blame upon them﴾ [al-Shura 41]. The lam in His saying ﴿And whoever﴾ is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), and (man) is a conditional noun of jazm (conditional particle), the verb of the condition is (intasara) (avenged himself), and its response is: ﴿those, there is no blame upon them﴾. ﴿And whoever avenges himself﴾ (meaning: takes his right for himself) ﴿after being wronged﴾ (i.e., after the wrongdoer wronged him).

Here we ask: (zulm) here is a verbal noun (masdar); is it added to the doer (agent) or to the object? The author's statement indicates that it is added to the object, i.e., "the wronging of the wrongdoer against him," and on this basis the verbal noun is added to its object, not to its agent. It cannot be added to its agent, because if it were, the meaning would be: "And whoever avenges himself after he wrongs people, those, there is no blame upon them." But the wrongdoer is not wronged until he avenges himself, so the verbal noun is added to the object: ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those, there is no blame upon them﴾.

It has already been mentioned that Allah the Exalted praised those who, when oppression befalls them, avenge themselves: ﴿those, there is no blame upon them﴾. He said (blame): (mu'akhadha, i.e., reproach or censure). The root meaning of al-sabil is "the way," i.e., there is no path for them to be blamed or censured.

We want one of you to parse His saying ﴿min sabil﴾: (min) is a superfluous (za'ida) preposition grammatically; (sabil) is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar) in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma at its end, its manifestation being prevented by the occupation of the position by the kasra of the superfluous preposition. The meaning: "those, there is upon them no way."

If someone asks: What is the benefit of the superfluous prepositions?
