They said to Fir'awn (Pharaoh): "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us and over Him who created us. So decide whatever you will decide. You can only decide concerning this worldly life" [Ta-Ha 72]. Allahu Akbar, Allahu Akbar! When faith enters the heart, do not ask about the resolve, determination, and strength. "You can only decide concerning this worldly life." And whoever does not die today will die tomorrow.

The point I am making is this: some people, when they see a situation in which evil prevails, become weak and withdraw. This is a mistake. Plunge into the midst of the people and support the truth. I did not join these people to agree with their falsehood. I will defend the truth that I believe in as much as I can. Furthermore, it is wise to divide the gathered people, meaning that they are taken one by one and each one is spoken to. It is said: "O so-and-so, what benefit do you get from this? This is a sin upon you. This is harm in this world and the Hereafter." This is what Quraysh did when they annulled the *Sahifa* (the document), those who had made a pact in it to boycott Banu Hashim. The story is well known. One of the opponents of this document would go to their chiefs, the chiefs who had signed it, and would come to them one by one and say such and such, until they fragmented. This is part of statecraft, because when you fragment a gathered group, what happens? Their strength disappears, their authority disappears, and you obtain good.

* Among its benefits also: people are divided into two types. One type: when a mercy from Allah reaches them, they rejoice in it with the joy of arrogance and insolence. The other type: when the mercy of Allah reaches them, they use it in obedience to Allah. This is derived from other verses as well.

* Among its lessons: a warning against rejoicing in the blessing of Allah when it is the joy of arrogance and insolence. As for the joy of gladness, happiness, and carrying out obedience to Allah, this is praiseworthy. Allah the Exalted said: "Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy, in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate" [Yunus 58].

* Among the lessons of this noble verse: whatever affliction befalls a person is due to his own deeds, as He says: "Because of what your hands have put forward" [Ash-Shura 48].

* Among its lessons: using a part to refer to the whole when that part has a great effect, as He says: "Because of what your hands have put forward."

* Among its lessons: a human being, insofar as he is a human, when an evil befalls him, disbelieves, meaning he despairs of the mercy of Allah that He would turn this evil away from him. As for the believer, he does not despair; rather he is patient and awaits relief, believing in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Know that victory comes with patience, that relief comes with distress, and that with hardship comes ease" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (2516) and Ahmad (2803), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas].

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: A hadith is related from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that a group came to him and stipulated that they would not pray the five daily prayers. He agreed to this and said: "Indeed, when they become Muslims, they will pray."

* Student: Some people make excuses for not performing all five daily prayers.

* Shaykh: They make excuses for what?

* Student: For performing them, meaning.

* Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: So does he leave the circle of disbelief if it is said to him: "Pray four prayers"?

* Shaykh: A hadith is related from the Prophet (peace be upon him) that a group came to him and stipulated that they would not pray the five daily prayers. He agreed to this and said: "Indeed, when they become Muslims, they will pray."

* Student: Some who write about *da'wah* (calling to Islam), O Shaykh, divide societies into categories. They say: the Meccan society, the Medinan society, the Abyssinian society, and they apply to each society verses that were revealed about the Companions in that situation (...) who had authority and a state.

* Shaykh: Without doubt, this is not (...) Abyssinian, Meccan, or Medinan. This is a general rule: the verses revealed, for example, in Makkah, apply to those who are like the people of Makkah, just as they were revealed about them. The consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

* Student: "Indeed, man is ungrateful" [Ash-Shura 48]?

* Shaykh: This is not an intensive form (*sigha mubalaghah*). This is an adjective of quality (*sifah mushabbahah*), meaning that disbelief is among his characteristics.

* Student: May Allah reward you well. Regarding the saying of the Exalted: "And when We..." (*wa-inna idha*). Someone says that when the first-person pronoun is used for plurality, with Allah the Exalted being the speaker, this is among the *mutashabih* (ambiguous) verses of the Qur'an, and it must be referred back to the *muhkam* (clear) verses. Is this correct, O Shaykh?

* Shaykh: No one said this except the Christians. Do you know the Christians? They say that Allah is the third of three. The evidence? They said: the Qur'an says: "Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder" [Al-Hijr 9], and "Indeed, We bring the dead to life" [Ya-Sin 12]. So Allah the Exalted used the plural pronoun in the legislative verses, "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder" [Al-Hijr 9], and in the cosmic verses, "Indeed, We bring the dead to life" [Ya-Sin 12]. Therefore Allah is plural! This is not in any doubt for the Muslims at all. The purpose is glorification, showing greatness, sovereignty, strength, and power (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verses 49–50:

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shura 49]. The sentence is declarative, and its predicate is placed first?

* A student: It indicates restriction (ḥaṣr).

* The Shaykh: Yes, restriction is intended, because the rhetorical rule is that placing before what should be delayed indicates restriction and exclusivity. So it is "to Allah" and not to other than Him. ﴿The dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ means creation and governance. Allah, the Exalted, is the Owner of the heavens and the earth in both creation and governance. For this reason He says: ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, and the words ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, here "mā" (ما) is a relative pronoun, and it is generally used for non-rational beings. The use of "mā" is to include both entities and attributes, since when attributes are intended, "mā" is used even for a rational being. Consider the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. He did not say "man ṭāba" (whoever is good), although women are rational beings, but since a woman is married for her attributes and not for her essence, He said ﴿marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. Here, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ [al-Shura 49]: we say that "mā" is used because what is intended is entities and attributes. As for entities, if we were asked: which is more numerous, the rational or the non-rational? On the earth, the non-rational; but in the heavens, no. The heavens are wider than the earth, and there is no place the size of four fingers in them without an angel in it. Taking everything together, the rational beings are more numerous. But considering what is on the earth, which is more numerous?

* A student: The non-rational.

* The Shaykh: The non-rational. Likewise, if we consider attributes, attributes include rational and non-rational beings, so "mā" is used. ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, that is, He brings it into existence after non-existence. But creation is not merely bringing into existence; it is creation according to a measure. ﴿He creates what He wills; He bestows on whom He wills﴾. This too is part of His creation. ﴿He bestows on whom He wills females﴾. Bestowal (hibah) is giving something freely as a gift. Allah, the Exalted, describes children as a gift because human beings have no power to bring them into existence; it is purely a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿He creates what He wills; He bestows on whom He wills﴾ (of children) ﴿females﴾. How does the phrase "of children" fit with ﴿females﴾? Because "awlād" (children) in the Arabic language includes males and females, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa 11]. ﴿He bestows on whom He wills females and He bestows on whom He wills males﴾. He did not say "dhukūran" (males) but used the definite article "al" (ال), which indicates the nobility of what it precedes, for males are considered more noble than females by people. Yet despite this, He compensated for their deficiency by mentioning them before the males. Or it may be said that Allah mentioned females first because a person's wish is for his children to be male, so mentioning females first is a sign that the matter rests with Allah alone, not with what a person wants and desires.

﴿Or He bestows on them males and females﴾ [al-Shura 49–50]. He said: (i.e., He makes them), but the correct gloss is "yuṣannifuhum" (He classifies them), because marriage here means classification, as Allah says: ﴿and other kinds of a similar sort﴾ [Sad 58], meaning kinds. So the meaning of ﴿yuzawwijuhum﴾ is that He classifies them, making them two kinds: ﴿males and females﴾, ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ (so he neither begets nor is begotten). He does not beget with respect to the female and is not begotten with respect to the male. These are four categories:

First: He bestows females on whom He wills.

Second: He bestows males.

Third: He bestows males and females.

Fourth: He makes a person barren, with neither males nor females.

This is because the matter belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and no one can create any of this. Rather, Allah alone is the Creator.

He says: ﴿And He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent﴾. ﴿Knowing﴾ (of what He creates), ﴿Competent﴾ over what He creates. He knows what He creates, Mighty and Majestic, and is capable of creating whatever He wills.

* In the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion over what is in the heavens and the earth, from His words ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the exclusivity of Allah, blessed and exalted, in this dominion. From where do we derive exclusivity?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Wrong, unless you did not understand the question. The question is: the exclusivity of Allah, the Exalted, in the dominion of the heavens and the earth?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The reasoning is that Allah placed the predicate first, and the predicate should be delayed, and placing what should be delayed indicates restriction.

If someone says: if you say the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusive to Allah, does a human being not have ownership? Allah says: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. So humans do have ownership. How can we reconcile our saying that the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusive to Allah with affirming ownership for other than Allah?

The answer: Allah's dominion, blessed and exalted, is complete and comprehensive. It encompasses comprehensiveness of disposal and comprehensiveness of place, meaning that Allah's dominion is complete in every respect and general in every respect. Human ownership is deficient, neither in the generality of place nor in the generality of disposal. We all own, but our ownership is limited. I own one bag and do not own another bag belonging to someone else, so it is limited.

Second: it is deficient. A deficient ownership, I cannot dispose of my property as I wish, correct? I cannot dispose of my property as I wish, correct? Correct. I cannot waste it, because I am forbidden to waste wealth. I cannot torture it if it is an animal, because I am forbidden from that. I cannot eat from my property whatever I wish and leave whatever I wish; an unlawful animal may not be eaten even if it is my property. The point is that human ownership is limited; second, it is deficient, limited, not covering everything, deficient in not owning every disposal.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah, blessed and exalted, creates what He wills of entities and attributes, in any manner and any form. Look at Allah's creatures: are they one? No, they are not one; they differ greatly in form, in hands, in feet, in food, in everything. Allah creates what He wills.

But know that Allah has guided every creature to what it was created for. Allah says about Moses when Pharaoh asked him: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation; then He guided﴾ [Ta-Ha 50], that is, He gave it what is fitting for it, then guided every creature to what it was created for. Therefore you find that one creature does not eat this kind of grass while another eats it; one creature does not inhabit this kind of land while another inhabits different land, and another creature is the opposite. Sand, for example, is not inhabited by ants, because they do not possess burrows; but it is inhabited by insects or reptiles that burrow into sand, since there are small reptiles that slip into sand as you would see a swimmer sink into water, and they have no burrows. There are things that do not inhabit this kind of land but inhabit hard ground where they can build their burrows. Strange things in Allah's creation, because Allah, Glorified and Exalted, gave everything its creation.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that children are a gift from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from His words ﴿He bestows on whom He wills﴾ and ﴿He bestows﴾, and a gift is a grant without return. So what is the return we owe for these blessings? It is gratitude.

Here is a question: may one name one's son or daughter "Hibat Allah" (the gift of Allah)? Yes, it is permissible. For this reason the jurists, may Allah have mercy on them, said regarding a miscarriage: if the miscarried fetus, after the soul has been breathed into it, is expelled, name it even if it died immediately. If you do not know whether it is male or female, give it a name suitable for both, by saying: this is "Hibat Allah," and name it Hibat Allah.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the perfection of Allah's power, blessed and exalted, in that from this one drop, which is a single kind, He created pure males, pure females, and a third group of mixed males and females, though the water is one. But Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is capable of all things.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that barrenness is considered a deficiency for the one to whom children would be born, from His words ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ after mentioning that children are a gift. So is the barren person one to whom a gift is given, or not? No; this is a deficiency.

From this principle it follows that if a woman's husband is found to be barren, she has the right to annul the marriage. That is, if someone marries a woman without knowing about his own condition, and then it becomes clear that he is barren, she may dissolve the marriage, either by herself, having two witnesses, saying: I have dissolved my marriage to so-and-so, or through the judge, where she and her husband go to the judge and he annuls the marriage. This is her right. If the husband says: I have no defect, I am able to have intercourse, I am sound in body and religion, why do you annul it from me? What do we say? We say: barrenness is a defect, and a woman has a right to children. For this reason it is forbidden for a husband to practise withdrawal (ʿazl) from his wife without her permission, because if he withdraws from her he deprives her of children, unless she permits it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: affirming these two noble names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, namely the All-Knowing (al-ʿAlīm) and the All-Powerful (al-Qadīr).

* Among its benefits also: affirming the attribute indicated by these two names. The All-Knowing (al-ʿAlīm) indicates what?

* Students: Knowledge.

* The Shaykh: And the All-Powerful?

* Students: Power.

* The Shaykh: Power. Every name of Allah includes one or more attributes, but not every attribute gives rise to a name for Allah. Every name of Allah includes what attribute or attributes? One or more. And not every attribute yields a name for Allah, and by this we know that the attributes are more numerous than the names.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: affirming Allah's will, Mighty and Majestic, from His words ﴿He creates what He wills﴾. No one compels Him to create a female or a male; rather, He, Mighty and Majestic, has complete will in His creation.

Know that whenever will is attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it is coupled with wisdom. Pay attention to this point: Allah's will is not bare will but is accompanied by wisdom. The proof is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insan 30]. He concluded with ﴿Knowing and Wise﴾ after saying ﴿And you will not will except that Allah wills﴾. From this we learn that Allah's will follows His knowledge and wisdom, and that He does not will anything with bare will; it must always be coupled with wisdom. This applies to every text in which the will of Allah is mentioned: know that it is coupled with wisdom.

Then, Mighty and Majestic, after mentioning His creation, and that He is the Creator who has absolute will, He mentioned something else: the Law (sharʿ). If you reflect on the Quranic verses, you will find that Allah mentions the Law before the decree (qadar). Read: ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Quran﴾ [al-Rahman 1–2], followed by ﴿created man﴾ [al-Rahman 3]. He began with the Law: ﴿taught the Quran, created man﴾ [al-Rahman 2–3]. ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging clot﴾ [al-ʿAlaq 1–2]. He began with reading. And you will find this pattern consistent, unless there is a reason to place creation before the Law. (...) We ask Allah, Exalted, to have mercy on us and on you with His mercy, and to grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verses 49–50:

I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shura 49]. The sentence is declarative, and its predicate is placed first?

* A student: It indicates restriction (ḥaṣr).

* The Shaykh: Yes, restriction is intended, because the rhetorical rule is that placing before what should be delayed indicates restriction and exclusivity. So it is "to Allah" and not to other than Him. ﴿The dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ means creation and governance. Allah, the Exalted, is the Owner of the heavens and the earth in both creation and governance. For this reason He says: ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, and the words ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, here "mā" (ما) is a relative pronoun, and it is generally used for non-rational beings. The use of "mā" is to include both entities and attributes, since when attributes are intended, "mā" is used even for a rational being. Consider the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. He did not say "man ṭāba" (whoever is good), although women are rational beings, but since a woman is married for her attributes and not for her essence, He said ﴿marry what seems good to you of women﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. Here, ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ [al-Shura 49]: we say that "mā" is used because what is intended is entities and attributes. As for entities, if we were asked: which is more numerous, the rational or the non-rational? On the earth, the non-rational; but in the heavens, no. The heavens are wider than the earth, and there is no place the size of four fingers in them without an angel in it. Taking everything together, the rational beings are more numerous. But considering what is on the earth, which is more numerous?

* A student: The non-rational.

* The Shaykh: The non-rational. Likewise, if we consider attributes, attributes include rational and non-rational beings, so "mā" is used. ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, that is, He brings it into existence after non-existence. But creation is not merely bringing into existence; it is creation according to a measure. ﴿He creates what He wills; He bestows on whom He wills﴾. This too is part of His creation. ﴿He bestows on whom He wills females﴾. Bestowal (hibah) is giving something freely as a gift. Allah, the Exalted, describes children as a gift because human beings have no power to bring them into existence; it is purely a bounty from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿He creates what He wills; He bestows on whom He wills﴾ (of children) ﴿females﴾. How does the phrase "of children" fit with ﴿females﴾? Because "awlād" (children) in the Arabic language includes males and females, as in the words of Allah: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa 11]. ﴿He bestows on whom He wills females and He bestows on whom He wills males﴾. He did not say "dhukūran" (males) but used the definite article "al" (ال), which indicates the nobility of what it precedes, for males are considered more noble than females by people. Yet despite this, He compensated for their deficiency by mentioning them before the males. Or it may be said that Allah mentioned females first because a person's wish is for his children to be male, so mentioning females first is a sign that the matter rests with Allah alone, not with what a person wants and desires.

﴿Or He bestows on them males and females﴾ [al-Shura 49–50]. He said: (i.e., He makes them), but the correct gloss is "yuṣannifuhum" (He classifies them), because marriage here means classification, as Allah says: ﴿and other kinds of a similar sort﴾ [Sad 58], meaning kinds. So the meaning of ﴿yuzawwijuhum﴾ is that He classifies them, making them two kinds: ﴿males and females﴾, ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ (so he neither begets nor is begotten). He does not beget with respect to the female and is not begotten with respect to the male. These are four categories:

First: He bestows females on whom He wills.

Second: He bestows males.

Third: He bestows males and females.

Fourth: He makes a person barren, with neither males nor females.

This is because the matter belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and no one can create any of this. Rather, Allah alone is the Creator.

He says: ﴿And He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent﴾. ﴿Knowing﴾ (of what He creates), ﴿Competent﴾ over what He creates. He knows what He creates, Mighty and Majestic, and is capable of creating whatever He wills.

* In the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion over what is in the heavens and the earth, from His words ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾.

* Among its benefits also: the exclusivity of Allah, blessed and exalted, in this dominion. From where do we derive exclusivity?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Wrong, unless you did not understand the question. The question is: the exclusivity of Allah, the Exalted, in the dominion of the heavens and the earth?

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The reasoning is that Allah placed the predicate first, and the predicate should be delayed, and placing what should be delayed indicates restriction.

If someone says: if you say the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusive to Allah, does a human being not have ownership? Allah says: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa 3]. So humans do have ownership. How can we reconcile our saying that the dominion of the heavens and the earth is exclusive to Allah with affirming ownership for other than Allah?

The answer: Allah's dominion, blessed and exalted, is complete and comprehensive. It encompasses comprehensiveness of disposal and comprehensiveness of place, meaning that Allah's dominion is complete in every respect and general in every respect. Human ownership is deficient, neither in the generality of place nor in the generality of disposal. We all own, but our ownership is limited. I own one bag and do not own another bag belonging to someone else, so it is limited.

* Students: Power.
