And you will find this pattern consistent, unless there is a reason to place creation before the Law. (...) We ask Allah, Exalted, to have mercy on us and on you with His mercy, and to grant us and you success in what He loves and is pleased with.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾ [Ash-Shura 51]. ﴿مَا كَانَ﴾ This form in the Noble Qur'an indicates that the thing is impossible in the extreme, either by divine decree (qadar) or by the Law (shar'): Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam 35]. That is, is it impossible or not impossible?

* The students: Impossible.

* The Shaykh: Impossible in the extreme.

Alright, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [At-Tawbah 113]?

* A student: Impossible (...).

* The Shaykh: Impossible in the extreme. By the Law or by decree?

* The students: By the Law.

* The Shaykh: By the Law; because it is possible for them to ask forgiveness, but it is forbidden for them.

﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him﴾: this is impossible by decree, indeed impossible by decree; that is, according to the report of Allah, mighty and majestic, for otherwise Allah is able to speak in a manner other than this, but according to Allah's report it is impossible.

﴿And it is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾. ﴿لِبَشَرٍ﴾ "Basharun" (human beings) are the sons of Adam. Why were they called bashar? Because their skin (bashara) is exposed unless they cover themselves. Other animals than humans are covered either by feathers, or by wool, or by fur, or by hair: by feathers like birds, by hair like goats, by wool like sheep, by fur like camels.

The human's skin is not covered, and the wisdom in that is that when a person feels his need for physical clothing, he moves from this to his need for spiritual clothing — note the wisdom of Allah, mighty and majestic — so that a person knows that he needs to cover his spiritual nakedness just as he needed to cover his physical nakedness. To this points the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts﴾: ordinary clothing; ﴿and [as] an adornment﴾: the beautiful clothing with which a person adorns himself; then He said: ﴿And the clothing of righteousness — that is best﴾ [Al-A'raf 26]. Is this clothing of righteousness spiritual or physical?

* The students: Spiritual.

* The Shaykh: Spiritual, good. It is also said: the human was called bashar because the effect of what is in his heart appears on his skin; when a person becomes angry, the effect of anger appears on his skin: his face and eyes turn red, his veins swell, and his hair stands up; and when he is given good news that pleases him, his face brightens and you find joy in it. And the apparent meaning — and Allah knows best — is that the first meaning is stronger: he was called bashar because his skin is apparent, unless it is covered.

﴿Except by revelation﴾ — he says: (﴿Except﴾ that He reveals to him ﴿revelation﴾ in a dream or by inspiration). This is one.

﴿Or from behind a veil﴾ [Ash-Shura 51]: that is, He speaks to him directly, other than the revelation placed in the heart, from behind a veil; as happened to whom? To Musa, peace be upon him, and it happened to Muhammad, peace be upon him, on the night of the Ascension, for Allah spoke to him from behind a veil.

So what is the veil with which Allah veils Himself?

The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: «His veil is light; if He were to remove it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches»[[Narrated by Muslim (179 / 293) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. This light is an extremely great light; no one can imagine it. This is the veil with which Allah has veiled Himself from creation, exalted is Allah. If this light, by its strength, veils, then what of the light of Allah, mighty and majestic?! He is greater and greater still. Allah said: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ [An-Nur 35], and no one can conceive of that at all.

Allah speaks to His servants from behind a veil only because if He removed the veil, the human would perish and would not be able to endure before the sight of Allah, mighty and majestic. When Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me that I may look at You﴾, he said this out of longing for Allah, mighty and majestic, not out of doubt. He said that out of longing for Allah, and Allah said to him: ﴿You will not see Me﴾, meaning: it is not possible for you to see Me, ﴿but look at the mountain﴾, the solid, firm mountain, ﴿and if it remains in its place, then you will see Me.﴾ ﴿So when his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain﴾: He manifested, not all of Him appeared; He manifested to the mountain ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾ [Al-A'raf 143]: the mountain was leveled in one instant and made equal to the earth. When Musa, peace be upon him, saw this, he fell unconscious from the terror of what he saw. Does a weak human endure the sight of Allah when the mountain did not endure it? No, by Allah. For this reason Musa was amazed, fell unconscious, and knew that it was impossible to see Allah, mighty and majestic.

His saying: ﴿except by revelation﴾: revelation is what comes to the Messenger by inspiration or by dream vision, because the origin of wahy (revelation) is informing swiftly and secretly; this is its root meaning in the language. So ﴿except by revelation﴾ means: through inspiration or through dream.

﴿Or from behind a veil﴾: that is, Allah speaks to him with a clear speech, but from behind a veil; and the veil mentioned is light, as the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: «His veil is light; if He were to remove it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His sight reaches»[[Narrated by Muslim (179 / 293) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. This is because a human cannot see Allah, mighty and majestic, in this world. Musa said to his Lord, mighty and majestic: ﴿My Lord, show me that I may look at You﴾, saying this out of longing and love. Allah said: ﴿You will not see Me﴾, that is, you will not be able to do that; ﴿but look at the mountain﴾. Musa looked at the mountain, and when Allah manifested to it, ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾: it was leveled until it became equal to the earth. When Musa saw this, he fell down unconscious, that is, he swooned from the terror of what he encountered and his inability to bear it. ﴿And when he regained consciousness he said: "Glory be to You, I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers"﴾ [Al-A'raf 143]. So when Allah wills to speak to any of the Messengers, there must be a veil.

The third category: ﴿Or He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 51]: this is Jibril, who is sent to the one addressed and reveals to that messenger, by Allah's permission, what He wills. We specified him as Jibril because Jibril is entrusted with revelation. The Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, used to begin the night prayer with this opening: «O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they differ; guide me to the truth in what has been disputed, by Your permission, for You guide whom You will to a straight path»[[Narrated by Muslim (770 / 200) from the hadith of A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her.]]. Each of these three is entrusted with what contains life: Jibril with what contains the life of hearts; Israfil with what contains the life of people for resurrection; Mika'il with what contains the life of the earth, by which animals and humans live.

﴿Then reveals by His permission what He wills﴾: ﴿by His permission﴾ means His permission by decree, ﴿what He wills﴾ means: of what Allah has revealed to this messenger whom He sent to the human messenger.

(﴿He is Most High﴾ [Ash-Shura 51] above the attributes of created things): this interpretation is wrong, because it gives the impression that every attribute of the created is not affirmed for the Creator; hearing is not affirmed for the Creator, nor sight, and every attribute of the created is not affirmed for the Creator. For this reason, if the author, may Allah have mercy on him, had said: ﴿He is Most High﴾ above the likeness of created beings and deficient attributes, it would have been easier. Yet we say: He is Most High in His essence and His attributes; His essence is above everything, and His attributes are the highest likeness. This is the correct view. But the author — may Allah pardon us and him — interprets the Qur'an through the Ash'aris, because he is one of them, so he distorts words from their places to agree with his false school. This is a affliction from which few scholars are safe: you find a man who holds some view in creed or in the legal rulings of obligation, then tries to twist the texts that oppose what he adopted, so that he makes the texts follow him, whereas the obligation is that the texts be followed. But this is an affliction that many people have been tested with. We say: ﴿Most High﴾ means in His essence and His attributes, free from every deficiency. As for (above the attributes of created things), this is strange.

The second says: (﴿All-Wise﴾ [Ash-Shura 51] in His creation). This too is deficient; rather He is All-Wise in His creation and All-Wise in His legislation, and wisdom in the Law is more eloquent than wisdom in creation, because creation is a cosmic matter in which a human has no power to change or to deviate; whereas the legal command is the thing in which humans may tamper. So we say to humans: do not tamper with the rulings of Allah, for they proceed from wisdom. Therefore the author's interpretation, which restricted it to the wisdom of decree in Allah's creation, is considered a deficient interpretation. So we say: ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what?

* The students: In His creation and His legislation.

* The Shaykh: In His creation and His legislation.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: the demonstration of the greatness of Allah, mighty and majestic, and that humans cannot speak to Him without an intermediary, either a messenger or a veil; by His saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: affirmation of Allah's speech, mighty and majestic; this has already been discussed, so there is no need to repeat it. We made clear that the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, is speech with letters and an audible voice, and that this is from its perfection, and not as those who claim it is a deficiency allege.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that Allah's revelation is of three kinds: revelation by inspiration; second, speech from behind a veil; third, sending a messenger who reveals to the one addressed what Allah wills.

* And from the benefits of this noble verse: affirmation of Allah's will, mighty and majestic, by His saying: ﴿what He wills﴾, ﴿then reveals by His permission what He wills﴾.

* And from it: affirmation of His elevation in its two aspects: elevation of essence and elevation of attributes; as for elevation of essence, He, glorified and exalted, is above everything; and as for elevation of attributes, all His attributes are lofty, with no deficiency in them in any respect.

* And from its benefits: affirmation of wisdom in His legislation and His creation, and affirmation of the cosmic and legal judgment; because it has passed that the word ﴿All-Wise﴾ means judgment and wisdom.

* * *

Allah divided people with respect to having children into?
* A student: Three categories.

* The Shaykh: Three!

* A student: Four categories.

* The Shaykh: Four categories, what are they?

(...) revelation, or [speaking to him] directly.

* A student: Or directly.

* The Shaykh: Two.

* A student: Or through an angel.

* The Shaykh: Or through an angel; ﴿He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾. These are three categories.

* A student: May Allah be good to you, O Shaykh, does this mean that Allah, glorified and exalted, will grant us on the Day of Resurrection strength in our eyes so that we may look at Him?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. The strength of people on the Day of Resurrection is not comparable to the strength of this world at all. Do they not remain fifty thousand years without eating or drinking?! That cannot be endured in this world. Does one not look at his dominion in Paradise for a distance of two thousand years and see its farthest point as he sees its nearest?! That is not possible for humans in this world.

* A student: May Allah reward you, O Shaykh, what is the meaning of ﴿revealed﴾ (tajalla)?

* The Shaykh: That is: appeared.

* A student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you, a hadith has come about the one in which there is the virtue of raising daughters and patience with (...). Does this virtue also apply to the mother, or is it specific to the father?

* The Shaykh: The apparent meaning is that it applies to everyone. But there is a hadith that it applies to women only: that if a woman loses three of her children, they will be a veil for her from the Fire[[Narrated by Muslim (2633 / 152) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, the men have taken your hadith, so set aside for us a day from yourself when we may come to you and you may teach us from what Allah has taught you." He said: "Gather on such-and-such a day." They gathered, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to them and taught them from what Allah had taught him. Then he said: "None of you women who sends forward three of her children before her will fail to have them as a veil from the Fire." A woman said: "And two, and two, and two." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "And two, and two, and two."]]. As for the matter of upbringing, it is because the father is the one responsible for raising the children.

* The student: (...) by the fathers?

* A student: What is the wisdom in mentioning creation after the Law in the verses?

* The Shaykh: I say: among what indicates that concern for the Law is more eloquent... and people were created only for the Law; people were created only for the Law. Allah said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat 56].

— Where is the questioner? Has Allah spoken to anyone other than Musa?

Yes indeed, He spoke to the Prophet ﷺ, He spoke to Adam. But Musa, peace be upon him, was called Kalim (the one who spoke with Allah) because the first revelation Allah gave him was speech; others received revelation first through an intermediary.

(...) creation first, then the Law began; this is because the Law is specific to the prophets. The Law mentioned here is the revelation specific to the prophets; this is the reason, the reason being that it is specific to the prophets.

* A student: (...) created?

* The Shaykh: No, he does not mean the created light. The created light is separate from Allah and is not an attribute of Allah. This is if we say that (nur, light) means "one who gives light (munawwir)", since some exegetes said: the illuminator of the heavens and the earth. But this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse. So it is said: Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth, and He is not created light; rather He, mighty and majestic, is Light, His speech is light, and His veil is light.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Meaning, in this case: ﴿to whom He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 49] — "whom" is general but intended specifically; is that so? I ask you: when we say ﴿He creates what He wills, bestows upon whom He wills﴾ [Ash-Shura 49], it means the prophets.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, look — may Allah bless you — if anyone claims something contrary to the apparent wording, we do not accept it from him; Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿He bestows upon whom He wills﴾, and did not say: upon the prophets. Then who is it that says the Companions were weary of some of them having sons and some not having sons, some having daughters and some having sons?! Who said this?! The verse is general, and whenever you find a statement that restricts the general, do not accept it without evidence.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, this is wrong. We have mentioned that He manifested; that is, some of Him, mighty and majestic — though I am uneasy about this, the view that what is meant is some of Him, because the basic principle is that it is all of Him. But it may be said that what prevents this is that nothing of His creation encompasses Allah, so He cannot manifest entirely while the earth is nothing in comparison to Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 52–53 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿And thus﴾, i.e., in the same manner as Our revelation to other messengers before you, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾).

﴿Thus﴾ (kadhālika) occurs frequently in the Qur'an. According to the words of the exegete, the kaf is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), so it is the object (maṣdar) of an omitted verb, and the estimate is: "like that." Then the verb is explained by what suits the context; i.e., like Our revelation to those messengers who came before, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, O Muhammad. By his saying "O Muhammad," he informed us that the address here is specific to the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and does not extend beyond him to anyone else.

﴿A spirit﴾ (rūḥan). He said: (It is the Qur'an, by which hearts come to life). Is the meaning of "spirit" here correct?
* Student: The Qur'an, because it is the life of hearts.
* Shaykh: The Qur'an, because hearts come to life through it.

And his saying: (﴿by Our command﴾ [al-Shūrā 52], which We reveal to you) means: from what We command, and it is possible that "amr" here is the singular of "umūr" (affairs), not the singular of "awāmir" (commands); i.e., from Our affair.

(﴿You did not know﴾, i.e., you did not know before the revelation to you, ﴿what the Book is﴾, the Qur'an, ﴿nor faith﴾ [al-Shūrā 52], i.e., its laws and landmarks). Allah revealed to His Prophet a spirit by His command, whether we say it is the singular of "umūr" or of "awāmir," and informed that Allah has the great favour upon him in this; because before this he did not know, i.e., did not have knowledge of or recognise, what the Book is, nor faith.

The phrase ﴿what the Book is﴾ may mean: what writing is, and it may mean what the author mentioned, which is the Qur'an. As for the first, it is because Allah, the Exalted, said of His Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: ﴿And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have had doubt﴾ [al-'Ankabūt 48]. As for it meaning the Qur'an, its examples are many. The point is that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, did not know; even writing, he did not write, peace and blessings be upon him, and he did not know revelation before it was revealed to him.

As for ﴿nor faith﴾, the author said: (i.e., its laws and landmarks), meaning: and you did not know about the laws of faith. Did the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, know what Allah had legislated for him in this perfect law before that? No.

Then the author said: (The negation suspends the verb from acting, and what follows fills the place of the two objects). This sentence concerns grammatical analysis: the verb ﴿you knew (tadrī)﴾ takes two objects. Is there anything after it in the accusative?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. After it comes (mā) as an interrogative, a subject (mubtadaʾ), and (al-kitāb) as its predicate; there is nothing in the accusative in it. When an interrogative clause occupies the position of the two objects, it suspends the verb from acting outwardly, but the clause is in the position of an accusative. So the interrogative here suspended the verb from acting, and what follows fills the place of the two objects.

﴿But We made it a light﴾ ((﴿We made it﴾, i.e., the spirit or the Book)); i.e., We made the Book that We revealed to you, or the spirit that We revealed to you, and the meaning does not differ.

﴿A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ (May Allah guide us by it). ﴿A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾. Light is that by which people are guided, and from it is the poet's saying:
..................... ∗∗∗ as if it were a banner with a fire at its top

And al-Khansāʾ's saying about her brother:
And indeed Ṣakhr, the guided ones take as their leader, ∗∗∗ as if he were a banner with a fire at its top

The meaning is that fire is made a sign for something: when people are in the desert, they kindle a fire at night on the top of a mountain or a hillock so that those who seek them may be guided by it.

He says: ﴿We made it a light, by which We guide whom We will﴾: We guide by this light whom We will, and this is based on the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insān 30]. Who is most deserving of being guided by this light? Whoever holds fast to it and acts upon what is in it, confirming the reports and executing the rulings. Whoever does this, the Qur'an becomes for him a light by which he is guided, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their righteousness﴾ [Muḥammad 17].

As for whoever turns away from it, may Allah protect us, it will be a proof against him and he will not benefit from it.

﴿By which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿of Our servants﴾: is the meant servitude general or specific? ﴿By which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ divides people into two categories: the guided and the astray, so ﴿Our servants﴾ here means general servitude, since He made servitude into these two categories: the guided and the astray.

﴿Of Our servants. And indeed you﴾, i.e., O Muhammad, ﴿are surely guiding to a straight path﴾ [al-Shūrā 52]. He said: (calling by the revelation to you). ﴿To a straight path﴾. If the author had said: ﴿you guide﴾ meaning "you point out," it would have been clearer and more concise; "guide" in the sense of "point out" is the guidance of indication. As for the author's saying "calling by the revelation to you," this is not sufficient, because if he merely called, would people be guided? But if we say "points out," then he has made the path clear and indicated it; then whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, it is only to its detriment.

﴿To a path﴾ (a way) ﴿straight﴾. He says: (the religion of Islam). And he is right: the straight path after the mission of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is the religion of Islam.

﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shūrā 53]. ﴿The path of Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿a straight path﴾.

As for His saying ﴿the path of Allah﴾, Allah, the Exalted, attributed it to Himself because He is the One who established it for His servants, and because it leads to Him. It is attributed to Allah for two reasons:
The first: that He is the One who established it for His servants and legislated it for them. The second: that it leads to Him.

﴿To a straight path﴾, i.e., upright, not crooked.

﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: ﴿to Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate placed first, and ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ is a postponed subject; placing the predicate first conveys restriction, i.e., to Him alone.

(﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in dominion, creation, and servitude). Had the author placed "creation" before "dominion," it would have been better, because creation precedes dominion; but the difference in this is minor. And his saying "servitude" means management: He manages them.

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Shūrā 53]. ﴿Unquestionably﴾ here is an opening particle, and its purpose is alertness and emphasis. And ﴿to Allah﴾ is the object of ﴿are returned﴾, placed before it to convey restriction; i.e., to Allah, not to other than Him, do matters return; i.e., the affairs of creation.

* In this verse: a clarification that this noble Qur'an is a spirit by which hearts come to life. On this basis, if you find your heart dead, or find it sick, or find it hard, then you should turn to the Qur'an, recite it with love and reflection, and the heart will change from sickness to health, from death to life, and from hardness to softness. Ibn 'Abd al-Qawī, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Preserve the study of the Qur'an, for it softens a heart that is hard like a stone.
That is, like pebbles, and this verse indicates it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Qur'an is from the command of Allah, and from this it follows that it is not created. The reasoning is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾ [al-A'rāf 54]. He separated creation from command and made it a counterpart to it, which indicates that command is not of creation, and this is the intended meaning. So this verse is among those used as evidence against the two groups, the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ariyya, who say that the Qur'an is created. The reasoning is that Allah made command a counterpart to creation, and the counterpart of a thing is not part of it. Is the part of a thing from it or not from it?
* Students: Not from it.
* Other students: From it.
* Shaykh: From it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the magnification by the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, of Himself; from His saying ﴿We revealed﴾ and His saying ﴿by Our command﴾. He is worthy of magnification, Mighty and Majestic, worthy of honour, and worthy of praise.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ, before this revelation, did not know what the Book is nor faith, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā 7]. ﴿Lost﴾ means ignorant, ﴿and guided﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a clarification of Allah's favour upon His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, by sending down the Qur'an, through which he became knowledgeable of the Book and knowledgeable of faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was unlettered, neither reading nor writing; this contains a refutation of the claim that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was a liar, since he could not have brought this Qur'an from himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, made the Book a light by which He guides whom He wills. From this benefit it follows that if you want your heart to be illumined and to come to life, then what should you do? By the Qur'an, but reciting with reflection.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that guidance and misguidance are by the will of Allah; from His saying ﴿by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, guides to the straight path; from His saying ﴿And indeed you are surely guiding to a straight path﴾.

If someone says: What is the reconciliation between this verse and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 56]?

The answer: the guidance in the second verse is the guidance of success (tawfīq), for the Prophet ﷺ cannot guide anyone; but the guidance in the verse here is the guidance of indication. Read His saying: ﴿And as for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 17]. "We guided them" — what kind?
* Student: Indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance of indication; i.e., We made the truth clear to them and pointed them to it, but they, may Allah protect us, preferred blindness over guidance, so they were not guided.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ is a straight guidance with no crookedness in it; from His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾. There is no crookedness in his reports, and crookedness in reports is falsehood; and there is no crookedness in the laws, rather all of them are built on justice and grace, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that whatever opposes the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is not a straight path; it is taken from the implication of His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾, i.e., whatever is other than what you are upon is not a straight path.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the exaltation of the affair of the religion of Allah to which the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, calls; from His saying ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

If someone says: How do we reconcile this verse with His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fātiḥa 6–7], while here He says ﴿the path of Allah﴾?

The answer: it is attributed to Allah in one respect, and attributed to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour in another respect. Its attribution to Allah is in respect of what? 
* Students: That He established it.
* Shaykh: That He established it, and that it leads to Him. Its attribution to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour is in respect of their being its travellers, the believers in it. O Allah, make us among them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion and its being exclusively His; the generality is from His saying ﴿whatever﴾, as "mā" is a relative pronoun indicating generality, and its exclusivity to Him is from placing the predicate before the subject.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that Allah, Exalted, judges as He wills, and that there is no objection to His ruling; from His saying ﴿to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. He brought the generality of dominion after mention of the straight path, indicating that what He, Blessed and Exalted, rules, there is no objection to it. Why? Because Allah has dominion over the heavens and the earth; He creates what He wills and legislates what He wills. Therefore you will find some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, when they do not discover the reason for a ruling, say: "This is ta'abbudī," meaning we must worship by it even if we do not know the wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a clarification that all matters return to Allah, i.e., they go back to Him, in creation, dominion, management, and judgment; everything returns to Allah. If we differ about a ruling in a question of knowledge, to whom do we return? To Allah. When the Day of Resurrection comes, creatures will be raised and return to Allah. So ﴿all matters are returned﴾ means all matters return to Allah, go back to Him; He is the origin from which they came and the end to which they lead, Blessed and Exalted.

* * *

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, the Sunnah has reported mention of some types of revelation; is that included in these categories or not...?
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: Like... he said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and sometimes the angel comes to me in the form of a man."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (3215) and Muslim (2333/87), the wording of the latter, from 'Ā'isha, that al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām asked the Prophet ﷺ: How does revelation come to you? He said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the sound of a bell, and this is the hardest on me; then it departs from me and I have retained what it said. And sometimes an angel comes to me in the form of a man, and I understand what he says."]]
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, whether it is a man or he sends a messenger.
* Student: And the first, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The first is by revelation; inspiration.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: I say: according to his activity. But the scholars said: one should set a specific portion (ḥizb) to recite each day, organising one's recitation, because if a person leaves it open like this, days pass and he has achieved nothing. Although this is not customary among the predecessors, unless a hadith indicated it, I think, from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Amr, that he "said: I can recite it in a month, in a week, in three days. He said: 'Do not recite it in less than three days.'"[[Reported by Abu Dawud (1390) with his chain from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Amr that he said: O Messenger of Allah, in how long should I recite the Qur'an? He said: "In a month." He said: I am stronger than that. Abu Musa repeats the words and reduces them until he said: "Recite it in seven." He said: I am stronger than that. He said: "One who recites it in less than three does not understand it."]]
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, he is not blamed. Praise be to Allah, a person recites the Qur'an every day in what?
* Students: The prayer.
* Shaykh: In the prayer. So there is no abandonment of the Qur'an.
* Student: (...) benefiting (...) the commentary of al-Nawawi (...)?
* Shaykh: No, this is a mistake on their part. How can we forgo benefiting from these great books, when the errors in them do not represent even a tenth of a tenth of a tenth? Ibn Rajab, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book al-Qawā'id al-fiqhiyya: "Allah refuses infallibility for any book other than His Book, and the fair-minded is one who overlooks a person's few errors amid his many correct statements." This is correct; this is fairness. And you hardly find any composition without error, whether intentional or unintentional: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisā' 82].

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Is everyone whom Allah, blessed and exalted, speaks to (...) a prophet?

* The Shaykh: Yes. If Allah speaks to someone with a law (shar'), he is a prophet. If He speaks to him in other than that way, he may be a devil (shaytan). Did Allah not address Iblis, saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad 75].

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: The best I know is the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him. It is trustworthy in matters of 'aqidah (creed), though it has some shortcomings: it mentions Israelite narrations (isra'iliyyat), and discusses many of them. The tafsir of Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di is good, especially in drawing out benefits (istinbat) from the verses. Yes, that is what I know now. The tafsir of Shaykh al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, is good, but it is only suitable for a student of knowledge who has firm command of the subject.

* The student: May Allah reward you well. It is said that Imam al-Shafi'i used to complete the Qur'an twice a day in Ramadan. Does this count as contrary to the Sunnah?

* The Shaykh: No, because this is an incidental matter (amr 'arid), and it does not contradict the Sunnah. Incidental matters are not treated the same as permanent ones.

* Student: When some innovators argue against us, they say: "You have now interpreted the Spirit (al-ruh) as the Qur'an. Why not say that the Spirit is a spirit from Allah, exalted is He?"

* The Shaykh: What do you mean: "a spirit from Allah"?

* The student: A spirit from the Spirit of Allah.

* The Shaykh: What did Allah reveal to the Messenger?

* The student: The Qur'an.

* The Shaykh: Very well, how are we interpreting it? We have not interpreted anything. This is what was revealed to the Messenger, and Allah named it a spirit (ruh) because hearts come alive through it.

Know that we do not deny ta'wil (interpretation). We may interpret, but when evidence points to an interpretation, there is no harm. For example, regarding His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 98], we say: "When you intend to recite." The apparent meaning of the verse is: "When you have finished reciting, seek refuge." The Sunnah has clarified this. So we do not deny ta'wil, because an interpretation that the wording indicates is tafsir (explanation). What we deny is ta'wil in the sense of tahrif (distortion).

* The student: Without evidence.

* The Shaykh: Yes, without evidence.

* The student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, he is not a messenger, any messenger.

As for the explanation of inspiration (ilham): either Allah casts it into his heart, like the words of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: «Indeed, it has been revealed to my heart (ulqiya fi rui) that no soul will die until it has completed its provision and its term»[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (8/166, no. 7694) from the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart (nafatha ruh al-qudus fi ruʿi) that no soul will leave this world until it completes its term and receives its full provision, so seek a good manner in pursuit (of provision)."]].

With this, the tafsir of Surah al-Shura is complete, and, Allah willing, the next session will be on Surah al-Zukhruf. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to end our lives and yours in happiness, to grant us understanding of His Book in the manner that pleases Him, and to make us among those who recite it with its due recitation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 42, verse 52–53 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿And thus﴾, i.e., in the same manner as Our revelation to other messengers before you, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾).

﴿Thus﴾ (kadhālika) occurs frequently in the Qur'an. According to the words of the exegete, the kaf is a noun meaning "like" (mithl), so it is the object (maṣdar) of an omitted verb, and the estimate is: "like that." Then the verb is explained by what suits the context; i.e., like Our revelation to those messengers who came before, ﴿We have revealed to you﴾, O Muhammad. By his saying "O Muhammad," he informed us that the address here is specific to the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and does not extend beyond him to anyone else.

﴿A spirit﴾ (rūḥan). He said: (It is the Qur'an, by which hearts come to life). Is the meaning of "spirit" here correct?
* Student: The Qur'an, because it is the life of hearts.
* Shaykh: The Qur'an, because hearts come to life through it.

And his saying: (﴿by Our command﴾ [al-Shūrā 52], which We reveal to you) means: from what We command, and it is possible that "amr" here is the singular of "umūr" (affairs), not the singular of "awāmir" (commands); i.e., from Our affair.

(﴿You did not know﴾, i.e., you did not know before the revelation to you, ﴿what the Book is﴾, the Qur'an, ﴿nor faith﴾ [al-Shūrā 52], i.e., its laws and landmarks). Allah revealed to His Prophet a spirit by His command, whether we say it is the singular of "umūr" or of "awāmir," and informed that Allah has the great favour upon him in this; because before this he did not know, i.e., did not have knowledge of or recognise, what the Book is, nor faith.

The phrase ﴿what the Book is﴾ may mean: what writing is, and it may mean what the author mentioned, which is the Qur'an. As for the first, it is because Allah, the Exalted, said of His Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family: ﴿And you did not recite before it any scripture, nor did you write it with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have had doubt﴾ [al-'Ankabūt 48]. As for it meaning the Qur'an, its examples are many. The point is that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, did not know; even writing, he did not write, peace and blessings be upon him, and he did not know revelation before it was revealed to him.

As for ﴿nor faith﴾, the author said: (i.e., its laws and landmarks), meaning: and you did not know about the laws of faith. Did the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, know what Allah had legislated for him in this perfect law before that? No.

Then the author said: (The negation suspends the verb from acting, and what follows fills the place of the two objects). This sentence concerns grammatical analysis: the verb ﴿you knew (tadrī)﴾ takes two objects. Is there anything after it in the accusative?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: No. After it comes (mā) as an interrogative, a subject (mubtadaʾ), and (al-kitāb) as its predicate; there is nothing in the accusative in it. When an interrogative clause occupies the position of the two objects, it suspends the verb from acting outwardly, but the clause is in the position of an accusative. So the interrogative here suspended the verb from acting, and what follows fills the place of the two objects.

﴿But We made it a light﴾ ((﴿We made it﴾, i.e., the spirit or the Book)); i.e., We made the Book that We revealed to you, or the spirit that We revealed to you, and the meaning does not differ.

﴿A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ (May Allah guide us by it). ﴿A light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾. Light is that by which people are guided, and from it is the poet's saying:
..................... ∗∗∗ as if it were a banner with a fire at its top

And al-Khansāʾ's saying about her brother:
And indeed Ṣakhr, the guided ones take as their leader, ∗∗∗ as if he were a banner with a fire at its top

The meaning is that fire is made a sign for something: when people are in the desert, they kindle a fire at night on the top of a mountain or a hillock so that those who seek them may be guided by it.

He says: ﴿We made it a light, by which We guide whom We will﴾: We guide by this light whom We will, and this is based on the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Insān 30]. Who is most deserving of being guided by this light? Whoever holds fast to it and acts upon what is in it, confirming the reports and executing the rulings. Whoever does this, the Qur'an becomes for him a light by which he is guided, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their righteousness﴾ [Muḥammad 17].

As for whoever turns away from it, may Allah protect us, it will be a proof against him and he will not benefit from it.

﴿By which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾. Regarding His saying ﴿of Our servants﴾: is the meant servitude general or specific? ﴿By which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾ divides people into two categories: the guided and the astray, so ﴿Our servants﴾ here means general servitude, since He made servitude into these two categories: the guided and the astray.

﴿Of Our servants. And indeed you﴾, i.e., O Muhammad, ﴿are surely guiding to a straight path﴾ [al-Shūrā 52]. He said: (calling by the revelation to you). ﴿To a straight path﴾. If the author had said: ﴿you guide﴾ meaning "you point out," it would have been clearer and more concise; "guide" in the sense of "point out" is the guidance of indication. As for the author's saying "calling by the revelation to you," this is not sufficient, because if he merely called, would people be guided? But if we say "points out," then he has made the path clear and indicated it; then whoever is guided, it is for his own self, and whoever goes astray, it is only to its detriment.

﴿To a path﴾ (a way) ﴿straight﴾. He says: (the religion of Islam). And he is right: the straight path after the mission of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is the religion of Islam.

﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shūrā 53]. ﴿The path of Allah﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿a straight path﴾.

As for His saying ﴿the path of Allah﴾, Allah, the Exalted, attributed it to Himself because He is the One who established it for His servants, and because it leads to Him. It is attributed to Allah for two reasons:
The first: that He is the One who established it for His servants and legislated it for them. The second: that it leads to Him.

﴿To a straight path﴾, i.e., upright, not crooked.

﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: ﴿to Him﴾ is a prepositional phrase functioning as a predicate placed first, and ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ is a postponed subject; placing the predicate first conveys restriction, i.e., to Him alone.

(﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in dominion, creation, and servitude). Had the author placed "creation" before "dominion," it would have been better, because creation precedes dominion; but the difference in this is minor. And his saying "servitude" means management: He manages them.

﴿Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Shūrā 53]. ﴿Unquestionably﴾ here is an opening particle, and its purpose is alertness and emphasis. And ﴿to Allah﴾ is the object of ﴿are returned﴾, placed before it to convey restriction; i.e., to Allah, not to other than Him, do matters return; i.e., the affairs of creation.

* In this verse: a clarification that this noble Qur'an is a spirit by which hearts come to life. On this basis, if you find your heart dead, or find it sick, or find it hard, then you should turn to the Qur'an, recite it with love and reflection, and the heart will change from sickness to health, from death to life, and from hardness to softness. Ibn 'Abd al-Qawī, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Preserve the study of the Qur'an, for it softens a heart that is hard like a stone.
That is, like pebbles, and this verse indicates it.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the Qur'an is from the command of Allah, and from this it follows that it is not created. The reasoning is the saying of Allah, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾ [al-A'rāf 54]. He separated creation from command and made it a counterpart to it, which indicates that command is not of creation, and this is the intended meaning. So this verse is among those used as evidence against the two groups, the Mu'tazila and the Ash'ariyya, who say that the Qur'an is created. The reasoning is that Allah made command a counterpart to creation, and the counterpart of a thing is not part of it. Is the part of a thing from it or not from it?
* Students: Not from it.
* Other students: From it.
* Shaykh: From it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the magnification by the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, of Himself; from His saying ﴿We revealed﴾ and His saying ﴿by Our command﴾. He is worthy of magnification, Mighty and Majestic, worthy of honour, and worthy of praise.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet ﷺ, before this revelation, did not know what the Book is nor faith, and this is indicated by His saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā 7]. ﴿Lost﴾ means ignorant, ﴿and guided﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a clarification of Allah's favour upon His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, by sending down the Qur'an, through which he became knowledgeable of the Book and knowledgeable of faith.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was unlettered, neither reading nor writing; this contains a refutation of the claim that he, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was a liar, since he could not have brought this Qur'an from himself.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, made the Book a light by which He guides whom He wills. From this benefit it follows that if you want your heart to be illumined and to come to life, then what should you do? By the Qur'an, but reciting with reflection.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation that guidance and misguidance are by the will of Allah; from His saying ﴿by which We guide whom We will of Our servants﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, guides to the straight path; from His saying ﴿And indeed you are surely guiding to a straight path﴾.

If someone says: What is the reconciliation between this verse and His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 56]?

The answer: the guidance in the second verse is the guidance of success (tawfīq), for the Prophet ﷺ cannot guide anyone; but the guidance in the verse here is the guidance of indication. Read His saying: ﴿And as for Thamūd, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 17]. "We guided them" — what kind?
* Student: Indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance of indication; i.e., We made the truth clear to them and pointed them to it, but they, may Allah protect us, preferred blindness over guidance, so they were not guided.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ is a straight guidance with no crookedness in it; from His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾. There is no crookedness in his reports, and crookedness in reports is falsehood; and there is no crookedness in the laws, rather all of them are built on justice and grace, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that whatever opposes the guidance of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is not a straight path; it is taken from the implication of His saying ﴿to a straight path﴾, i.e., whatever is other than what you are upon is not a straight path.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the exaltation of the affair of the religion of Allah to which the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, calls; from His saying ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

If someone says: How do we reconcile this verse with His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fātiḥa 6–7], while here He says ﴿the path of Allah﴾?

The answer: it is attributed to Allah in one respect, and attributed to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour in another respect. Its attribution to Allah is in respect of what? 
* Students: That He established it.
* Shaykh: That He established it, and that it leads to Him. Its attribution to those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour is in respect of their being its travellers, the believers in it. O Allah, make us among them.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the generality of Allah's dominion and its being exclusively His; the generality is from His saying ﴿whatever﴾, as "mā" is a relative pronoun indicating generality, and its exclusivity to Him is from placing the predicate before the subject.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that Allah, Exalted, judges as He wills, and that there is no objection to His ruling; from His saying ﴿to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. He brought the generality of dominion after mention of the straight path, indicating that what He, Blessed and Exalted, rules, there is no objection to it. Why? Because Allah has dominion over the heavens and the earth; He creates what He wills and legislates what He wills. Therefore you will find some scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, when they do not discover the reason for a ruling, say: "This is ta'abbudī," meaning we must worship by it even if we do not know the wisdom.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: a clarification that all matters return to Allah, i.e., they go back to Him, in creation, dominion, management, and judgment; everything returns to Allah. If we differ about a ruling in a question of knowledge, to whom do we return? To Allah. When the Day of Resurrection comes, creatures will be raised and return to Allah. So ﴿all matters are returned﴾ means all matters return to Allah, go back to Him; He is the origin from which they came and the end to which they lead, Blessed and Exalted.

* * *

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, the Sunnah has reported mention of some types of revelation; is that included in these categories or not...?
* Shaykh: Like what?
* Student: Like... he said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and sometimes the angel comes to me in the form of a man."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (3215) and Muslim (2333/87), the wording of the latter, from 'Ā'isha, that al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām asked the Prophet ﷺ: How does revelation come to you? He said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the sound of a bell, and this is the hardest on me; then it departs from me and I have retained what it said. And sometimes an angel comes to me in the form of a man, and I understand what he says."]]
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, whether it is a man or he sends a messenger.
* Student: And the first, O Shaykh?
* Shaykh: The first is by revelation; inspiration.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: I say: according to his activity. But the scholars said: one should set a specific portion (ḥizb) to recite each day, organising one's recitation, because if a person leaves it open like this, days pass and he has achieved nothing. Although this is not customary among the predecessors, unless a hadith indicated it, I think, from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Amr, that he "said: I can recite it in a month, in a week, in three days. He said: 'Do not recite it in less than three days.'"[[Reported by Abu Dawud (1390) with his chain from 'Abdullāh ibn 'Amr that he said: O Messenger of Allah, in how long should I recite the Qur'an? He said: "In a month." He said: I am stronger than that. Abu Musa repeats the words and reduces them until he said: "Recite it in seven." He said: I am stronger than that. He said: "One who recites it in less than three does not understand it."]]
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, he is not blamed. Praise be to Allah, a person recites the Qur'an every day in what?
* Students: The prayer.
* Shaykh: In the prayer. So there is no abandonment of the Qur'an.
* Student: (...) benefiting (...) the commentary of al-Nawawi (...)?
* Shaykh: No, this is a mistake on their part. How can we forgo benefiting from these great books, when the errors in them do not represent even a tenth of a tenth of a tenth? Ibn Rajab, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book al-Qawā'id al-fiqhiyya: "Allah refuses infallibility for any book other than His Book, and the fair-minded is one who overlooks a person's few errors amid his many correct statements." This is correct; this is fairness. And you hardly find any composition without error, whether intentional or unintentional: ﴿And if it had been from other than Allah, they would have found within it much contradiction﴾ [al-Nisā' 82].

* Student: Shaykh, may Allah bless you. Is everyone whom Allah, blessed and exalted, speaks to (...) a prophet?

* The Shaykh: Yes. If Allah speaks to someone with a law (shar'), he is a prophet. If He speaks to him in other than that way, he may be a devil (shaytan). Did Allah not address Iblis, saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad 75].

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: The best I know is the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him. It is trustworthy in matters of 'aqidah (creed), though it has some shortcomings: it mentions Israelite narrations (isra'iliyyat), and discusses many of them. The tafsir of Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di is good, especially in drawing out benefits (istinbat) from the verses. Yes, that is what I know now. The tafsir of Shaykh al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, is good, but it is only suitable for a student of knowledge who has firm command of the subject.

* The student: May Allah reward you well. It is said that Imam al-Shafi'i used to complete the Qur'an twice a day in Ramadan. Does this count as contrary to the Sunnah?

* The Shaykh: No, because this is an incidental matter (amr 'arid), and it does not contradict the Sunnah. Incidental matters are not treated the same as permanent ones.

* Student: When some innovators argue against us, they say: "You have now interpreted the Spirit (al-ruh) as the Qur'an. Why not say that the Spirit is a spirit from Allah, exalted is He?"

* The Shaykh: What do you mean: "a spirit from Allah"?

* The student: A spirit from the Spirit of Allah.

* The Shaykh: What did Allah reveal to the Messenger?

* The student: The Qur'an.

* The Shaykh: Very well, how are we interpreting it? We have not interpreted anything. This is what was revealed to the Messenger, and Allah named it a spirit (ruh) because hearts come alive through it.

Know that we do not deny ta'wil (interpretation). We may interpret, but when evidence points to an interpretation, there is no harm. For example, regarding His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 98], we say: "When you intend to recite." The apparent meaning of the verse is: "When you have finished reciting, seek refuge." The Sunnah has clarified this. So we do not deny ta'wil, because an interpretation that the wording indicates is tafsir (explanation). What we deny is ta'wil in the sense of tahrif (distortion).

* The student: Without evidence.

* The Shaykh: Yes, without evidence.

* The student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: No, he is not a messenger, any messenger.

As for the explanation of inspiration (ilham): either Allah casts it into his heart, like the words of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: «Indeed, it has been revealed to my heart (ulqiya fi rui) that no soul will die until it has completed its provision and its term»[[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (8/166, no. 7694) from the hadith of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart (nafatha ruh al-qudus fi ruʿi) that no soul will leave this world until it completes its term and receives its full provision, so seek a good manner in pursuit (of provision)."]].

With this, the tafsir of Surah al-Shura is complete, and, Allah willing, the next session will be on Surah al-Zukhruf. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to end our lives and yours in happiness, to grant us understanding of His Book in the manner that pleases Him, and to make us among those who recite it with its due recitation.
